CHESTER R. MACPHEE

Grand Master October 17, 1969-0ctob er 16, 1970
A review of the chronicle of his activities as Grand Master is a
reminder of the expression, "If you want a job done get a busy man
to do it," which was never more clearly illustrated than by the leadership
of Brother "Chet." It was a natural course of events that a man with
such an energetic, humble, imaginative and effective attitude should
become the executive officer of our Fraternity. Yet, while he made the
final decisions affecting the forward progress of the Fraternity, his
actions always reflected the results of discussions which elicited the
considered and collective judgment of his senior officers, as well as his
own estimate of the "grass roots" attitudes. The expression s-"What
do you think?" "Tell me about," "Let's see if we can't do this better,"
"Let's get some results on this," or "Let's extend kindness and consideration to others for it is only by personally forgiving that we are forgiven"
-were familiar to all with whom he came in contact. From Scotch
ancestry, which has been clearly traced to the early 1700s, he was born
into this active life in San Francisco on June 5, 1905. He attended public
schools in San Francisco and because of his father's illness worked
evenings while attending high school.

It is difficult to distinguish the major areas of his greatest concern
for he is a man of wfde and varied interests. His civic mindedness, his
love of family, his interest in youth, in the Masonic Fraternity, and
matters of broad spiritual development are evident in every contact
with him.
In 1924 he became a licensed real estate broker. His business interests and his natural concern for the welfare of people around him
led him into areas of leadership in civic activities in San Francisco. He
was elected and served for twelve years as a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. During the time he was Governor of California, Past Grand Master Earl Warren appointed him a member of
the California Real Estate Commission where he served for eight years.
He is currently a Director and Treasurer of the San Francisco Rotary
Club and has served as a director and held membership in many of the
prominent civic and social clubs, councils and foundations in San Francisco.

Grand Master
October 17, 1969 - October 16, 1970

In 1953 President Eisenhower appointed him Collector of Customs
for Northern California, Nevada and Utah, in which capacity he served
with distinction until 1958. Since then he has devoted his professional
interest to discharging the responsibilities as President of the Sandy
Estate Corporation . His managemen t of widespread and large interests

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

is indicative of the confidence which is placed in his good judgment and
breadth of knowledge.
On February 2, 1927, he married Marjorie Otton, his sweethear t of
DeMolay days. As the result of this mru:riage he is the proud father of
two daughters and one son, and now has eleven grandchildren. It has
been noted that in this Brother's busy life nothing comes between him
and the relationship with his family which is most important to him.
His interest in youth and the activities of iyoung people always has
demanded his attention. The encouragement which he has given to
Job's Daughters , Rainbow for Girls and DeMolay for many years
became most evident during his year as Grand Master of Masons. He
is a Director of the Red Shield Youth Center, Treasurer of the San
Francisco Boys Club and founder and Chairman of the San Francisco
Youth Association which later became the "Guardsm en." He has been
active as a Director of the Y.M.C.A. , a member of the San P.rancisco
Coordinat ing Council for Youth Welfare and in many other similar
organizations.
He became a Mason in 1940 and is a Past Master of Golden West
Lodge No. 455. His vital interest in fraternal affairs caused his appointment to numerous Grand Lodge committees and trusteeships. In 1967
he was elected to the office of Senior Grand Warden of this Grand
Lodge and served as its Grand Master during the term 1969-1970. The
basic thrust of his leadership was a challenge to each member to become
Masonica lly informed through education and to live responsible Masonic
lives. He has been and continues active in both York and Scottish Rites
and, by election of the Supreme Council of the Thirty-thi rd Degree, has
been coroneted a 33° Mason. On the ·retirement of Very Worshipf ul
Paul A. Pflueger as Grand Treasurer , Most Worshipf ul Chester R.
MacPhee was elected to serve this Grand Lodge as its Grand Treasurer .
This is truly an indication of the respect the Fraternity holds for his
ability.
Of special personal interest to Brother MacPhee is a "Thursda y
Morning Bible Class" of which he has been the leader for more than
twenty-se ven years. In his search for truth, a small group of f.riends.
who met originally to discuss the principles of the Bible, has grown to
a group consisting of more than 100 men of all faiths. The group is
favorably known throughou t San Francisco and California.
In the Book of Laws it is written, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God
with all thine heart and with all thine soul ..." Chet's total efforts have
been directed toward fulfilling this commandment. He has truly "set a
plumbline in the midst of" his people.

Invocation -Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
May I. at this time, declare how truly appreciative I am for the great
honor bestowed upon me by our Grand Master, Chester MacPhee, in appointing me to the office of Grand Chaplain. My walk with him and the
other Grand Lodge Officers has been an inspiration and I shall be
eternally grateful.
During the past year, the boundless energy, warmth, and love of
our Grand Master, and his personal reflection of true Masonry in Action,
has been a challenge to me, not only as a Master Mason, but as a minister. Also, he has not only been a teacher of Masonic philosophy and
practice, but he has taught all officers of the Grand Lodge the expertise
of cornerstone laying. In sun, wind, and rain, those cornerstones have

6

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

been laid perfectly with the square, the level. and the plumb line. In each
instance when I presented the prayer found in our cornerstone ceremonial. I was privately asked to pray for good weather, good attendance, and
for the brevity of the speakers. When the weather was not good, and
when the lecture of our Grand Orator was lengthy, my ability to pray
was definitely questioned.
In fact, many of our Grand Lodge officers had quite an experience
on Friday, October 2nd, when, with our Deputy Grand Master, we assisted him in laying the cornerstone at the Franklin Elementary School
in Redlands. Our Deputy Grand Master was eloquent and really
reached the hearts and minds of the children before us. He explained the
symbolog'Y of the cornerstone laying, explaining the difference between
the early days when Masons participated with George Washington,
Benjamin F1'anklin, in the laying of the cornerstones of our most historic
monuments. He stated that we did not have the cannon and the firecrackers they had in those days.
Within moments after those remarks there was lightning, tremendous
thunder claps, and rain fell. Again, many of the officers looked over at
the Grand Chaplain. Needless to say, my eyes were closed in prayer. To
me, it seemed a fitting climax for my last participation in cornerstone laying-on which I am now an authority-and a fitting introduction to the
year ahead.
As a small boy I remember sitting on the floor beside moy grandfather
and admiring the Past Master's Jewel that hung from the heavy gold
chain on his vest. Many times he would permit me to open the Jewel,
which revealed within the tools of the Master Mason. I remember well
the occasion when he said, "Some day, I pray you will become
a Mason, but, remember, you will have to prove yourself worthy before
you ask."
In later years, on many occasions, I wanted to ask for a petition of
membership, but my grandfather's words were indelibly imprinted on my
mind-first, I must be worthy.
M·y grandfather, my father, were not simply card-carrying Masons.
They were practicing Masons. They were not joiners: they participated.
Their word was their bond. Their faith in God was undeniable. Their
love of the home, their fidelity was constantly exemplified, and their love
of country and service to the community was inspiring to all. I thank
God for such a heritage.
·
Today, we are aware of a changing world. The material. the mechanistic changes are almost beyond belief. Social changes cause great consternation, and it is so easy for us to become indoctrinated in negation.
In fact, last week I had this devotional service well along in preparation, but after reading it over I found that I, too, had participated in stating only what is wrong instead of affirming what is right.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

The desires of our youth are far different than when we were teenagers. With my own son I had to declare only certain hours of the day
were proper for him to play the stereo. As you know, it has to be loud,
loud. and louder. Their way of dancing is certainly quite different from
our way. They don't hold each other in their arms anymore. In fad, after
observing them, it seems they hardly notice each other as they go through
their various gyrations.
This reminds me of the story of the two puppies who were watching
a group of teen-agers dancing-and they were really "turned on."
Finally. one puppy turned to the other and said, "If we did that, they'd
worm us."
Let us look on the positive side. There are dissidents among the
youth, but the majority of them are tremendous. Our youth are wonderful. and today they are demanding that we be forthright, honest, sincere.
There is a deep search by many for a spiritual experience, for a way of
life that contains real love, sincerity, and a feeling of belonging. They
have found it difficult to understand our spiritual relationships within
the church or synagogue. Many feel we wear one mask on our sabbath,
another mask at home, another mask in business, and many masks in
our social activities.
They are demanding realism-the realism of a father's love, a
mother's love, a family love. It is difficult for the young child, whose
mind is like a sponge, to quite understand the changes in their parents
which take place before their eyes at cocktail time when the mother or
father says. "What a day I've had. Pour me another double," or, when
they hear, "Get me a sleeping pill," or another pill to wake up, or a tranquilizer when nervous.
I point this out to us gathered here at Grand Lodge only for the purpose of Te-dedicating and re-consecrating ourselves to our obligations
that afforded us the opportunity of becoming Master Masons.
This morning, on the opening of Grand Lodge, I prayed that each
of us, including myself, would awaken to the truth that we, as Master
Masons, are a sufficient number of men for these times. But, a great
awakening is needed.
For instance, on my various lodge visitations, I have asked a Brother,
"What would your reply be if someone asked you, what is Masonry?"
One answer which came from a Junior Warden was, "That's simple.
We're a secret fraternal order." Another Brother answered, "It's a religion." May I ask you, what is your definition 1
To me, a Master Mason is one who, through qualification, enters
our Brotherhood as a man who believes in God, a man whose word is
his bond without question, a man devoted to his family. faithful to his
wife, and one who is a listener with his children, and truly an example
for them to follow. A Master Mason, to me, is one who loves his coun-

8

9

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

try and is will to stand up and be counted on behalf of its Constitution,
its Bill of Rights, but, even more, one who is willing to exemplify a government of the people, by the people, and for the people, not only in the
voting booth, but in the various community organizations that need his
help. Surely. a Master Mason is one who practices brotherly love, not
only to his Brothers, but to all whom he meets, regardless of their religion, their color, their philosophy. A Master Mason is a constant
builder of his own character and is one who readily examines the quality
of his thoughts, his ideals, his goals. A Master Mason is one who does
not judge by appearance, nor does he condemn easily, but seeks only to
exemplify the Truth. May I say that each one of these statements is a
never-ending mountain to climb, for no limit has been found for faith,
charity, love, and dedication. This demands constant analysis and examination. In my own life, daily. I am seeking to become a better Master
Mason.

us. and at this very moment, won't you, within the confines of your own
heart, pledge to do just this?

Have you ever stood before your mirror and looked at yourself as
you really are? Something responds, doesn't it? Have you ever asked
yourself, looking right into your own eyes, am I really honest with life?
Am I a forgiving person? Am I a happy person? Do I really believe in
Divine Providence? Am I grateful for my blessings?
As iyou ask these questions, a new i"eality is born that tells you of
work to do.
We take so many things for granted without ever giving thanks.
Sometimes that includes our families, our work, and especially our youth.
May I say one word here about the DeMolays, Job's Daughters,
and the Rainbow Girls? During the past year five visitations have been
made by these groups to the church where I am pastor. They were wonderfull I remember, on the occasion of the DeMolay annual "Go-tochurch" night, two boys spoke to me and both stated, "I sure wish my
parents had been here." I asked them if their fathers were Master Masons. One replied, "Yes." The other said, "Yes, in a way." Speaking
to others in the group. they remarked, "We know we can get financial
help. but we want Masons to attend our meetings who care." "Who
care," is quite a message, isn't it?
In speaking with Jobies, they did not complain, but one said, "The
only time we are really applauded is when we serve dinners."
Just think of the hundreds of thousands of Masons who could, this
day, dedicate themselves to help the youth. A Master Mason can attend
every DeMolay meeting. A Master Mason and his wife can attend every
meeting of Job's Daughters and Rainbow Girls. If the Masons of California would attend just one of their meetings each month, to greet them,
speak to them, listen to them, love them, we would find their organizations on the up-surge in a way beyond our comprehension. They need

How can I say all of us here this morning should be optimistic, that
many of the consternations we are facing will dissolve themselves? Because, I believe in God. I believe God re-enacts his nature through man,
and when man awakens to his true significance and has a reverence for
the spirit of God within him, changes for the better must take place.
We must attune ourselves to cosmic patterns which have been created
by the Supreme Architect of the Universe. I did not build mountains, nor
did I create my own heart. I could not change the Universal Idea
of hearts because thousands of hearts are being born in the world today.
Everything in this universe----every bird that flies, every fish in the sea,
every person-belongs to this one Universal Pattern of Life.
Isn't it true there is a universality to the pattern of the body, and isn't
it true there is a universal pattern to the mind, for we all can think, we all
can analyze, we can all learn from trial and error. To me, this conclusion
is inescapable. If we can know that we are One with the Divine Pattern
of Life given to us by our God, then you and I already have what we are
looking for within us. We already have the tools we need-the tool of
vision, the tool of brotherly love, of faith, of tenderness, compassion,
and courage.
We can abuse this pattern. We can abuse the ho~. We can abuse
the mind and we can deny God's Spirit Within. Still, there is hope. We
are going to have challenges on every hand but we must remember the
Bible says, "God hath made man upright, but they have sought out many
inventions."
We belong to God's Life and everything the Father hath is ours to
use. Think of it! Man only uses what God has already given. Man did
not create the cattle, the wheat, the trees, the fish of the sea, or the birds
of the air. He did not put the iron into the mounain nor the salt into the
sea. True, we change the form of the tree into a house, but it is still of
the Almighty God.
Last week I was quite aware of the universality of God's creativeness.
Mrs. Hornaday raises collies, and during the night I was awakened
because one of the collies was in labor. The first puppy was born enclosed
in a sack. This was the collie's first litter, but she broke the sack, bit the
umbilical cord in just the right place, turned the pup over a number of
times so it was breathing well, and then I observed the new-born pup,
that could not see or hear, immediately make its way to its mother's
breast.
This, to me, is the miracle of life. It is faf" beyond my comprehension,
but it was participation in that invisible pattern of knowledge that told
the mother what to do, as well as the little puppy.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Is it any less in man 1 I told this story to a man and said, "What do
you think? Isn't it wonderful?" He answered, "It's just instinct. That's
all it is." May I ask you, Master Masons, who created instinct?
Not one of us here is insignificant for these times. Man only becomes
insignificant when he is unaware that his life is part of the very Life of
God. God made a little humming bird and God made the great elephant.
The elephant is bigger than the humming bird, as we measure things, but
does the humming bird have less life than the elephant? There isn't any
big or little to the Thing we are talking about. nor hard, nor easy. nor
long, nor short. God's Directive Wisdom is available to us if we will only
permit our minds to be receptive.
We must remember there can be no happiness based on separation
or isolation, and our task in life is to know we are not separated from one
another, for God is Life and we are Life. Within the realm of that Life
is a Wisdom that seeks to use us, to bring peace and happiness to the
world God meant to be.
Here, I am not speaking of a church religion or synagogue ·religion. I
am not speaking of a dogma or a creed, I am speaking of the unlimited
potential within all of us to turn, in our own way, according to the desires and demands of our own hearts. and say. believing. "Thou art that
which I am. I am that which Thou art. Use me this hour, this day and
everyday to do Thy Will."
New unborn moments are dashing to greet us, and contained within
these unborn moments is the Divine Wisdom that sets us free from any
dilemma, from air pollution, water pollution, from the increase in crime,
from war, but this occurs onliy when we open our minds unto God, desiring to be a part of that Universal Pattern of God's Infinite Love that
brings us stamina and courage to meet the challenges ahead, that Oneness with God. omnipotent, omnipresent, and omniscient, revealed by
a little minister who was retiring after fifty years of labor in the Vineyard
of the Lord.
His parishioners knew that his favorite prayer was the Twenty-third
Psalm. To honor him on this occasion they sent for a professor of
speech in a university a few hundred miles away. It was to be the highlight of the program. He presented the Twenty-third Psalm with a background of beautiful organ music. It was perfect. Every word was distinct,
the phrasing was correct. At the conclusion of the program the little
minister was asked to say a few words. He thanked them for their every
kindness and requested permission to conclude biy repeating the Twentythird Psalm. Later. one of the church officials was driving the professor
of speech to the railroad station and thanked him for coming. The professor said, "I feel frustrated. May I ask you a question? Did they appreciate me, was it all right?" "Oh, yes," was the reply. "It was beautifully done." The professor then said, "Tell me, honestly, when the min-

ister gave the Twenty-third Psalm at the conclusion, people actually had
tears in thek eyes. His phrasing was poor, his pronunciation was not
good, but they seemed to like his rendition better." The official turned to
him and said, "In my opinion, if you will pardon me for saying so, the
difference between you is simply, you know the Twenty-third Psalm, but
our minister knows the Good Shepherd."
Today, we, as Master Masons, should all know the Good Shepherd
initimately, for, here, Divine Guidance begins. This Divine Guidance of
which I speak is available to every one of us, for everyone is significant.
Everyone is a Divine Expression of Almighty God.
Such realization of our signukance, our potential to become more, is
more than an intellectual conclusion. It actually is the feeling of a faith
that can make us whole: of a Divine Power available to man which
causes him to know he is sufficient, with God, to meet his needs. It is
an emotional awareness which should be felt every time we wear the
apron-the badge of a Mason.

11

This morning, what is your feeling as you sit with your Brothers
"":'earing their aprons? For a moment can it not return you to that prec10us moment when you were raised as a master of the craft proven
worthy. proven significant, proven righteous? Is there an emotional feeling of Brotherhood, Brotherly love and charity when you enter the lodge
room and see the letter "G?" There should be. When you return from
Grand Lodge to your family. are you a better man? Do your words, actions, communications within the family circle give evidence that you are
a practicing Maso!17
Today, as we wear our aprons, we are at work, at work with each
other, but, collectively, at work with the Good Shepherd. Our work is
to cleanse our minds of all pettiness and littleness, all prejudice and
hate, hypocrisy, bigotry of any kind, and stand tall with our Brothers
in behalf of the Truth that sets us free. There is work to be done in the
Vineyard of the Lord, and this means every home, every community,
every hamlet, every city, every state, every nation.
As we pass through each day, what monument have we left? Read
the history of Masonry. Be challenged and encouraged by the Master
Masons, who, throughout history, have given their All in behalf of education, in behalf of our Constitution and its Bill of Rights. Their Spirit
is still with us and we join the millions who have gone on to that Celestial Mansion not made by hands but Eternal in the Heavens. We become One with their ideals and declare, as they did, no form of anarchy,
no form of communism or socialism shall tarnish our government of the
people, biy the people, and for the people.
We believe in the separation of church and state. We believe that
every child born, regardless of race, creed, or color, was created equally
in Spirit and must be guaranteed the right to the pursuit of happiness.

There is time. It is not too late for us to become answerable to the
problems of these times. Through the philosophy, the ideals of Masonry,
we can bring influence and change. Masons are living and working in
every community, in law enforcement, in the judiciary, in our state, and
every state legislature and in the Congress of the United States of
America.
Through us, gathered here at Grand Lodge, may we affirm-"Hi s
·
Truth is marching on!"

Necrology
Another Masonic year has passed into history carrying with it the
record of our achievements and our failures. In its pages are recorded
the names of flve hundred and seven ( 507) of our Brethren who have
answered that last call, and have passed to that land to which we all must
go. We gather here in this solemn moment to pay a memorial tribute to
their memory. In death they are all equal, and we draw no comparisons
among them. Some have served the state and nation in the political arena,
others in the fleld of education, the judiciary and many other vocations,
but most of all we honor many of them for their labors in the vineyards
of Masonry. From the Grand Lodge Line we mourn the passing of our
Grand Lecturer, Hal Richards, and among our Inspectors, William Robusch, Inspector of the 582nd Masonic District and one of the most
loved men in the Corp. Separate memorials will be offered to them in this
program by Past Grand Masters, Theodore Meriam and Ellsworth
Meyer. Each year the list grows. Last year was the highest in our history and this year the toll has increased by forty-two ( 42) more. Time
will only permit the recitation of the \iistory of a few, yet all are worthy.
Their individual names and lodges will be appended to, and become a
part of the printed report. Four ( 4) Lodges: Washington No. 20, Sacramento: Sincerity No. 132, Greenville: Palestine No. 351, Los Angeles,
and Amity-Seal Rock No. 370, San Francisco, each lost flve ( 5) Past
Masters, and flve ( 5) other :Lodges each lost four ( 4) Past Masters.
Many others lost three ( 3).
Ralph Crockett Hine was a native of Chesterland , Ohio, where he
was born October 6, 1897. He died in Santa Barbara February 17, 1969.
He was a graduate of the University of Michigan. At the outbreak of
World War · I he enlisted in the navy. Shortly after his discharge he
came to California. He married Thelma O'Malley at Highland, California, in August 1920, and came to Santa Barbara in September of 1923
where he spent the balance of his life. He received the degrees of Masonry in Magnolia Lodge No. 242 in 1927 and served as its Master in 1933,
following which he served as its Secretary for three ( 3) years. It was
during his year as Master that the Santa Barbara Board of Relief was
formed and he served as its President for fifteen ( 15) years. He was

Frank Morrill Jordan, who died March 29th, served the State of
California as Secretary of State for twenty-eigh t (28) years, from 1942
until his death on March 29th of this year. He was first elected to that
office in 1942 upon the death of his father, Frank C. Jordan, who held
that office for near three decades. A father and son combination without
equal anywhere. Both father and son were members of the Fraternity.
The father was a member of Live Oak Lodge No. 61 of Oakland, the
son a member of Union Lodge No. 58 of Sacramento. He became a Master Mason on April 28, 1943 and he retained his membership in that
Lodge until his death. His grandparent s were pioneers who settled at
Haiycrafts Ferry, near Redding, and where his father was born in 1860.

On May 21, 1970 Grand Lecturer Richards had the unique privilege
of raising his two sons, William and Phillip, to the degree of Master
Mason in Washington Lodge. Those of us who were present saw a
justifiable proud father and two very pleased and proud sons.
One of Harold Richards' greatest ritualistic concerns was for the dignity and quality of our funeral service. His last official act as Grand Lecturer was the preparation of a directive to the Masters of the Constituent Lodges and to the Inspectors of the Masonic Districts for the purpose
of insuring the dignity and excellence which should characterize every
presentation of the Masonic Funeral Service. Here is the first sentence of
that directive-"The Funeral Service is one of the most important elements of our Masonic Ritual, and when well-executed it redounds to
the credit of Freemasonry as well as affording comfort to the bereaved,
and adds lustre to the esteem in which it is regarded." This was the concern and the expression of our late Grand Lecturer. The directive was
mailed on the day of his death. It arrived in the hands of its recipients
after his death. There can be no finer remembrance for Brother Harold
Richards than that every Masonic Funeral Service will be well executed
to redound to the credit of Freemasonry.
Brother Richards is survived by his beloved wife Betty, who shared
with full understanding and approval his busy Masonic life, by his two
sons William and Phillip, members of their father's lodge, and by two
daughters and another son, plus seven grandchildren. Surviving him also
are the brethren of Washington Lodge who have benefited so much from
the leadership of this truly distinguished Mason.
An illustrious Masonic career has ended. It was one which contained
a firm and never-wavering dedication to Freemasonry. It was one which
contained a compelling desire and di'ive for perfection--excellence was

Harold Newton Richards, Master Mason and master Masonic lecturer; Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of California from late in
1964 until he passed away on August 12, 1970. It was my privilege. my
pleasure and my honor to have appointed Brother Richards to that high
office and I have always been proud of the appointment. He was the
twenty-first man in the history of our Grand Lodge to serve as Grand
Lecturer. He, like his predecessors, added much to the stature and quality
of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii. A perfectionist at heart, he
taught well and thoroughly-and patiently, too--for proficiency was his
mission and his goal.
Harold Richards was a native of California, born in Sacramento on
September 3, 1910. He attended the public schools of that city and upon
graduation from Sacramento High School he entered the employ of
Holdener Construction Compny. He spent his working life with this firm
and was a co-partner from 1948 until his death. Many well-constructed
buildings. both public and private, in the Sacramento area stand as monuments to the quality of builder represented by our departed brother.
He was an active man-active in church, community and Masonry.
He served as President of the Sacramento Junior Chamber of Commerce, as President of the Sacramento County Society for Crippled Children, as President of the General Contractors Association of Sacramento, as President of the Sacramento Lions Club. There were many
other community attachments in all of which he was a leader. The list is
long.
From earliest childhood he was affiliated with the Methodist Church
in Sacramento. Here, too, he was consistently an active leader. High tribute to his church service and to his church leadership was eloquently expressed by Dr. Robert Panzer, who officiated at the funeral of Brother
Richards, when he described so clearly the strength and extent of Hal's
work with his church.
Freemasonry, though, was his consuming interest. He was raised in
Washington Lodge No. 20 on April 25, 1946. He became Chief Candidate Coach the following year and was Master of Washington Lodge
in 1953. His participation with the Grand Lodge began in 1952 when he

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

To inform each of the candidates as to the interpretation of what is
said and done in our degrees should be regarded as mandatory for our
Lodges. As we fail to do so, we fail Masonry; and we thus fail ourselves.
It's that simple.
As Masons we owe the candidate more than just the formal conferring of degrees and if we do not address ourselves to this very basic
responsibility we may expect to have weak Lodges, meager attendance
and little interest. On the contrary, those Lodges in California and
Hawaii which are working to bring Masonic Information, Masonic Education and Masonic Responsibility into their Lodges are finding a rebirth
of interest and a rebirth of activity.
I cannot stress strongly enough that most Masons want to know
more about Masonry. Each of us has a responsibility to meet this need.
We talk about Freemasonry being a force for great good in the
community.
Let me remind you that it is not this organization which is a force
for great good-it is the individual member-and that we, as individual
men, must exercise greater effort in teaching, explaining and exemplifying Freemasonry.
While we glory in the past, we live not for it. Throughout the ages
we have been importuned to search for greater light. Had the scientists,
the men of medicine, the farmers or the industrialists been satisfied with
the "status quo" they, and our world, would have become stagnant and
repressive.
Times change, people change, interests differ. What may have been
an adequate way to present Masonry in the past may not be adequate
today. What may have been enough to "get by" in the past is not good
enough in this day of competition and specialization. We are foolish
indeed if we think so. The more highly organized our society becomes,
the more it requires competent, self-respecting, well-rounded individuals
to make it work. The same applies to Freemasonry.
Unless we provide greater light through an expanded program of
developing knowledge. understanding and an irrepressable desire for
self improvement, we, too, become stagnant and in my judgment we
consign Masonry to mediocrity.
From reading the reports of my distinguished predecessors I have
learned that the Grand Master's Annual Message is intended to report
activities accomplished, decisions announced and recommendations. Between closing our Grand Lodge in this auditorium a year ago and its
opening here today much has occurred to report to you-and to this end
-subject by subject-I shall address myself.

My Brethren, for the privilege of serving this Grand Lodge, and for
the love and understanding of my fellow Masons, I shall be forever
grateful.
Many outstanding men of Masonry in California and Hawaii have
made great contributions to this cause to which we are all dedicated.
California Masonry today is probably at its highest level of effectiveness and credit is due to the men who have labored to make this possible.
Ritual, Lodge administration and Grand Lodge administration are all at
new peaks of efficiency. With the anticipated approval by Grand Lodge
of the work of the Code Revision Commission, the California Masonic
Code will provide better clarification of the laws of Masonry applicable
in this jurisdiction.
Serious problems exist, however, and in this report I shall discuss
them and offer some suggestions and recommendations concerning these
important issues.
There are those who will find portions of this message to be critical.
It is intended to be so. I firmly believe that Grand Lodge must reexamine and re-assess many of its procedures. It is hoped that although
critical, the contents may prove constructive.
After serving this past year I have become concerned that not enough
is done in our Lodges (beyond learning the ritual) to prepare our Lodge
officers to assume the important responsibilities of the Master's chair.
Despite this, many of our Masters do a creditable job.
As I see it, better preparation through a program of leadership
training would have a manifold benefit. It would produce better Masonic
officers and better citizens, both of which are our goals. Later in this
report you will learn of plans to meet this need.
An equally serious unsolved, and often unrecognized, problem exists
after conferral of our three degrees. At this time, too many of our
Lodges consider their responsibility of informing the candidate about
Masonry to be at an end.
The candidate applied for the degrees of Masonry because he wanted
a complete Mason. Unfortunately, in most cases, he becomes
become
to
only a member. There is a difference! It is my considered judgment that
the ritual is hut a foundation upon which one may build a personal
Masonic edifice. The ritual is indeed not the conclusion of instructionit is, in fact, only the base upon which to continue instruction. Thus, in
many instances, the personal Masonic edifice we seek to build stands on
a foundation hut with no super structure. A limited number of those who
come to us will, on their own, continue their study of Masonry and thus
better meet their responsibilities as Masons. Too many will not.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

CANDIDATES' EDUCATION

Grand Master of another jurisdiction stated, "We should have done
this a hundred years ago." It is hoped the contents of this pamphlet will
bring the Candidate's family closer to the Lodge and help in understanding that Masonic teaching will assist his loved ones in fulfilling the finest
hopes and dreams they have for him. This pamphlet is in no way to
replace the other materials used by coaches, such as the Handbook for
Candidates' Coaches. It is a supplement and hopefully fills a need that
now exists.

In a recent Grand Lodge Newsletter Grand Master Clinton H. Lang
of Illinois stated that "20% of all candidates on a national average received the Entered Apprentice Degree and never became Master
Masons." In California the record is much better. For an average of
five years approximately 4.6% of those receiving the first degree did not
receive the third degree in California. Let me suggest several reasons
which, according to my observations, account for these drop.-outs. On
most occasions this is due to the inability or unwillingness to learn the
required memory work. In other instances neither the candidate nor his
family had any knowledge as to just what participation in the Masonic
Order implies. It is the judgment of your Grand Master that the Master
and the Wardens of the Lodge should visit the candidate at his home as
soon as possible after he has applied for the degrees of Freemasonry.
This should be for the purpose of explaining to the candidate and his
family what Masonry is and what it is not. Care should be exercised
to inform the candidate that other members of the Lodge will visit to ask
questions. The Master should inform the individual that there is no
"horseplay" in the initiation and that he will be required to commit to
memory a portion of what is made apparent in the initiatory work. ·
Throughout the years of California Freemasonry, the wife or.- "in
some cases, the mother of the Entered Apprentice Mason has never
adequately understood what requirements, responsibilities and privileges
Masonry has created for her husband or son.
In many instances failure to progress is due to a lack of understanding on the part of the wife or mother. The family should be informed
there is work to be done and that for a short period of time his availability at home might not be exactly the same. While a portion of our
drop-outs may reasonably be charged to disinterested officers, inadequate ritual, uninformed coaches or for other reasons, I am confident that
much of it is due to the fact that the new Entered Apprentice Mason
does not know what his obligation permits him to tell his family about
Masonry. Accordingly, we have prepared a new pamphlet entitled
"Freemasonry-Does it Concern Me?" signed by the Master of the
Lodge, placed in an envelope addressed to the lady of the family and,
following the First Degree, is given to the new Entered Apprentice for
delivery to her. This booklet answers many questions for the family
which, when left unanswered, often create a competitive or resentful
attitude toward Masonry.
This pamphlet has been received enthusiastically by the Worshipful
Masters of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction and seems to fill that void
between the Lodge and the New Mason's family. Inquiries from practically every State in the Union have caused our Grand Lodge to issue
authorization for the reproduction of this particular pamphlet. One

MASONIC INFORMATION-MASONIC EDUCATIONMASON1c RESPONSIBILITY

Earlier in this report I made known my thoughts concerning the lack
of communication of the fundamentals of Freemasonry to our Brethren.
The Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility, under the chairmanship of one of California's outstanding
Masons, Brother William F. Poynter, P.M., has begun the long road
to remedy this fault.
This assignment has been undertaken in workshop format under
the direction of two unusually qualified Masons, Brother Arthur Dvorin,
P.M., in Southern California and Brother Louis I. Goldkind, P.M., in
Northern California. In addition, they have joined together for presentation of the program in Hawaii.
The response from the Lodges has been more than we anticipated
the first year. A contributing reason for the fast start is the unremitting
cooperation of the Inspectors and the members of the Ritual Committee.
The registered participants at our workshops probably do not number
more than 5,000 for this first year. These figures will include approximately 75% of the Lodge officers.
This year Masonic Information, Masonic Education and Masonic
Responsibility have been brought to the constituent Lodges with more
than fifty workshops held in various parts of California and Hawaii. Although no travel allowance was available for the Hawaii visitations,
several members of the Committee undertook two such workshops in
Hawaii at their own expense.
A subcommittee on the communication of 'Masonic fundamentals
was set up under the chairmanship of John R. Nocas, P.M., one of our
early supporters. This committee provided guidance and impetus to the
Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility.
The Deputy Grand Master advises me he plans to continue and
expand the entire program in the next Masonic year. I sincerely believe
the future will demonstrate that these dedicated efforts have been rewarding and fruitful.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

In addition to the workshops, the committee developed numerous
articles for bulletin use by each of the Lodges. Twelve separate articles
were prepared for the Lodges-o ne for each month. Twelve similar
articles were prepared and forwarded to the Scottish Rite Bodies in
this State, twelve different ones for the York Rite Bodies and twelve
different ones for the Shrine monthly bulletins. In addition, the Grand
Master's Bulletin became a reality, creating a direct correspondence and
informational medium with the Masters of our Lodges. The response
from many Masters has been most valuable.
In my opinion there is nothing of greater importance to California
and Hawaii Masonry today than Masonic education for its membership.
Because of this serious concern I have asked each constituent Lodge
to set up such a committee and to appoint all new Master Masons to
work on it. Progress is slow but a substantial beginning has been made.
Many years of hard work by dedicated Masons will pass ere we begin
to recognize the change from lack of education to knowledgeable
Masons, from mediocrity to superiority and from making members to
making Masons.
The sleeping giant of F£eemasonry, capable of producing great individual and collective good, can only be awakened by a continuous,
dedicated effort to learn, understan d and exemplify the truly great
principles of our Order. Knowledge is indeed the key. Man cannot
exempli!y lest he know the subject matter. To strengthen our Fraternity ,
therefore, let him learn/

dances, picnics and other meetings of a social nature or other social
events at which liquor, wine or beer may be used or served, in a
hotel, ·restaurant, dining room, club, convention hall, picnic area or
other establishment: provided, however, that, except for ritualistic
purposes, no liquor, wine or beer may be served in a Masonic Temple
or in any building or structure owned or operated by a Masonic
Lodge or any organization a prerequisite of membership wherein is
that a person be a Master Mason; and provided, further, that this
section shall not require a Masonic Lodge or Masonic-related organization to vacate leased premises prior to expiration of leases made
in good faith, or to violate leases, or to refuse to accept buildings so
received from an estate or by gift: but such building so received must
be sold or otherwise disposed of, or the offending use must be terminated, within a reasonable time. ( 1969)"
This permits the serving and consuming of alcoholic beverages at
purely social gatherings held by Masons in places away from Masonic
premises.
If, however, the meeting is for the purpose of transacting Masonic
or Masonic-related business, it is not a social event within the meaning
of the above-quoted section, even though held in a public place where
liquor is sold and even though the gathering may serve an incidental
social purpose.
It is the actual, not the declared, character of the meeting which determines whether or not it falls within the category of a social event.
Accordingly, meetings of District Officers' Associations, Boards of
Relief, Secretari~' Associations, Grand Lodge Committees and Boards
are for Masonic rather than social purposes wherever held and alcoholic
beverages may not be served or consumed at and during such meetings.
Whether the assemblage is of a voluntary group, such as a Secretaries'
Association, or of groups officially organized under the Grand Lodge is
not the controlling factor.
Special attention is directed to the law as it now stands with regard
to open installations of Lodge officers.
By resolution at the 1966 Communication, Grand Lodge repealed
and deleted from the Masonic Code Annotation 324g, which permitted
open installations in hotels and other public places where liquor is sold.
At the same Communication a new Section 324.2 was presented
which included the provision that a Masonic Lodge
"may hold an open installation of officers in a hotel, restaurant or
other establishment serving liquor or operating a bar: provided, however, in case of an open installation of a Masonic Lodge, the Grand
Master must first approve the location as suitable to the solemnity
of the installation ceremony; and provided further that no liquor
shall be.served to or consumed by members or guests during such
installation ceremony."

LIQUOR

At the Annual Communication in 1969 legislation was adopted
relative to the serving and use of liquor at Masonic functions. Shortly
thereafter inquiries were received concerning its signi.6.cance and application to specific cases.
With no intent to either add or subtract from the newly adopted
law, and after conferring with the Chairman of the Jurisprud~nce .Committee I issued a letter of interpretation as a matter of clariJkation. I
sugge~ted that the letter be made part of the Lod-ge Manual in ~~ss~s­
sion of each Lodge. I urge each of the senior officers to fam1har1ze
himself with the actual legislation as well as the interpretation.
"TO THE MASTERS
For the purpose of clarifying the legal effect of legislation enacted
at the 1969 Communication of the Grand Lodge regarding the serving
and use of liquor at Masonic functions, your attention is directed to the
following:
Section 324.2 of the California Masonic Code (see page 24 of the
1969 Pocket Supplement) provides as follows:
"Serving of liquor at social functions. A Masonic Lodge, or an
organization the prerequisite of membership wh.erein is. that a p~son
be a Master Mason, may hold social gathenngs, dinners, dinner

34

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

That proposed section, after being carried over on a majority af~
firmative vote, was defeated at the 1967 Communication.
There is, therefore, no present authority in the Masonic Code for
holding open installations away from Masonic premises or at places
where liquor is served.
I trust the foregoing provides adequate guidelines by which all concerned may follow a proper course.''
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

This magniflcent building, dedicated to the memory of those Cali~
fomia Masons who gave their lives in the service of our country, was
completed in 1958.
For more than twelve years the structure has served Masonry and
the community. Duxing these years there has been no major refurbishing. The carpets, drapes, curtains, etc. have received much wear and
tear. Likewise there has been no major repainting of the interior during
these years.
Floodlighting on the stage and elsewhere in the auditorium has been
inadequate due to the location established for the control of the flood
lights. Need for replacing the sound system and improved plumbing
facilities has been evident.
Regardless of its uses, this structure proclaims to the world the image
and emblem of Masonry. It should be maintained in the finest condition
at all times and its facilities should be above criticism.
The Trustees of the Temple Board unanimously recommended, and
your entire elective line concurred in, the extensive refurbishing program
which you now observe.
It is the judgment of all concerned that the substantial costs involved
and the adding of improvements will be returned to the Temple through
increased rental income over the years ahead.
The stage on which Grand Lodge is set up, you will notice, has been
reconstructed at a slightly lower level than heretofore. This was done
only after receiving the best recommendations of experts on acoustics.
lighting and auditorium usages.
As in all other matters of major importance this year, your elective
line made a thorough study and analysis of every proposed improvement
item and the cost involved. All were unanimously approved.
Special thanks and appreciation are due to the Temple Trustees. as
well as to Board Chairman, Most Worshipful Ira W. Coburn, Past
Grand Master, whose construction skills and know-how were made
available day and night without cost so the work might be completed at
a minimum of cost and with a minimum of delay.

MASONIC HOMES

They are the outward, physical manifestations of our attitude of
love and charity for those less fortunate than ourselves. Though we
never have been smugly self-satisfied, we have had a feeling of warmth
and pride in what has been accomplished.
Under the guidance of our Board of Trustees we have greater cause
than ever this year to be confident that our future Homes activities will
be even more effective.
Extensive studies of facilities which answered needs similar to ours
for young people were made throughout the United States. Where
methods which we have adopted have been applied, experienced psy~
chologists and sociologists have reported very successful experiences.
The old dormitory style Home at Covina has been replaced and
recently eight new, beautiful, individual home units have been built in its
place. We are confident the good judgment of your Trustees will be
demonstrated by the continuing aid to our youth.
A similar analysis has been made of the requirements for our guests at
Union City, particularly in considering the type and kind of needs that
may require answers ten, fifteen or twenty years in the future. Careful
and cautious consideration is being exercised so the most effective
method of charitable relief will be the end result.
Further details on both these matters will be included in the Report
of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes.

DISCRIMINATION

In early June of this year a brother requested a dimit from his Lodge
because, as he said, he "could no longer maintain membership in an or~
ganization which in fact gives lip service to the principles of brotherly
love, relief and truth, by discriminating on the basis of race or color •. · ·
and that our Fraternity would do better to orient itself to the outside
world and to the solutions of the very real problems which our society
faces today."
Earlier in the year I had received similar correspondence from a
young DeMolay boy who, having reached the age of 21, questioned the
policies of Freemasonry. During my term as Grand Master s~~eral
letters were sent to me from members urging that our Grand Lodge take
a stand" for this or against that.
Throughout the great history of our Fraternity, Masons have ~a.k.en
a stand as individuals, :reserving unto the Craft itself the responsibility
of strengthening the character of its individual members so that the
member's "stand" will be a "stand" based on integrity, perception and

37

character - built into the individual. through the learning and under~
standing of the basic principles of Freemasonry itself.
One need only recall Washington, Franklin, Roosevelt, Lafayette,
San Martin, Juarez, Garibaldi, Indian Chief Sitting Bull, Porfirio
Diaz, King Kamehameha, Simon Bolivar, the Rothschilds, George Tog~
asaki, and many other famous men, all of whom were Masons, and as
individuals were required to "take a stand." With every reasonable
justification, we believe their stand was a better stand because of their
Masonic background.
Likewise, in my response to these issues, I called attention to the
discrimination which Freemasonry has itself been subjected to throughout the years: that because Masons know what discrimination is, we
want no part of it! The laws and regulations of our Grand Lodge specifically prohibit discrimination against any applicant for the degrees in
this jurisdiction because of race, religious background or color.
My letter stated:
"There is no bar to a negro being elected to membership in a Lodge
in this jurisdiction. We are not aware that any have been elected or
rejected, for no record of this kind is maintained. If any have been either
elected or rejected it has not been by any directive or secret agreement
of this Grand Lodge but by action of the individual members of a Lodge.
"Regardless of how you, or any other person, may judge the action
of our Grand Lodge in the matter of recognition or non-recognition of
another Grand Lodge, this has nothing whatever to do with minorities,
race, religion or s:olor.
"The members who make up our Lodges are probably comparable to
many men in today's churches and synagogues. All are human; all may
err-all must be taught to learn and live the principles of their faith.
Most religious men have learned; so have most Masons. Thus the rea~
son you have set forth for requesting a dimit from your Lodge could
likewise call for a dimit from your religious beliefs, as well as from
other areas of society wherein men participate.
"Yes, Freemasonry has survived villification, hatred, intolerance and
persecution, and its striving for understanding is today the same as when
the early stonemasons chipped away the rough and superfluous parts of
the rough ashlars, seeking always to produce the perfectly polished stone.
"So it is with our members. We seek by Masonic Information, Masonic Education and Masonic Responsibility to develop greater under~
standing, to engender kindly consideration for others as a first step in
Brotherly Love, to help each member learn what Masonry truly means
in depth, to learn of its beauty, its perfection and its way of life to a
better future. We are not always successful because each man who
comes to us has his choice. He may lay down his tools and quit, or he
can better help mankind by the observance of good moral principles as

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

well as by personal and positive exemplification of Masonic love and
understanding.
"I have continuously called attention to the fact that Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth remain just words until activated. Undoubtedlry, there
are some of our members who give only "lip service" to these principles. This is unfortunate. It may well be that some have not learned
their meaning. We must try harder.
"Freemasonry today needs men who will become the teachers necessary to activate the words and lessons of our degrees-M~on~ w~o
will teach others, not only by interpretations, but by exemphficatlon m

Mry Brethren, racial or religious discrimination h~s ~o place among
Masons. When its ugly head is raised, men whose obligations mak~ t~em
Masons must be the first to speak out strongly against such_ pr~J~dice,
whether inside the Lodge or outside of it. What we do as mdlVlduals
is far more important than what we do as a Lodge or a Fraternity.
It is my continuing judgement, however, that the gr~atest servic~ w_e

HAWAII GRAND LoDGE

For a number of years, and particularly since Hawaii gained Statehood, there has been discussion by a number of our Hawaiian Lodge
members and others concerning separation from the Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of California and the forming of a new Grand Lodge
F. & A. M. of Hawaii. In such an event, the Lodges in the Hawaiian
Islands would become entirely dependent upon themselves.
For several years this Grand Lodge has made consultants available
to the Hawaiian Lodges to discuss the pros and cons of such a move.
In addition, the Hawaiian Lodges themselves, through studies of an
Inter-Lodge Committee, accumulated figures for their own consideration
to determine the practicability of such a move.
At last year's Annual Communication the Grand Master's recommendation on the Hawaiian matter was adopted by the Grand Lodge.
It provided "that the incoming Grand Master continue the Hawaiian
Advisory Committee to serve as unbiased consultants to the Lodges in
Hawaii in order that the best interest of Freemasonry and all Masons
in the Islands be served."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

With the assistance of that Committee your Grand Master for ..
warded to each member of the Hawaiian Lodges, in envelopes addressed
by each Lodge Secretary, a brief, unbiased summary of facts together
with answers to questions relating to the problem. A post card ballot
was also included with the request that each Hawaiian Lodge member
express himself concerning the formation of a new Grand Lodge of
Hawaii. Every effort was made by the Advisory Committee and your
Grand Master to present the facts in as complete a way as possible
and without bias. Before the mailing, drafts of the proposed fact sheet
were forwarded to the Hawaiian Lodge Masters, interested members
of the lnter..Lodge Committee, Inspectors and the elected Grand Lodge
Officers for their review and suggestions.
Of the ballots cast, a large majority indicated they were not in favor
of the formation of a new Grand Lodge of Hawaii. Seven of the ten
Hawaiian Lodges voted heavily against a new Grand Lodge. Three
of the ten Lodges voted in favor of such a Grand Lodge.
Perhaps at some future date further consideration of this question
may become desirable. However, the present overwhelming vote of these
members that a Grand Lodge of Hawaii not be formed is most apparent.
We are confident that the long established, warm fraternal relations
between these Lodges and the other Lodges in the Jurisdiction will con..
tinue undiminished. We :recognize, also, that there are special factors
of distance and isolation of Lodges in the Islands which require special
handling. However, as improved transportation shortens distances and
communication continues to improve, such problems will be minimized.

Pursuant to direction of this Grand Lodge the Berkeley Clubhouse
was sold on September 20, 1968, for $266,000.00, the sales price
being in excess of the appraised value. An agent's commission of
$9,900.00 was paid to Property Development, Inc., 1411 Grove St.,
Berkeley, California. The funds were in due time turned over to the
Foundation and invested by the Grand Lodge Investment Committee
according to guidelines set up for that purpose under the C.M.C.
With respect to the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse, on January 7, 1970, the
Foundation Board entered into an escrow agreement for the sale of that
Clubhouse. Problems developed precluding the immediate closing of
the escrow. The time for closing was extended to July 31, 1970. Un..
fortunately the prospective purchasers were unable to complete the
transaction. Releases between the Foundation and the buyers have
been executed and exchanged, and the property is once again being
offered for sale. A $25,000.00 deposit was retained by the Foundation
in accordance with the agreement. Detailed terms of the proposed sale
are not included in this report since terms and conditions of that offer
may have an effect on a future sale.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION

Grand Master Dayton, at the 1968 Annual Communication, recom..
mended that the Grand Lodge of California establish a foundation for
general purposes of Masonic interests. His recommendation was ap..
proved.
Officers and Directors were appointed and, on March 5, 1969, the
California Masonic Foundation was incorporated as a tax exempt, non..
profit corporation.
Its organization was slow and at times seemed to lack cohesive di..
rection. Some members of the Board believed the Foundation should be
separate and apart from the general function of the Grand Lodge. 0th..
ers considered the Foundation to be a vehicle of Grand Lodge with
which Grand Lodge should continue to be identified. I am pleased to
report that orderly progress in operation and functioning is being made.
Assets of the Foundation, by action of the Grand Lodge, consisted
of the two Clubhouses at Berkeley and U.C.L.A. respectively. Some
miscellaneous gifts were also received.

OPERATION OF FOUNDATION

It was anticipated that problems would arise in undertaking estab..
lishment of the new Foundation. After much consultation with the
Grand Lodge line officers, Past Grand Masters and others, I made cer..
tain recommendations to the Foundation Board, which I am pleased
to report were adopted at the meeting of February 15, 1970.
The implementation of the recommendation has done much to sta..
bilize the functional operation of the Foundation.
From time to time suggestions have been made to establish a cor..
respondence office for the Foundation in Southern California. Currently
both the President and Secretary of the Foundation reside there. It is
my judgment, after discussing this possibility with numerous interested
Brethren, that such a step be def erred and that the Foundation Directors
allow sufficient latitude for the proper officer to pay his personal secre..
tary for extra work, if required, or to employ a part time secretary as
needed. Hopefully the Foundation will some day reach a stage of de..
velopment which will justify a full time staff. In my judgment that time
is not yet here. In any event no office should be established without first
obtaining approval from the Grand Master.
Much has been accomplished to date. However, a great deal remains
to be done. It is my hope that when scholarships are presented they
may be presented through the local Lodge in the community where the
tteipient resides. This will identify the scholarship with the local Lodge
and its membership. There are other matters which should have atten..
tion. I recommend to my successor and his line officers that close coop..

I want to thank those responsible and dedicated members of the
Foundation Board for their continual devotion to the cause. This facility
can bring help to many young people and great credit to our Fraternity.
The challenge to our leadership is to properly direct it through the rough
seas during these formative years.
This Foundation can be an instrument of good will. This is our hope.
It is also our hope its effectiveness will be so recognized that its growth,
through bequests and contributions, will enable the Foundation to stand
on its own feet without subsidy of any kind from the Grand Lodge either
now or in the future. Such is the considered judgment of the current
progressive line officers.

Your progressive line officers became concerned with the increased
charges involved in the changeover from Lybrand's office to Andersen &
Co. Accordingly, we called for new audit cost estimates from four major
companies. As a result of this procedure the costs for our 1970 audits
approximated $10,000. The Brethren may be assured the current audit
has been equally as thorough as any other heretofore made of this Grand
Lodge and its entities.

i2

ANNUAL AUDIT AND RELATED MAITERS

In June of 1969 the then Grand Master ordered a change of our
auditors from Lybrand, Ross Bros. & Montgomery to Arthur Andersen
& Co. Unfortunately for our Grand Lodge, the change of auditors occurred after substantial work had been undertaken by the former auditors. This duplication resulted in extra costs. The new auditors were not
as familiar with our Grand Lodge procedures as they might have been.
This was occasioned by the short time available due to their late start.
Despite the handicap of delay, the audit report of Arthur Andersen
& Co. was efficient and thorough. In a so-called "Blue Back Report" the
company offered numerous suggestions for changes and modiflcations in
our internal controls and bookkeeping operations. Such suggestions by
an audit 6.rm after conclusion of their work is normal audit procedure.
However, after a personal study and investigation item by item, I became
convinced that our existing controls were excellent. Andersen & Co.
agreed.
When the report had been completed and 6.led with our Grand
Lodge, representatives of Arthur Andersen & Co. asked to meet with
me to discuss the report. I was informed, both verbally and in writing,
that the audit report was not to be construed in any way as a criticism
of our fine staff or of our operations.
I thereafter presented a written response containing my own personal
analysis point by point of the so-called "Blue Back Report" dated 10
March 1970. My analysis has been released to our Past Grand Masters,
the elective Grand Lodge officers and to the committees involved. Copies
of this report which speaks for itself are available for reading in the
Grand Secretary's office.
Our costs for the audit service of this Grand Lodge and its entities
were for each year 1965 through 1968 the sum of $8,975.00. However,
for 1969 the cost was $17,860.00.

IN-DEPTH STUDY COMMITIEE

Upon the recommendation of the Grand Master at the 1969 Communication, the Grand Lodge directed that "the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special committee to make an in-depth study of the administration and operation of our Grand Lodge and its entities toward effecting
any possible economy or increased efficiency."
In my own opinion this recommendation and the Grand Lodge action
was for the best interests of the Fraternity. I agree with the statement
made by the Policy and General Purposes Committee, "most successful
and well organized businesses periodically survey their operations and
procedures to see if any improvement can be made."
A report of this kind made to Grand Lodge, of course, would be only
as substantial as the members who compose the committee. It was therefore essential that members of that committee should be men capable
of this kind of analytical work. It should be composed of men whose
personal, professional background fitted them to the requirements; men
who could make an impartial, factual survey of our overall operations.
l~po~tant, also, was that their experience and knowledge of the Fratermty msured a background of understanding in fraternal operations in
general and the Grand Lodge of California and its entities in particular.
In s.elec~~ the appoi.ntees I chose men from as many of our separate
Masomc entities as possible. We were very fortunate with reference to
each appointee.
To chair this important committee I appointed Stanley Davis, Past
Master of Oriental Lodge No. 1i i and cllt'rently a member of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Taxation. As a Certified Public Accountant he
was inv~lved on a professional basis for a number of years in supervi~ing
the audits of our several entities and the record of the Grand Lodge
office. Although for the past nine or ten years he has not been thus
directly involved, his intimate knowledge of our accounting procedures
and the chronology of their development makes him completely qualified
for this responsible post.

qualifications is necessary. He is now retired but those who knaw his

Lodge. Prior to assumption of their new duties, the former property
and casualty coverage by Travelers Insurance Co. had been cancelled.
A new policy had been written with Pacific Indemnity Co.
At our invitation, the several insurance brokers of the companies
and the Insurance Committee of Grand Lodge presented differing views
of existing and proposed insurance coverage for less cost. Faced with
this dilemma, your elective officers requested the Insurance Departme nt
of the State of California to designate an unbiased rate expert who
possessed a knowledge of basic Masonry to advise us. The Junior
Warden of Parnassus -Presidio Lodge No. 388, Brother George E.
Frank. a rate expert in the Division of Insurance of the State of California, was selected to examine the several insurance policies and make
recommendations. After a prolonged study and analysis covering a
period of more than thirty days, Brother Frank concluded that the former
policy of the Travelers Insurance Co. provided greater coverage at less
cost for our Grand Lodge than did the replacement policy of Pacific
Indemnity. Before making any change to restore the coverage to Travelers Insurance Co., your elective line sought and obtained an experience
rate reduction from Travelers . Such a reduction in the sum of $11.850.00
was forthcoming. Based upon the recommendation of Brother Frank
and upon the further fact that a saving of $11,850.00 was available to
our Grand Lodge, your elective line ordered the Travelers policy reinstated.
Subsequen tly your elected line, recognizing the need for accident
Insurance coverage for those on Grand Lodge business. called for bids
for a policy adequate to meet this need. Four bids were received. Those
to be covered under this new accident policy are nearly 600 Grand Lodge
Officers. Inspectors and committee members of Grand Lodge. The low
bid of $8,700.00 annual premium from Kemper Insurance, representing
Lumbermens Mutual Casualty Company. was accepted. The savings
in our overall coverage was applied toward the purchase of the new
accident insurance policy which became effective May 1, 1970.
In 1953 Grand Lodge was successful in obtaining permission to
blanket all Workmen 's Compensa tion Insurance for Lodges under one
policy. A review of experience modification figures for the Lodges shows
a decrease from 100% in 1953-1954 to 75% in 1969-1970.
At that time ( 1953). Workmen 's Compensa tion Insurance required
by law would have cost at least $40.00 premium per Lodge. Some Lodges
that carried such coverage were paying higher minimums. By actual
survey it was found that a goodly number of Lodges had no Workmen 's
Compensation Insurance because of excessive cost.
Good loss ratio and elimination of high minimum premiums per Lodge
has resulted in very substantia l savings to Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE SYMPHONY

Masons in California are to be found in every conceivable profession and industry. The field of music is no exception. Without naming
any special group, I know there are numerous Masonic musical organizations in California- some large, some small-but none functioning
under the name of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California.
A number of our Brethren-s ome musicians and some interested in
the idea-have wanted to form a symphony for some time. Recently I
was approached and asked to formally endorse such a project. After
some discussion with our own Senior Grand Steward, Jerome B. Rosen,
a great leader in music and other interested Brethren I gave my wholehearted endorsement. I am now pleased to announce to all California
Masons that we are in the process of forming a Grand Lodge of California Symphony Orchestra. The orchestra is to be composed of members of the Masonic Fraternity, dedicated to bringing music to all who
~~~

.

Brother Phil Bovero, an outstanding conductor, has accepted our
invitation to serve as conductor of the symphony. There is a great deal
of work to do. Much enthusiasm has been exhibited by Brother Max
Slater, a musician in his own right, who has accepted the responsibility
as director of the orchestra. Rehearsals are to be scheduled weekly.
It is our hope that this project will result in pleasure to those who
love music and great credit to the Fraternity.

On 18 September the Grand Lodge of Baja California held a reception for the Grand Master of Masons in California at Tijuana, Mexico.
Almost five hundred California Masons accompanied your Grand
Master across the border where we were met by a like number of
Mexican Brothers for a dinner and reception. The event was held
during the week of the observance of Mexico's independence which is
celebrated at the same time as our Constitution month program. The
hospitality of our Mexican Brethren was exceeded only by their demonstrated love of Freemasonr y.

RECOMMENDATION No. 1
ASSISTANT GRAND LECTURER- HAWAII

There are ten constituent Lodges in the Islands of Hawaii. Three
Inspectors serve these ten Lodges. The Inspectors meet on occasion ~o
discuss mutual problems and ritual but the Assistant Grand Lecturer is
several thousand miles away. From time to time an Assistant Grand
Lecturer visits the Islands for an Inspectors' School of Instruction.
Consideration should be given to the appointment of an Assistant
Grand Lecturer in Hawaii. Arrangements for his attendance at several

Interest by visitors and Masons alike continues to be demonstrated
in our small library and museum. The registrar of names indicates an
increase in numbers of visitors each year.
Your Library Commission, with helpful suggestions by Past Grand
Master Hopp and the Grand Librarian, have again this year added
Judiciously to the volumes on our shelves and have even squeezed in a
few more shelves. But the limit has been reached.
The interest of the brethren in an adequate facility which might be
truly representative of the Fraternity, as well as being a source of knowledge and service to the community, has been evidenced in many ways.
One such manifestation is a resolution which will be considered later in
this Communication. The action you take on it will be for your own
determination. At the Annual Communication last year Grand Lodge
voted in the affirmative as follows: "Resolved that the Temple Board
Trustees be requested to acquire at the most reasonable price the two
properties needed to complete the area behind the Temple window and
that said Trustees prepare plans for the development of the property
which shall be presented to Grand Lodge for approval prior to any construction."
It is my recommendation that this Grand Lodge instruct the Trustees
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, together with the Library
Commission, to continue working on the plans for the development of
our Library and Museum as a part of this building and present a finalized
report for consideration at the Annual Communication in 1971. The
report should include consideration of feasibility, suggestions as to

per capita tax increase if needed, to effect the program. We should

RECOMMENDATION No. 3
MASONIC HISTORY

There being no Masonic History of our California Grand Lodge
available in booklet form, it is recommended that a special sub-committee
of the Committee on Masonic History be instructed to prepare a concise
history of our Grand Lodge to be available in a small booklet for members, visitors and other interested persons.

The Committtee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendation number three is that a sub-committee of the Committee on History "be instructed to prepare a concise history of the
Grand Lodge to be available in a small booklet for members, visitors and
other interested persons." The preparation of a history which could be
be printed "in a small booklet" would be a task to which the best talent
available among the Craft should be called and should not at the outset
be limited to a sub-committee of a committee.
To implement the recommendation, I move that the incoming Grand
Master be authorized to implement the preparation of a small booklet
on the history of the Grand Lodge of California.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes"
vote.
The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence in the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Adopted.
