to preparing a public ceremony for opening the copper containers removed from cornerstones of buildings where the cornerstone was previously laid by this Grand Lodge and for the replacing of such a cornerstone by a plaque wherever possible.
It is suggested that the proposed ceremony provide sufficient flexibility so that it could be adapted to a public ceremony for removal of
such a cornerstone if scheduling of such were possible.

The Committee on Ritual requested deferment of immediate action on
this recommendation for further study and subsequent report at the
1971 Annual Communication.
The proposal to defer was adopted.
RECOMMENDATION No. 5
RESOLUTIONS

We are proud of the democratic processes which are practiced
through each Annual Communication. The right of any member of
Grand Lodge to express himself through resolutions or verbally on any
matter which concerns the Grand Lodge should be carefully protected.
It is only through these channels that the true voice of the membership
is heard.
However, almost every year resolutions are considered which have
been presented at the last Communication or for the last several preceding Communications and which failed to obtain the required approval
for adoption. Frequently the language of the resolutions is identical to
that of those previously presented.
In view of so recent an expression of disapproval by Grand Lodge
and the demands upon the limited time of the Communication for the
study of new proposals as well, it is my recommendation that this matter
be referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on
Jurisprudence for their report to Grand Lodge in 1971. Such report
would deal with recommendations as to the appropriate number of years
to be required between presentations of an identical resolution or one
designed to accomplish the same purpose. In the event of the Committee's favorable recommendation, the JuJ:isprudence Committee would
submit jointly with the Policy and General Purposes Committee report,
proposed changes in our law to effect the intent of this recommendation.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendation number 5 is that the Committees on Policy and
General Purposes and on Jurisprudence be instructed to consider the
matter of a requirement that an identical resolution may not be again

56

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

presented until the lapse of a period of time. This recommendation requires study of the question and report next year. I so move and the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote.
Adopted.
RECOMME NDATION No. 6
MASONIC FUNERAL SERVICE

Your Grand Master, through the Grand Lecturer, has instructed the
constituen t Lodges that no Masonic funeral service shall be given where
the acting Master has not been certified as competen t by his Inspector.
The late Grand Lecturer, Harold N. Richards, prepared certificates of
competence which are being forwarded to the Inspectors for delivery to
those who are qualified.
I. therefore, recommend that this procedure be adopted as a policy
of this Grand Lodge.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Recommendation No. 6 provides that no Masonic
Funeral Service shall be given where the acting Master has not been
certified as competent by his Inspector. Presently, the Inspectors in the
several districts are requiring that the Funeral Service be memorized in
order to qualify for a Certificate of Competence.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees that the
Funeral Service is one of the most important elements of our Masonic
Ritual and when it is performed with dignity, understan ding, and feeling it adds lustre to the image of Masonry and affords comfort to the
bereaved.
If this recommendation is adopted, the performan ce of this Service
will be limited to those who have a current certificate. (It must be renewed every three years.) What will happen when the relatives of a
deceased Brother request that a good friend of the family, who has given
the service in the past and who has given it well, officiate at the Funeral
only to have the request turned down because he does not have a current Certificate of Competence? Our present Code provides that the
Funeral Service may be read by any Mason. Those who memorize the
Service, and give a good presentati on are to be commended. But should
we discriminate against the Brother who reads the service, and perhaps
gives a better presentati on?
What about the increased bt11'den on the officers? Under the requirements proposed here, there certainly will not be as many "competen t"
Brethern as there are now. In some areas, on a given daiy, there may be
none.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that this
recommendation will make the rendering of this Service more difficult
than it is now and we move that further considerat ion be given this mat-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

57

ter by the Grand Lodge at the 1971 Communication and that the implementation of this program be postponed until that date.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes"
vote.
The motion by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes to
defer action until the 1971 Communication was not adopted.
Adopted.
RECOMME NDATION No. 7
CORNERST ONE EXPENSE

During the 1969 Annual Communication this Grand Lodge adopted
a policy making it permissive for the Grand Lodge to reimburse a Lodge
for its expenses in connection with a Cornersto ne Ceremony . I am
pleased to report that most of the requests for reimbursement have been
nominal. There were a limited few where the costs seemed to be somewhat in excess of the average. At most of these ceremonies, if properly
approache d, the general contractor will provide the cornerston e or
plaque. The school district will frequently provide the sealed conta 'ner, etc.
In order that the Lodges may have a basic guideline, it is my recommendation that a ceiling of $250.00 be set as the allowance for such
reimbursable expense and that the actual be reimbursed but it is hoped
that the maximum will not become the minimum.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendatioa number 7 is that the Grand Lodge place a maximum on the amount of reimbursable expenses of a Lodge in connection
with the laying of a cornerstone, the maximum to be $250.00. I so move
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes"
vote.
The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence in the recommendation of the Committe e on Policy and General Purposes.
Adopted.

STUDY OP COMMITTEES AND BOARDS

In 1964 a Special Grand Lodge Committee on Committee Structure
reported to the Grand Lodge. Their report included, among other comments, recommendations concerning the functions of committees, includ~
ing the consolidation of certain committees, the numbers of members in
some, appointment of members to others, tenure of chairmen, and
expenses for their operations.
Although the various ·recommendations were adopted, it is my considered judgment that, since the recommendations were confined to
Standing and Special Committees of the Grand Lodge only. there was
no consideration of other related issues.
Further, it is my belief that the titles of certain of our committees and
boards should be reviewed in the light of their actual functions, viz.,
Board of Library Commissioners. Masonic Homes Endowment Board.
Board of Control. etc.
Further, the importance of the insurance program which affects
all entities, all constituent Lodges and all Masons in California and
Hawaii should be undergirded by a strong and continuing Insurance
Committee. Its membership should be of knowledgeable men in the
insurance .fteld. Terms of membership on the committee should be staggered and they should serve as an aid to the administrative office.
Further, under provisions of our present regulations there are variations between the several corporate entities with respect to the authority
of the Grand Master to appoint or replace members of the various
boards. The relationship should be uniform between the Grand Master
and the Boards of the Masonic Homes, California ·M asonic Memorial
Temple, California Masonic Foundation or other similar corporate
entities which might develop in the future.
It is my recommendation, therefore, that a study of these matters
be made by a committee during the coming year and appropriate legislation, where necessary, be submitted at the 1971 Annual Communication
to accomplish the intent of this recommendation.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendation number nine suggests changes in the names of certain committees of the Grand Lodge. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes this recommendation should be referred to the
Committee on Code Revision and I so move.
No action was taken on the recommendation of the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes.
Adopted.

59

MASONIC BLOOD BANK

In his Message to Grand Lodge the then Grand Master, Eugene S.
Hopp. recommended that "it would be possible to establish a blood bank
for our entire Grand Jurisdiction which would enable Master Masons
and their families to receive blood almost aniywhere in the world, ..."
His recommendation, which was adopted by Grand Lodge, directed the
appointment of a special committee to study "how blood banks shall be
organized."
Grand Master Robert A. Crigler appointed a Special Committee on
Blood Bank and Sojourner Relief who reported to Grand Lodge at the
1969 Communication. The report stated, "We recommend that a Grand
Jurisdictional Masonic Blood Bank for California and Hawaii should be
established under the supervision of the Grand Master."
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommended "That
it shall be the policy of the Grand Lodge to move forward the establishment of a jurisdiction~wide blood bank or two statewide blood banks
and that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee for
study and such action as he may authorize." This was adopted by Grand
Lodge.
Recognizing that this is primarily an administrative matter, it be~
came apparent that discussions with all blood banks in California and
Hawaii would be constructive. Mrs. Bernice Hemphill, national blood
bank authority, has been helpful in our effort to coordinate the many
individual blood b$lnk programs which had previously been established
to satisfy the requirements of local areas. To assist also in claxifying
details of procedure, I solicited the aid of Past Grand Master Eugene
S. Hopp, Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., Dwight N.
Deane, Chairman of the San Francisco Masonic Blood Bank Account,
and numerous other knowledgeable persons. A jurisdiction-wide Masonic Blood Bank is in the process of being established. Some administrative details remain to be resolved.
It is my recommendation that when the incoming Grand Master
considers the proper organization is completed he be authorized to declare the "Grand Jurisdictional Masonic Blood Bank for California and
Hawaii" functioning and that the Lodges be advised of all necessary
details.
Adopted.

PROCLAMATION
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK-APRIL 20-24, 1970
In observing the Fiftieth Anniversary of the founding of Public
Schools Week, we pledge our renewed interest and rededication of our
efforts toward the support of our public schools in California and Hawaii.
We firmly believe that this educational process is the finest example of
the kind of institution a true democracy demands and needs.
We should also renew our feeling of deep appreciation to the dedicated men and women who bear the responsibility of carrying out the
administration of education in our schools.
We realize that the State and Nation prosper in direct proportion
to the excellence and strength of the public schools and that only through
a strong Public School System can the ideals of freedom, the continuance
of the democratic process and the maintenance of free enterprise be
accomplished.
I. therefore, proclaim the week of April 20 through 24, 1970, to be
the Fiftieth Annual Public Schools Week and the theme of this annual
event to be "The Public Schools-Information-Education-Responsf..
bility." I further direct:
That all Constituent Lodges in California and Hawaii actively participate in an appropriate Public Schools Program.
That the suggestions offered by the Public School Committee be
followed whenever possible.
That no Lodge programs or meetings be held during this period for
purposes other than this Observance, with the exception of Stated
Meetings.
That publicity be given Public Schools Week in the Trestleboard of
the Constituent Lodges.
That this Proclamation be read at each of the Stated Meetings for
March and April.
Dated: February 10, 1970
Fraternally,
CHESTER R. MACPHEE
Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

GRAND MA.STER

PROCLAMATION
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
The warm heart of Freemasonry is enshrined by three jewels of
everlasting beauty-faith, hope and charity-"but the greatest of these
is charity." The word "charity" as used in the Bible and by Masons
means more than just giving. It means loving one another. This is
particularly applicable to Masons "who are linked together by an indissoluble chain of sincere affection."
Let us consider 1970 as the start of a new decade of renewed devotion to the tenets of our beloved craft. Let us take a giant step toward
charity!
To assist those placed in our care by divine providence is a priceless
privilege. Each of us should be proud of the parts we play in the maintenance and operation of the homes for our older folks at Union City and
our children at Covina.
Each year the Masons in California and Hawaii tangibly demonstrate, through their contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment
Fund, their belief in the principles of love and relief. Now is the time
for all of us to help! Help by contributing generously and help by
encouraging your Brothers to contribute. Such support is essential.
Our goal is to develop an Endowment Fund large enough to provide
sufficient income to cover the operating costs of our two wonderful
homes. I am confident that this year-"The Year of a Million Smiles"will exceed even our previous efforts. This is your opportunity for the
exercise of Masonic Responsibility.
I hereby proclaim the month of May, 1970, to be Masonic Homes
Endowment Month and direct that this proclamation be read in each
Lodge at its Stated Meetings of April and May. 1970. or that a copy
be sent to each member of the Lodge.
Dated: February 27, 1970
CHESTER R. MACPHEE
Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

In this year, 1970, the Constitution of the United States is the olde~t
Charter of republican government in existence. It is no accident that it
has survived these many years. The men who met in Philadelphia during
those trying days of 1787 were familial'. with world history: they had
first~hand information of tyrannical government: they were aware of
the weaknesses in the Confederation: and they knew they were meeting
to solve these problems without 'Compromising the rights of free men.
That they succeeded so well is self~evident after these many years of
success.
All citizens of the United States of America recognize the Constitu~
tion of the United States as the foundation of our governmental system.
Unfortunately. too many Americans have never read this important
document· and too few have studied it meaningfully.
One ~f the most distressing indications of spiritual sickness in
America is the spectacle of the gradual lack of Patriotism. There is a
poverty among us with which we are not successfully coping-a poverty
of patriotism, yet, there are men who do seek to preserve our heritage.
do proud men who defend a simple faith. My country, right or wrong.
They do a great work. Thank God the Masonic Fraternity is in the
forefront and stands out as one of the great leaders in this task. To the
credit of our Fraternity it must be said that Masonry has always advo~
cated the highest ideals of patriotism.
In this spirit and this end, I proclaim the Month of September 1970,
to be Constitution Observance Month and direct that every constituent
Lodge in California and Hawaii, participate in an appropriate ~bserv~
ance program, and wherever feasible, to plan an open community ob~
servance which includes other organized groups both Masonic and non~
Masonic.
I further direct that this proclamation be read at the Stated Meeting
next following its receipt and again at the Stated Meeting for September,
and wherever possible, it shall be reprinted in the Lodge bulletin.
Dated: April 6, 1970

Sincerely and Fraternally,
CHESTER R. MACPHEE

Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

Temple and the California Masonic Foundation. Each report is a com~
plete financial record of its individual corporate activity. They represent

of the audit firm, Touche Ross & Co .• I was particularly impressed with
the thoroughness of the work of the new auditors. Documents, invoices

office.

expenditures for both administrative and office expenses, and statement
of general expenses, are both well within the amounts budgeted. In the
statement of appropriations the Grand Master was requested to approve

recul'lring.
My sincere thanks and appreciation are expressed to our Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Chester R. MacPhee. His dedication to
Freemasonry is indeed an inspiration for all Masons to emulate. It was
a genuine pleasure to work closely with Brother MacPhee and our fine
cooperative office staff. My thanks and appreciation to you, my Brethren,
for the privilege and opportunity of serving the Grand Lodge.
RespectfuUy submitted,
PAUL A. PFLUEGER, Grand Treasurer

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In presenting my tenth annual report, in accordance with requirements of our law, I do so with the satisfying knowledge that this iyear
has been one of great progress and accomplishment for our fraternity
in California. Masonry in this jurisdiction will enter the new Masonic
year with increased strength and a continuity of enthusiasm.
The confidence in this forward surging year of action is re8ected
in the energetic support through words and actions of Grand Lodge and
Lodge officers, Inspectors, committeemen and the general membership.
The many program innovations; the expansion of our programs of Masonic information, Masonic education and Masonic responsibility; the
publication of the "mini-lectures": and the emphasis on the making of
better Masons out of members have all contributed to the rekindling of
the spark and light of true Masonic effort.
Brethren who have been members for years, and many new Masons,
demonstrate interest, dedication and the desire to learn. A continuation
and expansion of the programs so ably implemented this year will go far
in the future, not only to make better Masons of our present members
but to attract men to the fraternity who will make good Masons.
Your Grand Lodge staff has had an unusually busy year. Early and
late hours have been worked but all of it has been performed with the
desire to cooperate and the knowledge that such special effort is part of
the overall requirement in a year of action. All of us appreciate our fine
staff and its continued dedication in performing beyond the requirements of duty. Being a part of this "winning team" is a joy.
FUNDS RECEIVED

The Grand T,reasurer's Report again re8ects the recording of all
moneys received and credited to the various accounts under his direction for each entity.
The financial statements this year were audited by Touche Ross &
Co. The statements will be distributed with the advance reports.
Details of disbursements by Grand Lodge during the year have been
made available to and reviewed by the Grand Lodge Committee on
Finance, as required by our law. Supporting books, papers and vouchers
are on file in the accounting office.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE.
ACCOUNTING RECORDS

Each year for the past few years your Grand Secretary has been
pleased to report improvements and simplifkation in our accounting
procedures. The convenience and practicability of a centralized ac~
counting program for all Grand Lodge entities continues to confirm the
economy of such a program. The "team effort" on the part of Lodge
officers, Inspectors and our loyal office staff, has made this another year
of progress in 1"ecord keeping.
In accordance with a recommendation made at the last communica~
tion, a Special In~Depth Study Committee this year has reviewed in
detail the mechanics of your administrative office. The committee's
report will be presented during this communication.
1969TAxLAw
The California State Legislature last year adopted a law which
affects us as a fraternal group. A number of conferences were held
with the State Franchise Tax Board. As a result, a program was de~
veloped to assist all Lodges in completing and filing the forms re~
quired by the new law. Under the arrangements made the Grand Sec~
retary was permitted to make a single filing to answer certain questions
applicable to all Lodges. We express our appreciation to those dedicated
Brethren, Brothers Raymond B. Haizlip, Ivan Crase and Benjamin L.
Susman, who served as a Special Committee on Tax Study at the re~
quest of the Grand Master in analyzing the requirements of this tech~
nical problem.

GRAND LODGE. OP CALIFORNIA

National Grand Lodge of Denmark. It is not possible to adequately
describe that beautiful structure. Suffice it to say that it symbolizes
Masonry at its best.
I felt particularly honored to have been personally conducted through
the Temple by Brother Thaysen as it was his wedding day. He was
most gracious in showing me the Temple and also took additional time
to drive me to many points of interest in Copenhagen. I was most for~
tunate to have this wonderful Masonic experience.
LIBRARY AND MUSE.UM

The Chairman of the Board of Library Commissioners will give a
report of its activities for the year. As Grand Librarian, I have been
privileged to work closely with the fine, dedicated group of Masons
who comprise the Board and the volunteer staff which keeps the
facility open to the public. On some occasions, when programs or con~
certs were held in the Temple, the staff has had the library open in the
evening. We have had many reports from visitors expressing apprecia~
tion for the courtesies extended to them. This report would not be com~
plete without a special thank you to each of these Brethren for his con~
tinued dedication.
My special appreciation goes to all the Grand Lodge officers, In~
spectors, committeemen and the officers of our Lodges for their con~
tinued cooperation. To our dedicated staff my sincere thanks for another
year of cooperative effort.

VE.TE.RAN BUTTONS

Presentations of Veteran Buttons to eligible members continue to
increase. We are pleased that so many of our members continue to enjoy
good health and are reaching this landmark in Masonry. It would ap~
pear that for at least the next seven or eight years we will have the sat~
isfaction of presenting annually as many or more of these awards to
veteran Masons as were presented this year. (See Exhibit D.)
SECRET ARIES AssocIATIONS

Continuing interest is reflected by Lodge Secretaries, Officers and
Inspectors in these voluntary associations throughout the State. N um er~
ous meetings have been held. Much of real value has been gained, both
by the constituent Lodges and the Grand Lodge office, through the
results of these meetings. We are pleased that the Brethren have

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:
With five of its seven members present on Saturday morning.
October 10, 1970, your Committee on By-Laws began its Teview of the
matters referred to it. We were sorry that the Chairman of the Committee was not able to be present due to illness.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

85

Your Committee checked and rechecked one hundred twenty-one
changes made by constituent Lodges. to wit: ninety-nine changes in
by-laws and twenty-two changes in place of meeting. All of the reviewed amendments and resolutions were found to be in order. We
wish to commend the officers of the Lodges who carefully followed our
Masonic Code. and also the staff in the Grand Secretary's office for their
efficiency and diligence _in guiding those who needed assistance in
properly adopting the changes.
Exhibit B of the Grand Secretary's preliminary report, to which
members of the Grand Lodge may refer, sets forth one hundred twenty
of the changes. The one change, approved by the Grand Master after
said preliminary report was sent to the printer, was found to be in order
and your Committee moves that it be included in the Grand Secretary's
final report. Said change is :
Change date of stated meeting: Anchor Lodge No. 273.
In past reports your Committee has suggested that the Lodges review
Article X of their By-Laws which sets the maximum authority of the
Charity Committee of the Lodge during the interval between Stated
Meetings. In many cases the maximum amount is too low in view of
the times. This year eight Lodges increased the authority of their
charity committees and we commend them for doing so. We again
suggest to Lodge officers that Article X of your Lodge By-Laws be
reviewed to ascertain that the the authority of the Charity Committee
is realistic.
Even though all of the amendments reviewed were approved, your
Committee found tha( the matter of designating holidays in the By-Laws
remains troublesome. Article Ill of the Uniform Code of By-Laws,
which permits exceptions to the regular date of the Stated Meetings of
a Lodge, limits the exceptions to legal holidays and during the Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge.
With regard to legal holidays, these should be specifkally named
so that there will be no misunderstanding as to whether a particular
day is or is not a holiday. Further, the particular legal holiday should be
identified by NAME and NOT by date: that is, New Year's Day is
preferable to January 1 and Independence Day is preferable to July 4,
because such description leaves no doubt that the exception applies
when these days are celebrated on Monday in a year when January 1
or July 4 falls on a Sunday.
Particular attention should be paid to this point of designation of
holidays, and most especially for Monday night Lodges, because commencing this coming year of 1971, by action of Congress, several holidays will be celebrated on Monday even though they fall on another
day of the week.
Also, a Lodge should provide for an alternate date in case its Stated
Meeting falls during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. While

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

only those Lodges whose Stated Meeting is during the second week of
the month are affected, the date of any Annual Communication may be
changed for any year, so the contingency should be provided for.
In reviewing the resolutions having to do with the change of meeting
place by various Lodges, your Committee found that in several cases a
Lodge moved to a new location without following the formal procedures
set forth in the California Masonic Code, and when the Lodge notified
Grand Lodge it was meeting at a new location, such notice was the first
knowledge that Grand Lodge would have of a move having taken place.
Thereafter, the Lodge would have to take the necessary procedural
steps that it should have completed prior to any move. The procedure
for changing the meeting place of a Lodge is set forth in California
Masonic Code Section 372. We would like to impress upon all the
officers in attendance here that they should check the Masonic Code
and By-Laws of their respective Lodges before making any changes
in meeting places, so that the required formalities will be completed
before the move, rather than afterward.
Most Worshipful . we move that Grand Lodge approve the amendments and resolutions listed in Exhibit B of the Grand Secretary's report
distributed at this Communication, with the addition hereinabove
specified, and the report be adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
ALDEN FULKERSON, SR., Chairman

TRIAL RECORD No. 1973
The accused, a member of Barstow Lodge No. 682, was arrested
and charged with three counts of indecent exposure occurring on three
different occasions. He plead nolo contende re. He immediately submitted himself to a psychiatric clinic for treatmen t. Pronoun cement of
judgmen t was withheld and he was placed on three years probatio n on
condition that he continue psychiatric or psychological care or counseling. Charges were filed in the Lodge for the three counts and for
unmasonic conduct. The accused plead not guilty but at this trial admitted the acts charged. He presente d the report of the probatio n officer
and letters from doctors which showed cooperat ion and progress on the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

89

paTt of the accused and indicated eventual successful treatment. The
accused was found guilty of the charges and of unmasonic conduct and
the penalty was fixed at repriman d.
The procedur e was in all ways correct. Your Committee, however,
feels that in view of the evidence and the seriousness of the charges,
and the fact that the accused is not cured and that treatmen t is continuing, that the penalty should be raised to suspension, thereby leaving
to the Lodge the determination of the question as to when the accused
is rehabilit ated and entitled to be restored to the rights and privileges
of Masonry .
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOL VED that the findings of the commission in Trial Record
No. 1973 be approved but that the penalty be raised to suspensi on and
that the accused be suspende d from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry .
Adopted .
TRIAL RECORD No. 1978
A member of Heritage Lodge No. 764 made application for deg:rees
on Septemb er 9, 1963. His application concealed the information that in
1944 and thereafte r he served time in prisons of this State following
his conviction of a felony and, accordingly. charges were initiated
against him for unmasonic conduct.
The member defended on the ground that in 1961 he received a
pardon from the Govemo r and that his record was expunge d for all
purposes. The pardon was for reasons other than that the member did
not commit the offense.
The Lodge found the member guilty of all specifications and imposed
the penalty of suspension. On review of this record, your Committee,
although impressed by the sincerity of the recommendation of the Trial
Commissioners that the penalty not be increased, is bound by Section
513, C.M.C .. which forbids eligibility to apply for the degrees to a person
who has been convicted of a felony without being pardone d for the
reason that he did not commit the offense. We accordin gly are of the
opinion that the penalty should be raised to expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption :
RESOL VED, That the findings of the Trial Master in Record No.
1978 be approved but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that
the member be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry .
Adopted .

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.. F. & A. M. of California:
At the time of the formulation of this report, there was no reason to
expect that it would be written and delivered to this Grand Lodge by
any other than the late Very Worshipful Harold N. Richards. Such,
however, was not to be the case. The Supreme Architect of the Universe
decreed higher service for our Brother, and on the evening of Wednesday, August 12, 1970, Brother Hal Richards put aside the working tools
of this earthly life and went to labor in that Lodge which no time can
close.
The loss of this very dedicated Mason is keenly felt by all, but even
in our sorrowing we may all rejoice in the memory of the many accomplishments of this wonderful man, and the many gifts of love and devotion which he gave to us all.
I shall not elaborate upon our personal friendship, for his precious
gift of understanding, his invaluable assistance, and his deep spkitual
inspiration will live on in the hearts and minds of us all, and with the
passing of the years, we shall all remember with thanksgiving, the earthly
sojourn of our beloved Brother: the Very Worshipful Harold N.
Richards, Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of California.
To his memory is dedicated this report.
It is the requirement of the California Masonic Code, that it shall be
the duty of the Grand Lecturer, at each Annual Communicati~n of the
Grand Lodge, to render a full and detailed account of his services and
activities during the year, and to set forth therein, a complete report of
the condition of the Lodges within the Jurisdiction. Due to the extreme
brevity of my tenure in this office, I beg your forebearance and understanding as I endeavor to comply with those requirements in a manner
consistent with that tradition of excellence established by my worthy
predecessors.
RITUAL

Over the past 35 years, there has been developed within this Grand
Jurisdiction, an instru<:tional system designed to further uniformity of

107

our Ritual, from the Grand Lecturer, to the Assistant Grand Lecturers
and Inspectors, to the Officers and Brethren of the several Chartered
Lodges. Your Grand Lecturer is charged with the responsibility of administering this system which has established and maintains California
Freemasonry preeminent among fraternal organizations.
The past year has seen the light of understanding brought to many
areas of misinterpretation, and further inroads are being made into those
stubborn areas of resistance to total conformity. TowMd this end was
directed the following activities:
The annual meeting of the Ritual Committee was held in Long Beach
on December 5th to 7th, 1969 to consider many matters of Ritual. administration and duties and responsibilities of the Assistant Grand Lecturers
and Inspectors. This meeting was conducted by the late Harold N.
Richards, and aided materially in the presence and counsel of Past Grand
Lecturer, Very Worshipful Donald G. Campbell. Prominent among
those matters discussed were, Handbook for Candidates Coaches,
Offl~ers Monitor, Installation Service, Masonic Funeral Service, Inspectors Handbook Material, Protocol and Lodge room facilities and practices. Questions presented to the Grand Lecturer were discussed, and
all were satisfactorily resolved before adjournment. This meeting was
not only productive and stimulating, but the results of it were particularly
beneficial to all members of the Craft.
The Ritual Committee also held meetings at each of the six Divisional
Conferences, and a special meeting was held at San Clemente in the
month of February. Present at this meeting were all members of the
Grand Lodge elective line, as well as several members of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility.
Each meeting of the Ritual Committee this year has greatly added to
the understanding and harmony among its members, thereby creating an
atmosphere of complete cooperation within our instructional chain.
During the spring months the Inspectors held their Annual Conferences as follows:
Division 1 at Santa Rosa, April 17th to 19th, conducted by Worshipful Bertram C. von Konsky.
Division 2 at Lake Tahoe, June 19th to 21st, conducted by Worshipful Edward E. Seagle.
Division 3 at Los Gatos, March 20th to 22nd, conducted by Worshipful Ulysses G. Patropulos
Division i at Twain Harte, June 5th to 7th, conducted by Worshipful
Wallace H. Fiske.
Division 5 at San Diego, May 15th to 17th, conducted by Worshipful
Burton Meyer, Jr.

Division 6 at Pomona, February 27th to March 1st, conducted by

The Grand Lecturer's School of Instruction for the Inspectors was
held last Saturday, October 10th, in the California Masonic Memorial
Temple. This session was attended by all members of the Ritual Committee, and approximately 180 Inspectors. The Ritual and Lectures were
very ably exemplified by representative Inspectors of the various Divisions.
Regular schools of instruction for the Inspectors were held in each of
the Divisions by the Assistant Grand Lecturers, some being held as
often as nine times yearly.
The California Masonic Code, Section 161. sets forth the duties of
the Inspector: that of conducting regular schools of instruction for the
Lodge Officers. with a minimum requirement of covering the work at
least twice yearly. Some of the Inspectors have deemed it necessary in
some cases to hold individual schools in certain areas.

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

Schools of Instruction for the Inspectors and Officers Coaches of the
Hawaiian Lodges were conducted this year by our late Grand Lecturer,
Harold N. Richards. From his reports it is quite obvious that the light
of Masonry continues to burn brightly among the several Lodges and
the Brethren of our sister state. Brother Hal was very generous in his
pra.ise ~f the Hawaiian area Inspectors for their splendid leadership, and
their tireless efforts on behalf of Freemasonry. He also voiced great
admiration for the manner in which the work was being conducted in the
Islands, and for the compelling friendship of these warm and wonderful
Masons in the 50th State.
LoDGE ACTIVITIES

A study of the Inspectors Annual Reports brought to light a number
of facts which I felt were quite pertinent in reporting the condition of the
Lodges within the Jurisdiction. It is apparent that new records were
established this year in our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund Drive
with a g'reater number of our members making contributions toward th~
largest total contribution ever recorded. Of this we may be rightfully
proud.
From these reports, it would seem that the needs of the community
are being fllled by the Lodges, and that Masonry is advancing in all
Districts.
Programs of Public School and Constitution Observance were either
padicipated in, or conducted by, practically all of the Lodges this past
year. These activities will, of course, be reported upon in greater depth
by those Grand Lodge Committees involved.
To that portion of the reports concerning Lodge growth, leadership
and participation, my attention was especially directed, for it is in this
area where signs of trouble are being clearly evidenced.
In a large number of our Lodges, membership is on the decline. Areas

110

111

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of heavy population are rapidly becoming commercialized, thereby forcing the younger men of the community to seek suburbanization. Many
of our Temples are now in areas completely surrounded by an undesirable element and, in some cases, personal safety is risked by one's presence in the area after nightfall. In other areas we find a growing apathy
on the part of Lodge members concerning Lodge attendance and support
of Lodge activities.
A great number of the Lodges are reporting greatly increased diffi..
culty in finding new officer material. In most cases the younger members
seem completely disinterested in serving as Lodge officers, and more and
more often we are seeing Past Masters being forced to fill these positions
in an effort to bolster a sagging line.
Prominent among the reasons stated for unwillingness to serve is that
too great an amount of time is required to go through the chairs: extra
time is being required to compete in the business world: family ties are
demanding added time and attention, and other social commitments do
not permit the freedom of choice as in years past.
Recognizing the foregoing as valid reasons for reluctance of these
men to serve their Lodges and become active members, I would recommend that those Lodges which are experiencing this difficulty give very
serious consideration to filling the lower stations on a one year appointive
basis, with the progressive line commencing no lower than the Senior
Deacon's Station. This would undoubtedly create certain problems in
qualifying these one year appointees, but I feel that the advantages to
be gained in renewed interest would far outweigh any inconvenience
caused.

to all. Each year has brought the Inspectors many added duties and

bears the responsibility for all arrangements at Grand Lodge Ceremonies,

The ultimate in devotion to duty as an Inspector is revealed in the
story of Worshipful Alexander Duncan, who served as Inspector of District 101 from October 9, 1945, to his retirement in January 1968. In midyear 1970, his successor, Alfred Earl Pollard, found it necessary to move
from the State, leaving the Inspectorship of District 101 vacant. Brother
Alex, in the finest tradition of the Inspectoral Corps, resumed the duties
of Inspector and, while thus engaged, was stricken with a heart attack
and passed away just three weeks ago today.

INSPECTORS MANUAL

Not the least among the many outstanding contributions of our late
Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful Harold N. Richards, is the longawaited and very welcome Inspectors Manual. This very comprehensive
guide for the Inspectors is truly a magnificent piece of work and is just
one more token of the great love of this wonderful Mason for his Brethren. It was his desire that the Inspectors of this Jurisdiction be given
this valuable working tool, and to this ideal he devoted his time and
talents unsparingly. This manual, which was commenced by Brother
Hal in 1966, was placed in the hands of the Inspectors in February, 1970
and even in the short time it has been in use it is quite evident that it will
be most invaluable to the Inspector in the discharge of his duties.

FUNERAL SERVICE

To Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee, I offer my deep appreciation
for the many wonderful opportunities which he has granted me. I shall
be forever grateful for his inspiration and guidance throughout this year
and my heart will warm at the memory of having served with this truly
great man of Masonry.
To the Grand Secretary and his wonderful staff, my personal thanks
for their many courtesies and their warm friendship. Without their assistance I could not have done those things required of me.
And finally, my Brethren, to you for your many expressions of good
will, for your very generous offers of support and for the opportunity of
serving you in Masonry, my very deepest gratitude and my humble
prayer that God may grant to us all many additional years of Masonic
association.
Respectfully submitted,
H. DOUGLAS LEMONS, Grand Lecturer

One of the problems discussed at the December 1969 Ritual Committee meeting was our 'Masonic Funeral Service. The then Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful Harold N. Richards, presented to the Committee
a statement from the Grand Master in which he voiced grave concern
at the manner in which our Masonic Funerals were being conducted. He
further directed that a system be developed by the 1Ritual Committee
whereby only those who are well qualified and proficient would be permitted to conduct the Funeral Service.
His directive has now been complied with, and the program which
was developed will require all who intend to conduct Masonic Funerals
to appear before the Inspector of his District and there demonstrate that
they are qualified and proficient in the Funeral Lecture and its delivery.
The Inspector, upon being satisfied of their qualification, will notify the
Grand Secretary's Office who will cause to be issued a Grand Lodge
Certificate attesting to the fact that the bearer is well qualified in the
Funeral Lecture. This Certificate, signed by the Grand Master, and
counter-signed by the Inspector of the District, will permit the recipient
to conduct the Masonic Funeral Service for a period of three years following its issuance. The Inspector will see that all Masters in his area
are provided a current list of those qualified and the Grand Secretary's
Office will notify well in advance of its expiration date. This program is
presently under implementation and should become fully operational by
year's end. Thanks are due the Grand Master for his astuteness in recognizing the extreme gravity of this situation and for his unrelenting
determination to remove this blemish from the face of Masonry.
CONCLUSION

From this point my performance, and that of the Ritual Committee,
can only be judged by service rendered to the Fraternity and to you, the
Brethren of California Freemasonry. It is my .6rm resolve as Grand Lecturer that I shall constantly endeavor to maintain the excellence established by my worthy predecessors. That no deviation from our established Ritual will be tolerated but, rather, that even g,reater effort will be
expended in teaching the Ritual as it has existed from time immemorial.
I am sure that the Brethren here assembled will join me in recognizing
those great men who have given so unselfishly of their time and talents
in establishing and maintaining the dignity and high purpose of this office: Our three living Past Grand Lecturers: Most Worshipful Leslie E.

FINANCIAL
The operation of our Homes is truly big business. With over four
hundred men, women and children under our loving care, with housing,
feeding. clothing, medical and hospital services to supply, we have a
major operation. For proper investigation and medical examination
of applicants, we have added expense. To give our guests and children
an expanded life rather than a confining life and to account for and
administer the gifts and trusts which make this possible, demands a
proper accounting of our trusteeship.
To accomplish this accounting and to properly budget expense
against income, the Budget and Accounting Committee was appointed.
Trustees Mitchell, Mize, Price, Revitt and Smith, working closely with
the Secretary, Edward H. Siems, and his accounting staff, and ably
assisted by Assistant Treasurer Linsk, who is a Certifled Public Account, as consultant, have evolved accounting practices and account

116

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

designations which will clearly show to the Craft where their money
goes and will enable the Superintendents to better control their expendi·
tures, getting more rather than less for our guests out of the dollar
spent on their behalf. Our thanks go to this able group who have given
unstintingly of their time and business talent.
It should be noted by all of the members of the Grand Lodge that
the low per capita charge on our lodges is a direct result of the success
in the lodges of the Endowment Fund each year and the accompanying
increase in gifts and bequests going to the support of our Homes. The
present per capita supplies less than fifteen percent ( 15%) of the cost
of operation of the Homes. None of the cost of redevelopment now or
forseeably in the future is a charge on our lodges. Generous and dedicated Masons and their families have and are making this all possible.
Our thanks to you for your dedication to the endowment principle and
to the Endowment Committee and the lnspectoral Corps for keeping
you on your toes. The continuance of the love of giving shares the
heart of Masonry with those of our own most in need of comfort and
consolation.
By reason of this continued generosity and the businesslike administration of our Homes we anticipate no change in the per capita and
therefore recommend the continuance of $1.00 per member for the support of the Homes.

COVINA
The present-day story of Covina is, of course, the story of Covina
redevelopment. Chronologically and operatively, the progress of redevelopment is divided into steps.
Step I has now been completed. Although delayed by strikes which
have affected the whole building industry, our contractor, Brother Leonard Fullmer, Jr. of Arcadia Lodge No. 547, delivered the project on
August 3, 1970 and Notice of Completion was flied by Trustee Myron
E. Smith on August 10th. Final cost under the contract was $765,787.67,
an increase of only $8,737.67 over the initial bid. All of the increase resulted from decisions of the Board to incorporate additional needed work
in this contract rather than deferring it. Our t"elations with Brother
Fullmer reflected his deep desire of "who best can work and best agree.''
The beauty, style, utility and arrangement of the cottages also reftect the
dedication of our Master Plan Architect, A. Quincy Jones, and his associates, particularly Brother William A. Laffin of Cahuenga Lodge No.
513, in general charge of the project.
Even as the former dormitories had seen their day, so the furnishings required replacement. Under the guidance of the Covina Redevelopment Committee with its members, Trustees Campbell, Head and Smith,
with invaluable assistance given by Robert H. Mason, Past Master of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

117

Harding Lodge No. 584, and with full expression of the children's needs
and desires interpreted by Superintendent Blaine and Mrs. Blaine, the
new cottages have been completely carpeted, draped and furnished.
Thanks go to John Biren, Past Master of Ionic Lodge No. 520 and
Allen Price, member of Home Lodge No. 721, who were low bidders
on carpeting and drapes respectively, saving thousands of dollars for
the Homes.
Our thanks go to the Westerners of Twentieth Century Fox, to the

who supplied refrigerators, washers and dryers for each cottage, and to

receiving.
Step II, just at completion, consisted of the demolition of the sixtyyear-old dormitories, site development, including new perimeter roadway, parking areas for visitors, a new picnic area and the moving of the
displaced baseball and tennis facilities from the cottage site to the general ·recreation area. The cost of this Step II work has been covered by
money set aside in Covina Reserve and from the Meserve Trust Fund
which was specifically designated by the donor, Alida 0. Meserve, to
be used for athletic and recreational facilities for the children of Covina.
Total cost of demolition and of these improvements in Step II will be
approximately $285,000.
Step III envisages the replacement of the remaining original buildings, the Administration Building and the Infirmary with a new Community Center. Basic layouts were presented to the Board at its September meeting and the architect was instructed to proceed with drawings which should lead to construction, commencing in the spring of
1971.
With the steady progress thus made, the Home at Covina should,
before the close of 1971, stand as the finest home for children and
young people in the Masonic world. Those of you who have the opportunity should plan to spend part of the time you expect to have in
Disneyland making a detour to see this, our own "Magic Kingdom.''
We are proud, because it bespeaks the quality of our young people,
to announce a greater attendance at college and university under our
scholarship program than ever before. You are not only assisting our
new graduates but extending a helping hand to t'eturning service graduates who recognize the value of education. All of this aid in education
comes from gifts made to the Student Aid and Scholarship Fund. This
fund also supplies educational assistance and tutoring to the members
of our Home Family relieving the operating funds of this expense.
We urge you to read the Superintendent's report to get the full
impact of the work you are doing at Covina.

DECO TO
After declining for several years. the population at our Home at
Decoto has risen steadily to approximately 350 men and women. At
the same time. the age at admission has continued to rise. With the
relaxation of the physical requirements for admission reported to you
at the 1969 Communication, a greater proportion of space is necessarily
allocated to those unable to fully care for their own needs. To solve this
problem. alterations have been made in the South Wing to comfortably
house our married couples and Adams Hall has been given over to those
in the so.-called non-ambulatory category. This means that we have actually three groups of guests: those fully capable of self care. those
able to move about with mechanical aids such as cane. walkers or wheelchairs, and those largely or totally confined to bed care by reason of
age or physical condition.
This changing, ever older population was never contemplated by
our predecessors when the Home was located in its present setting.
Recognizing the changing needs, the Decoto Redevelopment Committee
was appointed consisting of all Trustees near Decoto. After its report
made at the July meeting and several hours of discussion. a Steering
Committee, Chairman Alfred W. Odle with Trustees Dayton, Price
and Smith brought a final report for action to the September meeting.
The report is of such importance that we have had it printed as a supplement to this report. The truths set forth, the obligations so eloquently
expounded and the opportunities for Masonic service so gloriously
shown make it "must reading" for you, your officers and the Craft. We
cannot too strongly urge your serious and understanding study of it.
The decision of Trustee Laurence E. Dayton, P.G.M., to retire from
the Board does not mean that we will lose his wise counsel and inspirational view of Masonry. He has promised to be available for special
projects and we hope to use his talents. His service has been above the
call of duty and as he devotes more time to his old craft of writing, we
wish him well.
Trustee Guy B. Mize, P.G.M., has announced his inability for personal reasons to continue his service. As a member of the Budget and
Accounting Committee and the Real Estate Committee, as well as ably
representing the Board as Chairman of the Employee's Pension Plan or
Retirement Committee, he has given generously of his time. Regretting
his decision, we wish for him a well deserved rest.
Each year we extoll the virtues of our able Secretary, M.W. Edward
H. Siems. Grand Secretary, and his staff. They continue to merit our
gratitude and the satisfaction which comes of work well done. In like
manner, Maria Workman and Martha Quick give more than a full
measure of devotion to their tasks. Superintendent James C. Blaine at
Covina continues to be a devoted father to his Covina family.

DECOTO REDEVELOPMENT

A Reaffirmation of Masonic Relief
Relief is central to Freemasonry. The obligation, whether of the
individual or the lodge, is primary. not contingent upon what others may
or may not do.
"To relieve the distressed," we are told, "is a duty incumbent upon
all men, but particularly on Masons. To soothe the unhappy. to sympathize with their misfortunes. to compassionate their miseries, and to restore peace to their troubled minds is the great aim we have in view."
Within these broad dimensions lie the whole range of charitable acts,
which are not limited to the relief of poverty.
When the Home for the Aged was established. indigency was the
principal need to be served. The alternatives for the individual Mason
and his wife or widow were to go to the county poorhouse or depend
upon the uncertain bounty of friends. In the intervening years, changes
have occurred which have an important bearing upon the kind of service
the Masonic Homes of California should render its elderly. Social Security, pension plans in government and private industry, old age public

120

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

assistance, and the more recently inaugurated Medicare program have
only partially reduced the financial hazards of old age.
Additionally, care in a Masonic setting for those with health problems has emerged as a major contemporary need. Until we liberalized
our admission policy to include the non-ambulatory, it was necessary to
turn away for physical reasons many who deserved our help. We may
reasonably foresee that the ratio of non-ambulatory and nursing home
cases to ambulatory will increase for us as it has elsewhere.
The demands raise the question as to the kind of facility required,
and the type of site suitable for the purpose. We must have a facility designed in terms of structure and equipment to provide the multiple services needed to meet the physical, social, and medical needs of our
residents.
Our present facility at Decoto was well planned and situated for its
early purpose. Although geared to the past, it has served adequately
until more recent years. It is the opinion of the Trustees that it will not
be readily adaptable to the changing requirements of the future. Any
conversion toward modernization is not practical or feasible. Alterations,
repairs, and maintenance are becoming increasingly costly because of the
ravages of time and inflation. Changing building code requirements
relating to safety become increasingly expensive and more difficult to
meet. The design and layout coupled with the rolling and undulating
terrain are no longer suitable to the ambulations of our residents, within
the home or around the outdoor areas. The average age of our guests
has increased steadily during the past ten years and there is every
indication, because of medical science, that the median will continue to
rise. It becomes increasingly obvious that those of advancing age should
move about laterally as much as possible with a minimum use of steps,
stairways, and ramps. They are now required to traverse many different
levels in walking from their rooms to dining room and to recreational
areas, thus continually exposed to the possibility of accident.
Obsolescence, both functional and economic, together with physical
deterioration, is depreciating our Decoto facility at an accelerating rate.
Decoto lacks the requisite ingredients the Fraternity desires to meet
future needs in the care of its elderly brethren, their wives and widows
in light of changing conditions. Of increasing importance is the responsibility on California Freemasonry to make their declining years as
meaningful and viable as possible.
Terrain is hilly. It restricts all outdoor activities, except for a hardy
few and thus prevents our guests from enjoying such activities as walking, croquet, lawn bowling, gardening, or even basking in the sun.
The increasing encroachment of heavy industry militates against the
present site. There are many particularly obnoxious days as a result.
It is obvious that our multi-story complex on hilly terrain in an area

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

121

becoming industrialized is definitely not the answer. It does not and
will not meet the requirements of those needing a protective environment because of approaching or advanced infirmity.
Clearly we must emerge from an institutional-type complex which
is gradually but inexorably becoming obsolete. It has served its purpose
and served it well. It has furnished the basic requirements of food and
shelter and has, for many years, provided a pleasant community fot
those who have sought its sanctuary. We must begin now to take the
first steps in a journey of a thousand days which will lead toward a more
gratifying, gracious, and happier way of life for those who are in the
long twilight of their years.
The solution is a one-story facility on level ground-a modern home
-truly a home in every respect-not just an institution. Our home must
provide cheerful living-an environmental area conducive to maximum
outdoor enjoyment within a framework having ease of accommodation
to the changing needs of the elderly. It must be homey yet efficiently
functional. The locale must be in proximity to necessary medical facilities, shopping areas, and other conveniences for our residents. The site
must be of sufficient size to provide for necessary future expansion.
Steps are being taken by your Board of Trustees to study and survey
available sites in the Bay area so that within the coming year a suitable
site may be acquired. Meantime, plans are being formulated for the
orderly development of such a site when acquired.
We say again: "To relieve the distressed is duty incumbent upon
all men, but particularly on Masons. To soothe the unhappy, to sympathize with their .misfortunes, to compassionate their miseries, and to
restore peace to their troubled minds is the great aim we have in view."
Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth! How appropriate that our keystone is Relief, flanked and supported by the other two cardinal principles.
Our Fraternity needs and calls for the best in man and mankind.
It calls for Relief-True Relief nurtured by Brotherly Love.
Board of Trustees

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodg~ F. & A. M. of California:
The Annual Message of the Grand Master and the Reports of the
Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary. the Grand Lecturer and the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes have been referred to the Committee
on Distribution. We submit the following report:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

We recommend that portions of the Grand Master's Message be referred to the Grand Lodge committees as noted herein:
1. To the Committee on Jurispurudence-Recommend ation No. 5.
2. To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes-Recommendations Nos. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, and 9.
3. To the Committee on Finance - Recommendations Nos. 1, 3, 7,
and 8.
4. To the Committee on Ritual-Recommendations Nos. 1 and 4.
5. To the Temple Board Trustees-Recommendation No. 2.
:Regarding Recommendation No. 10, your Committee on Distribution
commends the Grand Master for his interest in the Grand Jurisdictional
Masonic Blood Bank for California and Hawaii but feels that no further
action by the Grand Lodge is necessary.
GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT

We recommend that the portions of the Grand Secretary's Report
be referred to the committees as indicated:
1. That portion relating to changes of meeting place to the Committees on Charters and By-Laws.
2. That portion relating to consolidation of Lodges to the Committee
on Charters.
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT

We recommend the Report of the Grand Treasurer be referred in its
entirety to the Committee on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES TRUSTEES' REPORT

We recommend the Report of the Masonic Homes Trustees be referred in its entirety to the Committee on Finance.
REPORT OP THE GRAND LECTURER

We recommend that the portion of the Grand Lecturer's Report relating to finance be referred to the Committee on Finance.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK P. LEMEN, Chairman
NILES 0. MILLAR

Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
"Let thy benevolence be as an unfailing light
for all generations."
"Every man shall give as he is able."
••• Deuteronomy 16: 17
In this year of social unrest, strikes, political campaigns and major
economic policy changes, it is with a spirit of fraternal pride, pleasure
and appreciation to this Grand Lodge that our Board presents its 38th
Annual Report for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1970.
We enjoyed the most successful year in the history of our Board.
We have moved into new dimensions of Masonic brotherhood and our
horizons of fraternal charity have widened.
F,reemasons belonging to Lodges in California and Hawaii contributed through their Lodges a total of $919,392.16. This is $33,272 more
than was donated last year. The sum was the largest ever raised since
the Fund was established in 1932.
This year a total of 113,260 contributors participated in the most
energetic and total effort ever in behalf of the Endowment prog,r amdespite the fact that our total membership of 233,855 is the lowest in
the past decade.
Statistically speaking, the percentage of participants increased by
one percent to 48.1~% of the entire membership. In 1969 there were
111,745 donors (47.17%) who contributed $886,120.14.
Another new all-time record was set this year with the determination
of $8.12 as the overall actual average contribution. Last year's average
was $7.93. The average donation, among the entire membership, also
set a new record of $3.91 each compared with $3.66 in 1969. Our appreciation for their dedicated effort is extended to a volunteer army of
committed Craftsmen who were instrumental in helping to achieve these
record results. These became a reality through the untiring efforts on
the part of Masons in every section of California and Hawaii.
Each of us should feel a deep satisfaction with what has been
achieved. However, each of us should renew his determination to
reach even greater heights by increasing the percentage of individual
contributors participating. This is our lifeline. We must keep faith with
that historic covenant between the Freemasons of California and our
principal charity-that of maintaining our two fine Homes.
Our Grand Master, a most ardent champion in the cause of Masonic
Charity, ~b~erved that the achievements of 1970 "have set a new plateau
for a re-mv1gorated and more keenly aware Masonic enthusiasm.'' He
paid SJ>ecial tribute to Brother Guss for his outstanding leadership and
complimented the Brethren for their continuing support.

INDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTIONS THROUGH l.oDGEs
A total of $919,392.16 was the new record in contributions this year,
$33,272 greater than last year. Of the 703 Lodges in the jurisdiction,
the 1970 report included participation of 701 Lodges.
A study of statistics points out the following interesting facts: The
total of annual contributions between 1960 and 1970 swelled by
$368,244.82. There was an increase during the decade of more than
12,994 members participating annually in the donations. The average
gift per contributor rose from $5.50 in 1960 to the new high of $8.12 for
this year. All of these increases occurred, however, regardless of a decrease of 8,285 in total membership from 1960 to 1970. This year ~epre­
sents not only the beginning of an exciting new decade but also a pivotal
year in the fraternal battle against a persistent foe--decrease in membership. Latest membership figures as of June 1970 show a total of 233,855
-lowest in a decade, compared with a high of 244,914 in 1965.

164 in Sierra City with 32 members. This venerable Lodge was chartered in 1864.

INCOME PROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND
The income from the Homes Endowment Fund this year was
$1,021,849.61 and that amount has been transferred to the operating
account of our two Masonic Homes.
BEQUESTS AND GIFTS
Gifts and bequests in the amount of $336,249.48 were received into
the Endowment Fund during the past iyear.
In addition, $1,311,360.28 in bequests was received by the Homes
direct from estates wherein the Endowment Fund was not specifically
mentioned in the will. Thus, a total of $1,647,609.76 was received in
bequests during the fiscal year. With each year's passing, the importance of relating full particulars regarding bequests and wills to the
members while in Lodge and featuring such information in Lodge publications will do much in the future to benefit the growth and development
of our two Masonic Homes.

THE YOUNG AND OLD HAPPILY ANNOUNCE ...
This year Grand Lodge pays its fraternal homage to its · newest
Lodge-Kern River Valley, U.D., with 72 members and a contribution
of $208.18 from 36 donors, representing a 50% participation and an
average gift of $2.89. The "oldest" Lodge is California No. 1, chartered in 1850 and now having 377 members. This year "Old No. One"
donated $2,533 with 34% participating and $6.72 as the average gift.
STANDARDIZED REFERENCE TO OUR HOMES
In order to unify reference to and properly identify each Home, the
Endowment Board has adopted the following names as befitting our
"crown jewels":
MASONIC HOME FOR OUR GUESTS AT UNION CITY
MASONIC HOME FOR CHILDREN AT COVINA
Brethren, let us uniformly use these names when referring to our
Homes.
ALOHA! CONGRATULATIONS TO OUR l.oDGES IN HAWAII
The Endowment Board is proud of this year's achievement by Lodges
in our newest State. Nine of the ten Lodges reported a gain in their annual collections, while half announced an increase in their membership.
The Endowment Board is grateful for the cooperation shown by
Masters of the Hawaiian Lodges, ably assisted by the Inspectors of the
382d, 384th and 385th Districts.
This year's contributions through Hawaiian Lodges amounted to
$13,053.71, the largest amount in a number of years. In 1968 the total
was $11,211.82 and in 1969 it was $12,258.66
Of 3,174 members this year's contributors numbered 1.561. or approximately 50%-two percentage points higher than their mainland
Brethren. We are proud of our Island Lodges and look to them for
greater gains in membership and Masonic scope.
MEMBER PARTICIPATION COMPARISON
In 1968, 331 Lodges reported 50% or more "member participation.''
Seven Lodges reported contributions of 100%.
Last year 295 Lodges Teported 50% or more participation, while eleven
Lodges made the coveted 100% goal. This year we are proud to announce that 337 Lodges reported 50% or more participation. A dozen
Lodges-large st number ever-were honored as being 100%.

RECOGNITION TO INSPECTORAL CORPS
The six lnspectoral Divisions in the jurisdiction provided excellent
on-the-spot support to our state-wide program and the Board wishes
to acknowledge their cooperation. The Assistant Grand Lecturers of
these Divisions were always receptive to our needs and provided suggestions, cooperation and sustained interest throughout the campaign.
All of the Inspectors deserve our thanks and recognition.
The Board is grieved over the untimely passing of Very Worshipful
Harold N. Richards, Grand Lecturer. He was a constant interested
"sideliner" at our regional meetings and his advice will be missed.

MASONIC LoDGE SERVICE ROLL

When we can say "It is good" of our work, our acts, our decisions,
our life-we have reached the highest expression of dignity of Masonic
labor and commitment.
For the first time Lodges in the jurisdiction having attained an "aver~
age gift" goal of $3.00 or more per member are placed on the "Service
Roll." This designation replaces the former "Honor Roll" listing of
Lodges that attained a $2.00 or' more average gift. The idea of terming
the list as "Service" instead of "Honor" is in keeping with present~day
evaluations of the economics of Masonic Charity.
Service Roll status of $4.00 or over average was attained by 274
Lodges. These Lodges, in developing a new and greater appreciation of
the acts of love and charity, deserve our fraternal thanks and congratu~
lations. These are listed below:

SERVICE ROLL SIOELIGHTS-1970
In 1970 there were 131 Lodges that reported an "average gift"
of $5.00 or more. compared with 114 in 1969.
The largest group this year. as in 1969, was the $3.00 to $4.00 category: 207 this year compared with 227 in 1969. This indicates that most
Lodges experienced minimum trouble in reaching this new and higher
plateau. The new Lodge "Service Roll" is a goal within reach of all
Lodges whose members exert reasonable effort and commitment in the
practice of Masonic Charity.
Lodges attaining "Service Roll" status will be presented with the
~amiliar gold stars for their Lodge certificates.
The statistics below show that the average gift per individual has
increased and that the "old-fashioned" $2.00 average which has been
in vogue for more than 40 years is no longer a real incentive.

HIGHLIGHTS OP A TOTAL 1970 CAMPAIGN
The year's varied activities in behalf of the all-out effort centered
about the theme "Make 1970 the Year of a Million Smiles."
Spurred on by the Grand Master's admonition in his annual Proclamation for Endowment Month-"Let us take a giant step toward
charityl"-the program began with the free distribution to the Lodges
of approximately 275,000 convenience envelopes as an aid to stimulate
donations when members paid their annual dues.
Over 1,000,000 mailing "stuffers" were circulated during the year.
Monthly mailings proved of inestimable value as point-of-interest reminders to contribute to the Fund. This year .6.ve distinct pieces of literature were available for distribution, including several original ideas
that were well received by the Brethren.
It is apparent that the total of contributing participants increases
slightly each year: Your Board is concerned. however. about the "Forgetful 50%" and seeks their interest and support. Several new approaches to the problem were instigated this year and the Board is gratified
with the initial results. By recognizing that Charity is a year-round
responsibility and not just confined to the Endowment Month of May,
a number of Brethren who remained on the sidelines are now actively
supporting the annual effort.
The Board is deeply appreciative of the publicity appearing in our
Cal.ifomia Freemason. Next year we hope to develop this approach even
further. Plans are being made to introduce caravan tours from various
areas to view each of the Homes. This year, for the .6.rst time, we perfected an unusual and highly pleasing manner in which to display the
report of Lodge contributions through enlarged 36" x 24" pages. identical to the copy in the annual Endowment Board Report. These were
posted on four large tackboards and were easily the "hit" of Grand
Lodge Week exhibits and displays.
SPOTLIGHT ON PERSONNEL
To our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Chester R. MacPhee. we
all express our thanks for his continuing and enthusiastic interest. At

140

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

every meeting or social event which he attended, he mentioned the activities of our Homes and the efforts of the Lodges to contribute to the
Fund. He has been an inspiration to our cherished cause.
Comment also must be made of the cordial cooperation extended the
Board by members of the Grand Master's "official family" and to the
Assistant Grand Lecturers, Inspectors, and our Grand Lodge office. All
played important roles.
The annual program would not have been such a "smiling" success
without the wholehearted cooperation of the Lodge officers, committeemen, "sideliners" and especially the Secretaries who play a vital role
in our annual charitable endeavor.
The Grand Lodge office staff was superb. It was a real pleasure to
work with the charming and efficient ladies and Brethren of our Grand
Secretary's office.
We have been particularly fortunate that our Board has been composed of Brethren who, through their untiring service to the fraternity,
have demonstrated true commitment to the cause of fulfilling a Masonic
need.
Some will be terminating their service on the Board. Others will take
their places. It is not possible in the space allotted to adequately express
our appreciation. Suffice it to say they have indeed squared a good stone
in the quarry and earned Master Masons' wages!
The fraternal philosophy of our Masonic Homes exemplifies Masonry's greatest tenet-Charity. This belief gives to every Mason the
honor and opportunity to be his brother's keeper.
It is my fervent hope and prayer, as I leave the Chairmanship of
this Board, that the two Masonic Homes help strengthen and perpetuate
our belief in the dignity of man to the Glory of God. Let us continue to
bring the light of Charity and Love to an all-too-often bleak and dismal
world.
My most sincere thanks to all Masons for such splendid support.
"For the greatest of these is Charity."
Respectfully submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT
BOARD
MORRIS C. Guss, Chairman
