REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. &A. M. of California:
We present herewith a factual report of the activity in your Boards
of Relief since our last Communication.
During this year we have continued our policy of furnishing copies
incoming and outgoing correspondence to the Grand Master,
all
of
Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, and by di~
rection of the Grand Master, have added the Grand Secretary to the list.
This policy has permitted the elective Grand Lodge Officers to be
completely informed at all times of the problems and progress of the
Board of Control and Boards of Relief.
We have again asked that all Boards comply with your Law as it
now appears on the record, nothing more, nothing less. This endeavor
has not met with the enthusiastic support of some of the Boards. This
lack of support is evidenced by the reluctance of those Boards to comply
with the Law. In other Boards, compliance has been immediate and
complete.
Due to your approval of a statewide Blood Bank at our last communi~
cation, we have reversed a former directive to now permit Boards to con~
tinue serving non-member Lodges in Blood Bank operations, pending
development of a program by the Committee working to establish the
statewide Blood Bank.
Continuing our policy of visiting Boards of Relief and conferring
with their officers ;md members, in order to be of assistance to them and
to carry out our responsibility of standardizing the operation of Boards
of Relief, we met with the following Boards, Long Beach, Fresno, Sacra~
mento, and two times with the Los Angeles Board.
Our visitations indicated that copies of the Rules and Regulations
sent to the Boards in October 1969 were not being used. On June 26,
1970 we caused to be sent to each Master, Warden and Secretary of
each Lodge in the jurisdiction, and each Grand Lodge Officer, Inspector
and Committeeman, additional copies of the Rules. These were mailed
by the Grand Lodge Office, with a cover memo signed by the Grand Sec~
retary. It is hoped that all have or will make themselves familiar with
these Rules.
SAN GABRIEL VALLEY BOARD OF RELIEP

We can report to you that the problems of this Board as outlined in
last year's report have been resolved, and with the election of new offi~
cers and hiring of a new Executive Secretary, per capita has been re~
duced, mileage to those attending funerals has been eliminated, payment
to the Acting Master discontinued, and operations are now being con~
ducted in a conformity to the Law.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

164

165

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
LoNG BEACH BOARD

On February 7, 1970 your Board of Control met with the P.resident,
Secretary. and members of the Executive Committee to examine the operation of the Long Beach Board.
We were anxious to find out why the per-capita of this Board was
the highest permissible amount of all of the Boards in the state, and why
this Board required a full time stenog·rapher.
Examination revealed that one of the rooms in the suite of offices was
sublet to the Long Beach Benefit Club, and that the telephone served both
the Board and the Club, with incoming calls being handled by Board
personnel. It was also found that the voluminous clerical work of the
Club was handled by Board personnel. (quote) "during off hours," (end
quote) and payment for this work in addition to the Board salary was
made by the Club directly to the personnel.
No factual evidence could be found to indicate just what constituted
"off hours" as being separate from regular Board work, and it appeared
that the Long Beach Board was subsidizing the operation of the Benefit
Club.
This service to a non-member organization appearing to be in violation of Sec. 333 e, C.M.C .. and Article XVI, Sect. 3 b of the Rules and
Regulations, the Board of Control directed that the tenancy of the Long
Beach Benefit Club be terminated by June 30, 1970, and further. that personnel of the Board of Relief immediately cease to do work for the Club
on Board premises.
Last year the Long Beach Board reported 6405 sick visits to sojourners. We asked for an explanation as to how this Board conducted
79% of the total sick visits made by all Boards in the state.
. This was explained as follows: "Each of the Lodges, members of the
Board, rotated on a pre-determined schedule, visitations to the VA Hospital on Sunday afternoon. This Committee, usually five in number,
would visit for example three sojourners in the Hospital. The calculation of the five visitors times the three sojourners would equal fifteen
visits, and was so recorded."
Your Board of Control. while in agreement that 5X3 equals 15. did
not feel that this computation presented to you the proper work of the
Board.
We therefore directed that future reports contain only the number of
sojourners visited by the Board Committee, without being multiplied by
the number of visitors.
Brother Clayton Heinz, newly elected President of the Board. has
exemplified a sterling quality of leadership and administration in correcting the above items. On April 11, 1970 he notified the Board of Control
of the removal of the Benefit Club from the premises, a termination date

for the stenographer, a reduction in per capita, and advised that a new
Executive Secretary had been hired.
This prompt action by Brother Heinz and the Executive Committee,
without fanfare, protest or request to the Grand Master for decision is
somewhat unique, and much appreciated by the Board of Cont•rol.
Los ANGELES BOARD

On February 7. 1970 your Board of Control visited the Los Angeles
Board to review operations.
In the discussion which ensued, the President remarked "that he had
serious doubts about the authority of the Board of Control to supervise
or make Rules binding upon the Los Angeles Board."
The President stated "that the Los Angeles Board was operating under compact with the Lodges dated in 1917 and since this pre-dated the
formation of the Board of Control. it was his feeling that the Board of
Control lacked authority."
The Board of Control is of the opinion that all Boards of Relief, including the Los Angeles Board, are subject to the authority of the Board
of Control regardless of the date of the formation of the Board of
Control.
Search of the Board of Control files revealed Compacts signed by
the Lodges dated 1950 and 1951 disproving the validity of the President's contention. Subsequent correspondence advised the President of
this fact.
Our visitation !evealed the following facts indicating that the operations of the Los Angeles Board were illegal according to the Rules, and
apparently had been so for many years.
1. That the Lodges of the Los Angeles Board did not appoint representatives as provided in the Rules for their protection.
2. That elections for Executive Committeemen were held, without
the presence of duly appointed representatives, candidates being elected
by a majority vote of those present. Some Lodges were recorded as
having five or more present, and others having as many as thirty-two.
3. That the Executive Committee, without the required Resolution
giving them authority, conducted all of the business of the Board, including election of the President, Vice-president, and Secretary-Treasurer.
The result of the above has been the operation of an organization,
Masonic in name and nature, representing the members of the 106
Lodges of the Board, without a legal process of election or legal delegation of authority.
This fact was communicated to the Grand Master, and he forthwith
directed that the Lodges appoint proper representatives, after which a
legal election was to be held.

166

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Under date of September 15, 1970, we were notified by the Los Angeles Board that the election directed by the Grand Master had been held
with 190 of the 318 legal representatives voting. Your Board of Control
notes from this reported figure, that 40% of the representatives of the
106 Lodges did not, could not, or would not attend even though this election was directed by the Grand Master. We ask an obvious question, Do
those Lodges whose representatives were not present realliy have an interest in the Board of Relief or the manner of its operation?
Another visit was made by the Board of Control on March 21, 1970.
Routine examination was made of the records from July 1967 to the
date of the visit, indicating a consistent pattern. Check stubs were
audited for the period August 30, 1969 through the date of the visit in·
dicating further violations.
1. That a Board of Control directive prohibiting lump sum payments
for mileage to the Secretary was not being observed. Check numbers in
our flies indicate the payee and amounts to substantiate this statement.
2. That funerals were being conducted by the Board in disregard of
Sect. 605 C.M.C.
The President and Executive Secretary made strong protest to the
effect that due to the large size of the Board, and alleged inability of the
Masters of the Lodges to perform the funeral service, it was impossible
to require the Lodges to conduct funerals in accordance with Sect. 605
C.M.C.
Your Board of Control has noted that the Los Angeles Board has
reported 173 funerals for the year just ended June 30, 1970, and can not
see that the performance of approximately two funerals per year for each
of the 106 Lodges would cause a great hardship on those Lodges.
It is also interesting to note the Executive Committee minutes of December 14, 1969 records the passage of a motion, that the Los Angeles
Board conduct funerals only at the direction of a Lodge, and with no fee
paid to the acting Master.
Why then, was this practice continued until March 21, 1970? Other
Boards in the state are operating properly in this respect so why not
the Los Angeles Board?
3. That payment of $10.00 per funeral was made to the Brother conducting the funeral in violation of Sect. 604m C.M.C. Check numbers
in our file indicate the name of the paryee and that in addition to the
$10.00 fee, mileage was also paid.
4. Check numbers 20563 and i0564 indicate that gifts of $100.00 and
$75.00 were given to the Executive Secretary and Assistant Secretary
respectivdy at Christmas time as a bonus. The generosity of Boards of
Relief in giving gifts is a privilege denied the Lodges.
5. Publishing a Clearing House Report, not provided for as proper
work of a Board of Relief. This matter was reported to you last year.

The Board of Control in examining figures for budget approval for
1970-71, rejected an item of $750.00 for printing this report.
On receipt of this rejection, the Los Angeles Board appealed the
ruling to the Grand Master, pleading that compliance with our ruling
would be detrimental to the Lodges since no time had been permitted to
find an alternate.
From the time of the report made to you last year until the rejection
of the budget item, a period of approximately eight months, during which
time the Los Angeles Board did nothing to find an alternate.
The Board of Control, after consultation with the Grand Master, and
though still of the opinion that this was not proper work for a Board of
Relief, and further that ample time had already been provided, had an
alternate been sought, extended permission for this work to be continued
until December 31, 1970. The Los Angeles Board, to our knowledge,
is the only Board in the jurisdiction, publishing such a 'l'eport.
During the previous fiscal year ending June 30, 1969 the Los Angeles Board received an income of $14,926.00 in excess of expenses. During the fiscal year ending June 30, 1970, the excess in income over expenses was $7444.95, in spite of budgeted salary increases to the Executive Secretary and Assistant Secretary totaling $1 700.00 The surplus is
increasing year by year.

167

RECOMMENDATIONS

Many of the problems arising from Board of Relief operation are
caused by individual interpretation of the words used in the C.M.C. and
Rules. Your Board of Control feels that written defiinition of certain of
these words will clarify and make possible more unifO'l'mity of operation.
We therefore make RECOMMENDA TION No. 1.
That the words "relieve the distress" contained in Sect. 603 C.M.C.
shall mean only "the furnishinng of food, clothing and shelter," unless
other specific items are requested by the sojourners Lodge.
We have searched thoroughly through the C.M.C. and find no specific authority for Boards of Relief to engage in funeral activity. The
long standing practice of all Boards in the area must therefore be without legal consent.
The conduct of funerals is under the jurisdiction of the Ritual
Committee, and permissibility to conduct funerals is carefully spelled out
in Sect. 605 C.M.C. We do not propose any change in these respects.
We can see however, that the administrative work connected with a
sojourner funeral could be beneficial to all if made legal for a Board of
Relief.
We therefore make RECOMMENDA TION No. 2
That Boards of Relief be authorized to do administrative work in
connection with sojourner funerals. Such administrative work shall be
limited to, contact with the sojourners Lodge for authorization for the

169

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

funeral, order such floral emblems as are approved by the sojourners
Lodge, billing same to the Lodge, contact a member Lodge to furnish
qualified officiants, notify sojourners Lodge of time and place of burial
together with the name of the Brothers and the Lodge conducting. The
Board is expected to display the formalities expected of our Fraternity in
contacts with the family before, during and after the service. Many
Boards make no contact with the family, dealing only with the Mortuary.
Last year we reported that two Executive Secretaries were drawing
pensions from the Grand Lodge fund while continuing full time employment with a Board. The fact that the employees salary might be reduced
by the amount of the pension at the time the pension was taken is negated
by the fact that future raises in salary, in effect, reinstates the reduction.
Budget ['equests indicate raises to both of these Secretaries.
The normal purpose of a pension is generally to provide an income
after retirement, and not as a supplement to continue on the job.
The principle of including Board of Relief Employees in this pension while excluding Lodge Secretaries, building custodians, and other
employees of the Lodge, is in our opinion discriminatory. Many of those
excluded contribute as much in work, and many are employed at a much
lesser salary.
We therefore make RECOMMENDATION No. 3
That Board of Relief Employees be removed from eligibility in
the pension and health insurance benefits. This recommendation is
made with the reservation, that those now receiving pension funds, and
those now employed by a Board of Relief, shall continue to receive the
benefits now provided. Only future employees shall be removed from
eligibility.

MEMBERSHIP IN BOARDS

Last year we reported that cases existed where Lodges meeting in the
same Temple belonged to different Boards, also ·cases where one of two
or more Lodges meeting in a Temple belonged to a Board, the others ['efusing to join, and. cases where a Lodge in a City or Town belonged
while others in the same City or Town refused to join.
Since none of the Lodges have taken the initiative to correct this disparity and infraction of the Rules, the Board of Control must therefore
make ['ecommendations to the Grand Master for compulsory membership
or surrender of membership in a Board, as each case merits.
Normal jurisdiction of a Lodge is determined by its meeting place.
This then, must be the determining factor in such decisions. It is not
feasible or proper that Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction belong to
different Boards of Relief, or that one having concurrent jurisdiction belonging to a Board, the others not joininng.
Your Board of Control has a definite and serious ['esponsibility imposed upon it by your Law. All decisions and directives have been made
by either a majority or unanimous vote of all of the members of the
Board, without rancor or personal vengeance.
Your Board of Control is mindful of the splendid service provided
by some Boards, but is gravely concerned that others continually endeavor to disregard or circumvent your Law.
Your Board of Control has found that some have a contention that
services offered by a Board of Relief should be expanded in various
measure.

170

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The responsibility of making Law is yours and yours alone. Your
Board of Control does not have, nor does not desire the power to make
Law.
We would charge you therefore, that in the discharge of your t"esponsibility, that you exercise your own good judgment that the Craft
as a whole be benefited by any change of Law. without subverting the
interest of all Lodges and Boards to the interest of a few.
We request the sum of $3,500.00 to cover expenses during the com·
ing iyear.
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Retirement:
Recommendation No. 3 in the Report of the Board of Control relates to eligibility and participation of Board of Relief employees in the
amended retirement plan adopted by Grand Lodge in December, 1958.
The recommendation of the Board of Control is to the effect that
benefits of the Retirement Pension Plan adopted by Grand Lodge for
the benefit of employees of the Masonic Homes of California and of the
Grand Lodge of California and its component organization s be continued for present and retired employees of Boards of Relief only and
not for future employees of Boards of Relief.
This recommendation definitely requires further study as to policy
and also consultation with the Internal Revenue Service who must approve changes in the Retirement Plan which affect the rights of employees, past. present or future, before changes can be implemented.
Your Retirement Plan Committee recommends that action on Recommendation No. 3 as offered by the Board of Control be deferred pending necessary study and consultation with actuaries for the Plan and
governmental agencies and that report be made to Grand Lodge at the
next Annual Communication.

At the first meeting of the Board, the Grand Master, the line officers
of Grand Lodge and all members of the Trustees of the Temple unanimously agreed upon the following:
1. The Building and the Auditorium are primarily and fundamenta lly for the use and occupancy of the Grand Lodge of California
and Masons in general. Nothing should be done to change the
basic purpose of the Building and the Auditorium and it should
always be home in mind that the Building was designed as a
Masonic Temple.
2. The Temple Building should be constantly maintained and kept
in excellent condition and repair.
3. Certain alterations should be made for the accommodation of
patrons who rent the Auditorium for events authorized under
the policy of the Board of Trustees and subject to the approval
of the Board.
4. The Temple Board should follow any specific instructions of
Grand Lodge in the matter of acquiring properties.
Taking up these points, the Temple Board gave consideration to the
following:
1. Raising of present stage floor and, after study, to obtain proper
height for best sight lines; and developing a design which would
facilitate its removal and reinstallation if necessary.

173

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

2. Detailed study of any necessary repairs such as leakage, drain~
age and general maintenance of building.
3. Study of the acquisition of further real property purchases as
directed by the Grand Lodge.
4. Refurbishing and alteration of main Auditorium:
a. Painting
b. Carpeting
c. Sound system
d. Lighting
e. Dressing room facilities
f. Redesigning stage and back stage
5. Study and report on conditions affecting the Temple arising from
proposed construction of a new hotel west of the Temple.
In order to expedite the above work, the following were designated
by the Board to make studies, create designs and secure all necessary
data to carry out the work:
1. H. M. Engle & Son, Structural Engineers: All structural design
and maintenance;
2. Millard Sheets: All design, architecture and interior decoration:
3. Lyle Patton, Electrical Engineer: Wiring installation, lighting of
stage and auditorium and control panel;
4. Electronic Media, Inc.: Sound system;
5. Robert Batchelor, A.I.A.: Foundation Study;

Using this experience as a guide, a survey of A, B, C, D, E and G
floors was made during the rainy season, in the first few months of
1970. Cracks, due to leaks, were marked for future identification. A
contract was let to pressure~treat these walls. It is believed that the
work done will be effective in stopping most of the leakage. Periodic
inspections will be made next winter ( 1970~71) and any additional
leaks which may develop will be treated. Water seepage always has
been heavy at the east end of "E" floor. Portions of the floor slab were
removed and subfloor drains were installed. Future seepage, if any,
will be minor. Additional subfloor drains can be installed, if necessary.
The four exit doors of the building leading to California Street,
th•rough constant use, have become defective. Rain seeps in and damage
to the carpet has resulted. A cost estimate is being obtained to remedy
this condition.
A small utility room on the third floor at the west end of the view
porch had a badly leaking floor slab. This had caused considerable
damage to the contents in the storage room below. These leaks have
been repaired.
Inspection disclosed some leaks in the marble facing on the California Street walls. Periodic inspections will be made to ascertain the
cause of these leaks and they will be corrected.

172

STAGE RENOVATION

The original movable stage had a height above the main Auditorium
floor of 3'6". Experience, over several years, indicated that for the best
sight lines the stage should be lowered. The original stage was dis~
mantled and each of its 4'0" x 8'0" units were lowered and replaced
with a new maple floor. The old drape skirting around the stage was
replaced with attractive wood paneling. If the Grand Lodge requirements make it necessary, the stage can still be dismantled and the
4'0" x 8'0" units stored until reassembled.
BUILDING MAINTENANCE

Since completion of the Temple there has been considerable leakage
in the south and west walls. A few years ago the walls of the boiler
room were waterproofed by pressure treating the cracks with "epoxy."
This solved the problem in this particular location.

REDECORATING AND REFURBISHING
MAIN AUDITORIUM

Due to the beauty, character and location of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, we have increasing demands for outside rentals. In
order to accommo<late concerts, ballet performances, corporate meetings, lectures, etc., it has been necessary to redecorate and improve the
lighting in the auditorium. Our first and of course primary concern has
been to maintain the character, spirit and function of the building for
the Grand Lodge annual meetings. Every effort has been made to
preserve the dignity and the beauty of the Auditorium. In order to
maintain a facility worthy of the Masonic name, it has become imperative to provide proper entrance and exit from the stage, a better
balanced sound system and lighting control.
REDECORATING

The new color scheme for the Auditorium harmonizes with the existing color of the seats, which are in good condition. The walls and
ceiling have been redecorated to insure an overall effect of harmony
and to guide the eye to the stage. The coloring of the central oval
ceiling has been carried into the surrounding wall areas.
The installation of new carpet was necessary to !replace badly worn
floor covering. In the foyer a color combination of recarpeting and new
vinyl wall covering has been selected to create the important "first

impression" as one approaches our magnificent Auditorium. Planters
will be placed in the main lobby with permanent plants, which will give

The former sound room was rewired and all new solid state power
amplifiers installed. The former gondola mounted speaker system has
been augmented and designed into the new stage left and stage right
prosceniums.

174

ELECTRICAL WoRK AND RELIGHTING
The major items of electrical work involve installation of new lighting
and sound control systems, including the installing of new control consoles in a booth constructed at center-balcony of the Auditorium. The
former lighting control system was installed when the Temple was constructed. It consisted of motor-operated auto-transformer dimmers
located in the equipment room, at rear of Auditorium. These were controlled from a console located at the stage left balcony of the Auditorium
opposite the organ ,console. The components of this system were fixedmounted, making it very difficult to remove parts for servicing. This type
of dimming system has become obsolete and is slow in response, there
being a lag between the time when the console control is positioned
and the time when the motor-driven auto-transformer dimmer corrects.
The new dimming system consists of Skirpan silicon controlled
rectifier ( SCR) or solid state dimmers which, with the control console
components, are all modular plug-in construction, permitting easy
removal for servicing. The SCR equipment is instantaneous in response
and thus will meet the most exacting demands for theater lighting.
In addition, a new Kliegl "Safpatch" panel is being provided, permitting over one hundred stage lighting circuits to be cross-patched to
any of the twenty-four 6 KW SCR stage lighting dimmers.
Changes were also made in the lighting which serves the first floor
audience area. This consists of the removal of lamps in the six multibeam downlights which formerly were a source of ·glare in the eyes of
the audience. These were replaced with twenty-nine 1000 watt Kliegl
ellipsoidal reflector lens type downlights.
The additional lighting and light control units will insure, at all times,
£rom the full lighting of the Auditorium to the high concentration upon
the stage. The effect will be both effective and pleasing. Lights have
been installed above the rear of the stage. This will provide balanced
stage lighting.
SOUND SYSTEM
Another phase of the remodeling program in the Auditorium may be
categorized as ... Modernization of the Sound System." The original
system has become obsolete. Those who use the facility have required
additional and more modern sound equipment. The new srystem will
provide a specially designed mixing console, incorporating the latest
state of art features, such as stereophonic sound, echo, variable equalization, feeds for broadcast, TV news, and the Auditorium sound system.

SOUND AND LIGHTING CONTROL BOOTH
A new gondola has been added in the center of the balcony in order
to insure perfect sound balance and light control. The new consoles
bring the present lighting and sound up to date by replacing the now
obsolete equipment of the original installation. It will eliminate the continuous hauling of specialized heavy equipment in and out of the building.
ENTRANCE SCREENS AND REDESIGN OF CANOPY OVER STAGE

In order to allow proper entrance on stage. two gathering areas
have been created on the right and left sides of the stage. New teak
screen panels frame the architectural treatment of the canopy. They
will house the speakers and result in the elimination of the unsightly
gondolas suspended from the ceiling. The panels have been designed
as an integral part of the whole unit formed by the canopy and its side
pilasters. The new canopy treatment houses gold curtains which cover
the travertine wall and Masonic Sunburst when the Auditorium is used
for purposes other than Grand Lodge. The canopy also houses a motion
picture screen (electrically controlled) and two mounting bars that
can be used for extra curtains. signs, special effects and down lights.
New dressing ·rooms and toilet facilities for women back stage have
been installed and, in addition, the conference rooms have been redecorated and better ventilation has been provided for the entire con£erence room area.
In planning the improvements to the interior of the Auditorium
every attempt was made to create a better aesthetic response. At the
same time nothing has been done that was not concernd with improving the primary function of the building-that of its use by our Grand
Lodge. With the improved lighting, sound equipment and the stage
remodeling, it is our firm belief that the California Masonic Memorial
Temple is now the most modern and efficient auditorium facility in this
part of the world. It is indeed well worthy of the name, California
Masonic Memorial Temple.

INCOME

Each year the income from the use of our facilities has shown a
continuing increase. During the fiscal year ending June 30, 1970, the
increase on rental and other charges to the public amounted to 41.6%
above last year. The rental on our garage, in which we participate with
the operators, amounted to an increase of 14.4% Rental on other real
estate increased 14.8%. As in previous years, much of the income from
the garage results from the occupancy of our Auditorium and Exhibit
space.
Convention and tourist business continues to play an important part
in the rental of the Auditorium and Exhibit Hall. The Yerba Buena
Center, south of Market, which was expected to bring additional con~
ventions to San Francisco, was delayed in construction due to legal
problems. However, there are four new hotels or additions to present
facilities in the planning stage or under construction in the immediate
area of our Temple. One of these structures will be as high as forty~
three stories. As these hotels are opened to the public, we may expect
profit from increased use of our facilities.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK APRIL 20-24. 1970
"The Public Schools-Information-Education-Responsibility" was
the slogan chosen by the Grand Master for this year. The slogan was
very well accepted throughout California and Hawaii and was used extensively by both Masonic and non-Masonic groups. The results of
some of the Public Schools Week activities follow:
Over seven million milk cartons carried a panel urging visitations of
public schools during the week of April 20-24.
Billboards situated on major California highways carried the message
to millions of motorists.
All of the major food chains were contacted by the Committee requesting that they use some space in their weekly food ads to publicize
Public Schools Week. The response was good.
Proclamations were obtained from the vast majority of public officials
and State legislators in both California and Hawaii declaring the week
of April 20-24 as Public Schools Week and urging the citizenry to visit
their public schools.
Television and radio stations were again generous with air time and
several committee members, the Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers
and other prominent Masons appeared on radio and television.
More than 3,000 bus cards were posted in buses throughout the State.
Thirty thousand official posters, printed at Los Angeles Trade Technical College, were distributed through the office of the Grand Secretary.
This represented an increase of 11 % over last year. The Public Schools

GRAND ORATION
TOMORROW
AND TOMORROW
AND TOMORROWDONALD R. FRETZ, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Sir, My Fellow Officers, Visiting Dignitaries and
Brethren:
Before we talk about tomorrow I would like to reminisce about yesterday and talk about today. To work with a great man is inspiring and
working with our Grand Master this year has been an inspiration to
those of us fortunate enough to have been elected or appointed. There
are moments or times all of us would like to preserve. I would like to
wrap this year in some beautiful cloth and carefully keep it for all time to
come. I thank you, Most Worshipful Sir.
In saying these things, I am mindful of the strength of the Deputy
Grand Master and the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens and that
their years, too, will be excellent years for this Grand Lodge.
But now about tomorrow.
Do you remember when you were introduced to the concept of infinity? Do you remember being bewildered? I do. You were told to
think of the largest number you could think of and then keep going on
and on, and when you had thought of the new largest number you could
think of you went beyond that. It didn't make any difference how far
you went, there was a number beyond that and beyond that and beyond
that. Think of the farthest star you can see, then keep going out and out
and on and on into space, and where does space end? Who knows? Just
keep going on and on and on.
As of today, tomorrow will be October 1i. But when tomorrow becomes today, tomorrow will be October 15. And on any given future
day there will be a tomorrow. Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow-.
It is this infinity of time that I want us to think about today. Let's
think about the problems that will be facing the world and Freemasonry
thirty years from now and then, if we can do it, 100 years from now.
Tomorrow and tomorrow. We might ·rightly be concerned whether
there will be anyone here to enjoy that tomorrow. We've lived for the
last 25 years or more and do live now at the threshold of disaster. Circumstances in the world are such that the catalyst of such a disaster may
now exist. Some people have lived so long in conditions which seem to be
on the borderline of catastrophe that they no longer build fallout shelters.
Others are so frustrated by what they believe is their inability to control

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

183

their own destiny that they want to exist only for themselves, to "do their
own thing." Most of us assume tomorrow and that it and we will meet.
If we assume that we will be here, we need to take stock of what tomorrow will bring and to determine what we can do to make it what we
want it to be. And if we are not going to be here, then we may assess
what we will not experience.
We frequently think of what may happen or what we would like to
have happen next year or five or ten years from now. But how many
times do we try to see beyond our own lives and plan for the long term
future of others or of our organizations.
Let's take a look at the problem. There are now 3Yz billion people
in the world. By the year 2000-only several tomorrows away-there
will be 7Yz billion people on the same-sized earth. Some wise men predict
that the earth will not be able to accommodate its future population.
Others. equally wise, rely upon the adaptability of man.
But when there are 7Yz billion people, or more billions than that, how
can their physical needs be met? Can you picture even twice as many
cars on Los Angeles freeways? Or twice as many freeways? Can you
picture doubling our world housing, doubling our world food supply,
doubling our world rate of fuel consumption? What new methods of
travel. what new housing construction, what new sources of food, what
new sources of fuel will be found to meet the needs of these people?
Assuming that people continue to exist, can you imagine the immensity
of the urban problems when 400 million people instead of 200 million
people inhabit this t:ountry? That could happen sometime soon after
the cyear 2000. What will the year 2070 bring?
Can you imagine the problem in parts of the world where population
growth is more rapid than ours? The physical problems-food, housing,
transportation-pre sented by such numbers of people seem prodigious.
But what of the social problems? Let's take c·rime and law enforcement.
Crime rates are now tremendously high. But we know that crime rates
are highest in the low income, urban areas. What then will happen in
the future when urban areas increase in density? As crime increases,
courts are busier and court congestion results because we are unwilling
to pay the price for new judges and of new methods. Then picture the
medical problems, mental health, welfare. When we double the number
of people, we many times more than double the problems.
It strains our imagination to try to think of the year 2000. What
then of the year 2070, only a hundred sets of tomorrows away? Picture
the problems of that day! Even with all of the vast changes and improvements which may be made in mental health. medicine, law, courts
and social organization. can you picture the regulation of peoples lives
in that day? It's not difficult to picture a governmental communications
system which watches the conduct of everyone. It is not difficult to

185

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

imagine that the mental attitudes of people will one day be controlled
by adding something to the air they breathe, or the water they drink,
or the food they eat. The real problem is to preserve such freedom as
makes life worthwhile, while yielding to such necessary regulations as
may be required to enable people to live in peace and harmony. This
will not be easy.
The immensity of the problems to be faced creates the challenge of
tomorrow, and the challenge of tomorrow is really the challenge of today.
There are three parts of the problem. The first has to do with human
beings. Human beings, by their numbers, create the problem. They
will also solve it or be destroyed.
Man is a creature of dignity, of God-given attributes. He is worth
saving, and he must believe it. This assertion conditions governments,
as our Declaration of Independence says. It conditions our way of life,
the manner in which we organize ourselves economically and socially.
Man may need to change, but he must not lose his dignity or his
freedom. Attempts to cope with increasing numbers of people will focus
upon restrktions upon freedom of activity. It is more likely to come in
the gradual erosion of rights than it is by some revolution which will
suddenly impose restrictions upon activity.
Where you find the present indication of such future restriction will
depend upon your point of view. Some may find it in the fact that the
treehouse of their youth has been sacrificed to zoning ordinances for the
"benefit of all." Others may find it in a new "no knock" law which
permits law enforcement officers some new freedom of action. Others
may find it in higher taxes. All of these may be right or none of them
may be right. But this is an area in which we must be vitally concerned
and vigilant.
The second problem area is that of economic conditions. Economic
conditions can change causing people who have existed comfortably for
many years to lose their comforts, to become fearful. While we have
taken many of the valleys and hills out of the economic road, new chuckholes are constantly being made and need repair. One economic challenge is to find new ways to market new products in a new age. Economic institutions have added to the problem by giving us numbers
instead of names. We can ill-afford such depersonalization. The more
anonymous a man becomes, the less dignified he is, and the less responsible he may hold himself for his actions. The psychology of the mob is
too well known to us for us to permit such anonymity.
The third phase of the problem is that of organizations. Man's organizations are changing. Some forms of government have ceased to exist:
others have taken their place. Even our form of government, which
purports to be the same as it was when this country was founded, is not
really the same as it was fifty years ago or one hundred years ago. It
has changed to meet the needs of the times. Other organizations have

faced challenges, some have ceased to exist. The challenge to institutions is to remain alive and useful.
I have presumed to believe that the challenge which warrants this
discussion is the challenge to this institution-Freemasonry-to remain
alive and useful thirty years from now, one hundred years from now.
Freemasonry has met challenges in all its history. Persecution has
not daunted it. But today we face a new danger.
All institutions are threatened today. There are people who advocate
revolutionary overthrow of the establishment, which includes organizations, governments, businesses. At least some of these people are
dangerous. Many others are simply expressing youthful discontent.
But the greater threat to institutions today comes from the people
who are far from violent revolutionaries. The danger comes from boredom, from a lack of enthusiasm, from apathy, from doing nothing. The
opposite of this is enthusiasm, activity, involvement.
Governments, whether federal. state or local. control much of our
lives. But how hard it is sometimes to get able men to subject themselves
to election to office. How hard it is to interest people in local issues. The
apathy of voters, of potential office-seekers, creates bad government.
It can be remedied by involvement.
Churches of dozens of denominations have affected the moral and
spiritual lives of most of us. Now the question is raised as to whether
the church is relevant. When was it ever more relevant? When did it
ever need to have more people involved?
Schools-universities and colleges have become so politicized that
instead of being re.iJarded as places of education, they are regarded as
places where political opinions are expressed by violent and destructive
confrontation.
We need government. We need churches. We need schools. If
these organizations were destroyed today they would somehow be recreated. They are •relevant.
And I say to you today that if Freemasonry were destroyed, it would
be re-created. It is essential. It is revelant.
It has been said that WHAT WE MUST REACH FOR IS A
CONCEPT OF PERPETUAL SELF-DISCOVERY. PERPETUAL
RESHAPING TO REALIZE ONE'S BEST SELF, TO BE THE
PERSON ONE COULD BE. What organization could be more relevant to this task? Our principles must be discovered and interpreted
by the individual. Our method of teaching permits, and even requires,
interpretation by the individual of the lesson which is taught. To listen
one time, then again, then again-is to hear, to learn a new lesson each
time. Masonry's chief goal is to aid each man by helping him find and
keep his best self. The principles are wonderful.
But as we face tomorrow, and tomorrow and tomorrow, is this
enough? Does the practice conform to the principles?

184

186

187

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We teach brotherly love. But we witness instances in which the
lesson is not learned. I recognize the need to screen and admit men
cautiously to membership in our order. But I pray that when a qualified
black man has the courage to apply to my lodge, that no one will say NO
because of his color.
We teach brotherly love, and are influenced by the teaching, but are
we influenced enough to make all members feel welcome in a warm
and friendly place, to reach out to sojourners and make them part of our
group?
We teach relief, but give so little. We teach truth, but do we always
know it or tell it?
How do you measure your life against the virtues of temperance,
fortitude, prudence and justice?
The greatness of this lodge has been the greatness of men freely
united who share moral commitments. Our society now suffers because
we have keedom without moral commitment. Never was there a time
when society more needed this organization than now. We need, both
here and in government, a vigorous sense of individuality and a sense
of shared purpose.
It is good for us to be proud of the organization to which we belong,
but unless we kindle such pride and belief in our institutions in others,
our organization, too, may wither and die.
We need to be diligent in making men Masons, for it is only by their
actions that other men are attracted to our order. Our Grand Master
has been saying this through this entire year. And we know it is true.
We are not looking for quantity, what we are looking for is men of
integrity who by their very existence rekindle faith. Such men will be
interested in Masonry when Masons follow the principles taught. But
such example, by even the most dedicated Mason may not be enough.
In his book, SELF RENEWAL, John W. Gardner speaks of
growth, decay and self renewal. He says a society decays when its
institutions and individuals lose their vitality. But he also points out
that we have the knowledge now to create an ever renewing society.
In that society, what matures is a system or framework within which
continuous innovation, renewal and rebirth can occur.
If we translate his language to our organization-and it seems appropriate to do so--we say that for an ever ·renewing organization, a
vital force, some programs are being born, other things are .flourishing,
still others are dying.
Because some programs surely die, we need to innovate in order to
renew.
We apparently pride ourselves on being a conservative institution.
The conservatism that preserves continuity, moral principles and our
basic beliefs is an important ingredient of Masonry.
But fewer men are attracted these days by a passive institution.
To protect tomorrow we may need to find new avenues of activity.

Let me suggest two such innovations.
FIRST:
We are vitally concerned with public education and the public
schools.
There are those who say that education might be more effective and

less expensive.
Would it not be a project worthy of this organization to undertake
an in-depth study of educational effectiveness, expense and goals by
laymen and professionals, educators and technologists? We would not
do this as partisans or advocates of change, but to provide a public
service.
The •resulting informed citizens would become the people who would
be satisfied there should be no change, or that there should be change.
It would be expensive, but not more than we could afford. It would
restore our belief in the importance of the public school. It might come
at a time critical to us and to public schools.
A SECOND such possible innovation:
Thursday morning we are hosting a breakfast dedicated to the
observance of law. The breakfast itself is an innovation. What about
going further. Why not finance and promote studies of the waiys in
which law enforcement could be more effective and justice more certain.
Again, not as advocates or partisans of the recommendations which
might result, but as a public service.
You will think of other possibilities. Do not hesitate to mention
them to the Grand Master.
Wouldn't thes~r some other programs-be innovations which
might tell people of our interest in the renewal of society? And might
they not renew us?
We believe in the social responsibility of man for man. Our principles are strong. But to protect tomorrow, we need to innovate. Few
people these days desire to belong to a passive institution.
Tomorrow is a challenge. So is the day after that. And next year.
And all the tomorrows to come. You and I as individuals will not be
here to see all of them-perhaps not even many of them-but we can
aid in preserving this institution which has from time immemorial been
dedicated to the task of aiding men aid themselves. We must innovate
and create, we must be enthusiastic, active, involved in our unique way
in the problems of our day. This institution is needed, is relevant. But
we as individuals must constantly remind ourselves of what it is that
makes it so.
We must do the things that will make it so and keep it so--tomorrow, and tomorrow and tomorrow.

proud men who defend a simple faith. My country. right or wrong. They

programs presented this year would be a difficult if not an impossible
task. We shall, therefore, make no attempt to single out any one Lodge

being fought within our communities. in our press, on the radio and
television, in our schools, in our courts, everywhere.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
The California Freemason has now completed 17 years of publication. Its purpose is to provide Masonic information and inspiration to
the Craft in California and Hawaii. Every member receives a copy. Each
Grand Master is the arbiter of the contents during his administration.
There has been a gratifying number of paid subscriptions from sojourners and from interested persons in other states. Commendation of
the California Freemason has been forthcoming from many parts of the
world. It is interesting to observe that an ever increasing number of
Grand Jurisdictions now provide a magazine for their members. Many
of these are excellent and do much to increase interest in !Masonry.
The publication and distribution of the California Freemason is administered by a board comprised of the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and the Editor-in-Chief who is appointed by the Grand Master.
The present per capita of 35 cents has been just sufficient to cover
the cost of preparing, printing, distributing and mailin9. This will suffice
for the future until such time as rising costs overtake us. Costs are
increasing and there is the prospect of increased postal rates.
The financial figures for the past year will be found in the auditor's
report.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.. F. 0 A. M. of California:
Under the appointment of Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee, the
Commission has endeavored to carry out his wishes for the administration of the Library and Museum of the Grand Lodge.
His dedication to instilling a spirit of Masonic Education into the
hearts of all Masons has been reflected in your Library's endeavor to
serve all the Masons in California and Hawaii. With the conviction that
a library is only as good as its capacity to serve the needs of an inquiring
mind, your Commission has CC11:'efully selected 24 new research volumes
for general use. In addition, we have received donations of 333 volumes.
Of special interest was the acquisition of the first five. unexpurgated,
volumes of the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California, an extremely rare addition to our holdings. A collection of pertinent volumes
of one of the most famous contemporary Masonic scholars, an active
California Mason, is now available to any member.
An interesting group of statistics deserve mention. During the year
of July 1, 1969 to June 30, 1970. the library supplied 230 books to Masons
in our Jurisdiction, while signed visitors reached an exciting level of
1,008. even though our basic schedule limits us to a five-day week. Part
of our unusual increase in visitors must be attributed to a carefully
selected experiment over a 60 day period under the guidance of Commissioner, Brother Stanley Butera. On several occasions when specific
cultural events wer~programmed on weekends at the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the Library and Museum were open for inspection.
The response was extremel<y favorable and besides the personal attention extended by our qualified personnel. brochures, such as the Grand
Lodge publication "Masonry-A Way of Life," were available for distribution. It has been the desire of your Commission and its staff to
maintain a facility which not only serves the needs of the inquiring
student and the newly inspired member. but also to present an image of
culture and dedication to the finer thoughts and spiritual philosophies of
man to the public.
Your Museum received during the same reporting period 20 new
items for display. Our facilities and Museum may be personally observed
on the second floor of the California Masonic Memorial Temple during
Grand Lodge Sessions. as well as the Monday through Friday hours of
10:00 A.M. to 3:00 P.M.
Your facility has been staffed as usual by a most dedicated group of
voluntary librarians who serve not only as assistants to the members
and guides to visitors, but also as technical workers in various labors as
catalogers of books and Museum acquisitions and repair specialists.
Their roster has grown to include: William H. Scott, William

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.. F. & A. M. of California:
The members of this Committee wish to express their appreciation
to the Grand Lock.Je and to our Grand Master, Chester R. MacPhee
for the privilege of serving. The cooperation of the Grand Master and
the Grand Lodge has again made this year a pleasure.
Your Committee held a special meeting on June 13th, 1970, for the
purpose of coordinating the activities of its members. The main topic of
the meeting was the pictorial indexing of all Lodge buildings within our
jurisdiction. A new questionnaire is being prepared for this purpose. The
members of this Committee will fill in the answers on the questionnaires
as much as possible with the information we have on hand in the Grand
Lodge files of the Masonic History Committee. Various plans were then
discussed as to the best way in which to obtain the balance of the information needed. It was decided the best way would be to send it directly
to the individual Lodge for completion. In this way no duplication of
material will be requested.
It was the consensus that this meeting was constructive and will be
helpful to each member in attendance.
This Committee was again 1'equested by Grand Lodge to report on
another historic site. This was the site of Quittman Lodge No. 88 (extinct) in North Bloomfield, Nevada County. This is in the Mother Lode

194

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

country, which is so rich in Masoni c lore. This town and Lodge site is in
the Malakaff Diggings State Historic Park. During the gold rush days
this was the site of a large placer mining operation.
The community of North Bloomfield was the adjacen t town and at
its peak had a population of about one thousan d. Quittma n Lodge No.
88 received its dispensation under the name of Unity Lodge on July 27th,
1855. It was chartere d as Quittm an Lodge on May 8th, 1956. It took its
new name from John A. Quittma n, P. G. M. of Mississippi. It first met
in Orleans Flat in Nevada County. When the digging s played out there
it moved to Moore's Flat where it met until 1887. As the gold again ran
out the Lodge moved to North Bloomfield, which was about five miles
to the southwest. It stayed in North Bloomfield until the gold of the
Malakoff ran out. In 1910, because of its dwindling membership, Quittman Lodge consolidated with Nevada Lodge No. 13. The State of California, in making this site a State Park, has marked out the site of many
of the early buildings in North Bloomfield. The site of Quittma n Lodge
has been duly marked. There is nothing left of the building except two
or three foundation posts.
At the present time the State Departm ent of Parks and Recreation
has authoriz ed the restoration of the town of North Bloomfield to its
"Gold Rush" eloquence. The Catholi c church is already in the process
of being rebuilt. The Genera l Store, which is still standin g, is being
restored . There is a museum depicting scenes and displaying artifact s
of that era. This has all been done with private or institutional funds.
It is the underst anding of this Committee that no State funds are to be
available in the near future for any of these projects.
Several Masons of Nevada County are interest ed in seeing Quittman Lodge rebuilt and restored on its original site in North Bloomfield.
They have had Mr. Robert F. Uhte, Supervisor of the Design Section
of the Departm ent of Parks and Recreation, do an estimate on the rebuilding of the Lodge. According to Mr. Uhte's research it was a two
story wood frame building. The first floor contain ed a commercial business with all of the Lodge facilities being on the second floor. The
estimat ed cost of construction is $60,000.00. This does not include the
furnishings of the Lodge room. A memorandum to Mr. Ray B. Hunter,
Deputy Directo r of the Departm ent of Parks and Recreation by Mr.
Uhte, giving a complete breakdo wn of the propose d building and its
costs is being submitted with this report.
On June 14th, 1970, Brother Paul Cowgill, of this Committee and
your Committee Chairm an attende d a Homecoming celebration at the
Park to view the site first hand. We also had the opportu nity to speak
to members of the Park Departm ent, the Forest Ranger and several of
the Brethre n interested in this project. We also had the honor and the
pleasur e of speaking to Brother Charlie Gaus, now a member of Nevada

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

195

Lodge No. 13, who was the last man raised in Quittm an Lodge No. 88 in
1909 or 1910. He is 92 years of age and is still quite active. In fact,
Brother Gaus still drives his 1924 Dodge touring car around the area.
We have asked the Brothers up there to try and get his story down on
tape.
We have since tried to contact the Departm ent of Parks and Recreation as to what other improvements are to be made in the Malakoff Park
area in the way of roads, facilities and other projections. Thus far we
have been unable to get any definite answer from them.
We, therefore, conclude our report on the restoration of Quittm an
Lodge as follows:
We believe there is historical value in the restoration of the building.
We suggest that all control of the :rebuilding and its maintenance be
in the hands of Grand Lodge. We leave all financial matters in the
hands of the Committee on Finance.

its work for the coming year we submit the following budget:

REPORT OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS
CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 6 A. M. of California:
The California Masonic Foundation has now been in existence for
a period of approximately one and a half ( 1Yi ) years, as a charitable,
non-profit corporation, tax exemption having been granted to it by both
the Federal and State governments. Reference is made to the report of
this Board published in the proceedings of the 1969 Communication of
Grand Lodge as to the details of the Foundation's organization and
functions.
Suffice it to say, at this point that the Board of Trustees is composed of fifteen ( 15) members who came from all parts of the State and
Hawaii.
The officers are as follows:
President........................................................ JOHN S. HuNT
Vice President... ......................................... LYLE E. PATTON
Secretary.............................................. HERBERT W. SMITH
T reasurer............................................................ FRED HACK
The primary purposes and objects of the foundation are to receive
gifts, devises, and bequests, and to hold, use administer, and disburse
the same in a manner not in conflict with the laws, rules, and regulations of Grand Lodge for all phases of education, including scientific
research.
SCHOLARSHIPS

In carrying out these objects and purposes, we have concentrated
during the past year on finding worthy students who, for one reason
or another, are unable to finance their educations without help from
some source other than their own families. Recommendations of these
students have usually come from the constituent Lodges. When a recommendation is received, it is followed up by our scholarship committee, the
members of which are:
HERBERT W. SMITH, Chairman
PETE FLORIO
RALPH FENSTER

The investigation of the student's eligibility for the scholarship is
thorough and comprehensive, and yet is designed to avoid embarassing
the applicant or his family. Eligibility is based upon several factors,
including the student's scholarship rating, financial need, leadership
qualities, recommendation by faculty, etc.
During the past fiscal year scholarships have been authorized for
approximately 40 students at $400.00 per scholarship. The procedure
adopted for making the actual awards will bring each Lodge which has
recommended a successful scholarship applicant directly into the picture.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

197

In each case, it is planned that the award will be made by the Master
of the Lodge in a ceremony held at the Lodge, with such members of
our Board in attendance as are able to be there.
This affords the Lodge an opportunity to accumulate some good will
in the community, and likewise give the members of our Board an opportunity to disseminate information as to what the foundation is doing
by way of assisting qualified students in the particular area to further
their educations.
This plan has been very effective insofar as the awards already made
are concerned, and as time goes on it is believed that the foundation
will become a vital force in spreading the Gospel of Masonry throughout
California and Hawaii.
Parenthetically, I would like to state that, upon the vote of our Board,
a substantial scholarship was awarded to Kristine Paymiller, one of the
young ladies who spoke today.
FINANCIAL INFORMATION

At the close of the fiscal year, (June 30, 1970), the net balance of
assets on hand was $363,983.49. This is after disbursing $15,000.00 for
scholarship grants and, we are pleased to report, after reimbursing
Grand Lodge in the sum of $14,679.31 for funds allocated to us during
the 1969 Communication.
The major portion of said balance was invested in bonds valued at
$333,003.30, and common stocks valued at $7,426.00, such valuations
in both instances being at cost. The U.C.L.A. Clubhouse property is
carried on the books at a valuation of $1.00. The foundation relies upon
the Investment Committee of Grand Lodge for advice as to investments.
Revenue during the past fiscal year totalled $21,416.43 consisting
of interest - $20,681.14, dividends - $551.83, and miscellaneous $183.46. Expenditures were: Educational grants - $15,000.00, clubhouse expenditures - $10,178.92, a total of $25,178.92. Expenditures
exceeded revenues by $3,762.49.
We regret to report that the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse has not been sold.
During the year, we had every reason to believe that a sale of this
property would be consummated on or before May 5, 1970. The buyer
was Jewish Federation Council of Greater Los Angeles and they desired
to purchase the property for the use and benefit of their students at
U.C.L.A.
We are informed that, due to objections by the students themselves,
the buyer's officers did not believe that the purchase should be completed,
and pursuant to the terms of the escrow instructions, paid the sum of
$25,000.00 to us as liquidated damages and reimbursed us for the second
half of Los Angeles City and County taxes which had been paid by the
foundation, and the escrow was mutually cancelled.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Lodge Financing is pleased to submit its annual
report for the 1969-1970 Grand Lodge year with the observation that
operative Masons are hard at work throughout the jurisdiction on the
planning, building and improving of Masonic Temples.
Even during a period of so-called tight money, with a slower rate of
building and real estate activity generally, it is rewarding to note the
diligence and tenacity with which Masons in so many areas demonstrate
their ability to house their Lodges in functional and attractive facilities
and on a fiscally sound basis. The Committee on Lodge Financing feels
privileged to work throughout the year in the vineyards of Masonry and
to share in the accomplishments of the constituent Lodges and Temple
Associations.
Great emphasis has been placed on seeking solutions in those few
cases where excessive debt has been incurred against a Temple property
or where other financial difficulties exist, as well as on avoiding a repitition of such problems in other cases. As the Committee reviews and
acts upon a constant stream of applications to purchase, lease, build or
modernize, it is gratifying to note the care and thoroughness with which
most of the applicants approach such programs.
During the last Annual Communication, while sitting in formal session, the Committee interviewed representatives of almost forty Lodges
and Temple Associations, and during the year since then has either met
with, or processed material received from , an equal number. The formal
actions taken by the Committee since its last annual report was submitted
are listed in the attached Appendix. On examining it the inference should
not be drawn that the Committee consents to every request it receives.
On the contrary, many submittals are questioned or denied, then resubmitted, so that all are finally satisfied that a sound and prudent solution
has been reached.
Also, under the direction of the Grand Master, a special committee
has been investigating the procedure for applying to the Franchise Tax
Board of the State of California for tax exempt status, and the Lodges
and Temple Associations are alerted to watch for a communication on
this matter which should be distributed shortly.
Lastly, the Committee expresses apprecation to the Grand Master,
Most Worshipful Chester R. MacPhee, for personal interest, guidance
and support: to the Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Herbert
A. Huebner, who has served in a liaison capacity between the Committee and the elective Grand Lodge line; and to the Grand Secretary, Assistant Grand Secretary, and their staff for continuing cooperation and
assistance.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It has been a busy and demanding year, and as this report is written
many additional submittals and applications are pending. The Chairman
could not possibloy handle the work load without the diligence, patience
and help of the Committee members, for which sincere appreciation is
expressed. It is hoped that the work of the Committee on Lodge Financing has been acceptable, and at this time the Grand Lodge is requested
to app:ropriate $2,000.00 for the operating expenses of the Committee
for the ensuing year.

REPORT OF CODE COMMISSIO N
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Each year for the last thirteen years, it has been the responsibility
of this Commission to prepare the Cumulative Pocket Supplement to
the California Masonic Code Annotated after the Annual Communication.
In November 1969, changes were made reflecting the legislation
passed in October of that year. Because the Pocket Supplement could
no longer have just page changes it was necessary to rearrange and reprint. Thus, this occasioned the delay in disseminating the Supplements.
It is expected that when the revised Code is adopted the loose-leaf
form will expedite preparation of amendments.
The Committee requests a budget of $500.00 for the coming year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M . of California:
The Columbia Temple Committee met twice in Columbia during
the past year. We discussed a new roof, an interior paint job, underground wiring, and a salary raise for the Custodian.
At the June 6th Conference meeting in Sonora I asked three of the
line officers to visit the Temple. I explained to them the poor condition
of the roof. It was the original roof that was put on approximately
twenty years ago. I asked if there were funds available to reroof the
building before the fall rains. They agreed that this work was advisable
and in August a new paper and tar roof was put on the Temple. The
new roof is guaranteed for twenty years. This amount is included in
our 1970-1 971 budget.
On further inspection of the building it was noted that a basement
steel door was in very bad shape and on account of the widespread vandalism at the present time it should be irebuilt.
The ceiling in the Museum has cracked in several places and it was
suggested that a structural examination be made of the building. Five
hundred dollars is in the budget for this purpose.
The Pacific Gas and Electric Company is installing underground
wiring in Columbia. This will be an improvement to the Temple, as the
unsightly power pole in front of the building will be removed.
We are asking that the salary of the Custodian be increased to eight
hundred dollars per year. When broken down this is about two dollars
twenty cents per·day.
During the past year twenty-one Lodges visited the Temple to confer degrees, also Job's Daughters Bethel No. 263 held a meeting there.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL IN LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge~ F. & A. M. of California:
The Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles with its revered atmosphere
and symbolical treasures was the site of more Masonic activity the past
year than during any other year since the State Historical Landmark
was created in 1962.
Ten special meetings were conducted in the Hall and were about
evenly divided between regular Masonic Lodges. the International
Orders of DeMolay and Job's Daughters. Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge
No. 814 meets there regularly.
Over 2,000 visitors were conducted through the Hall the past year.
They were chiefly visitors to the City of Los Angeles. A gi'eat number
of them, who are members of the Craft, identified their Lodge affiliations
as they signed the Visitors' Roster.
The Hall promises to be an even greater attraction next year with
the increased activity planned in the old Plaza section which will be
further refurbished. The opening of additional establishments will di'aw
interested spectators. The focal point of redevelopment presently is an
area near our Hall that will be created into a modern restaurant available
for banquets.
This Committee was fortunate to receive the services of Brother
Homer M. Glick, who has performed admirably in his capacity as guide
and caretaker of our old Temple at 416Yi North Main Skeet in Los
Angeles.

207

Brother Glick has made a trunk for all of the old paraphernalia,
installed new electric boxes outside the building as well as safety cables
all around the baseboards. Being a student of Masonry and Tiler of
Moneta Lodge No. 405, Brother Glick demonstrates his ability as .a
speaker when conducting tours in the Temple. He presents a Masonic
Pin to all candidates raised in the old Hall, serves coffee and donuts
when the Lodge is called from labor to refreshment, and performs maniy
duties not connected with his position as caretaker. All of this is done on
his own time and with his own money. Indeed, he is a true member of
our Craft.
The Old Temple is open Thursday, Friday and Saturday from 10:00
A.M. to 2:00 P.M. The regular Plaza guide who conducts tours around
the Old Plaza sector always stops at the Old Hall for interested and
curious sightseers to visit the site.
A plan is currently being developed by the members of this Com~
mittee to further publicize the old Temple as being an ideal site for spe~
cial Lodge meetings and for regular meetings of concordant bodies.
The old Hall was the site of the first meeting place of Los Angeles
Lodge No. 42, now in its l l 7th year since being chartered.
The budget of $1,560.00 will be sufficient to cover the caretaker's pay
and supplies for the ensuing year unless we are required to keep the
Temple open all week, instead of the regular three days, due to the
increased flow of traffic in the Plaza sector where it is located.
The year 1970 will go down in history as having been a busy season
in the annals of our Old Temple. Brethren are cordially invited to visit
this California Masonic Shrine when in the neighborhood.
Respectfully submitted,
BENJAMIN M. WEISS, Chairman
HERBERT HARGRAVE, JR.

MELVILLE H. NAHIN

WALTER H. WAYMAN

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Correspondence Committee respectfully ~ubmits this . Repo~t
covering its activities for the Masonic year which closes with this
Communication.
All proceedings of Grand Jurisdictions of the Unite~ State_s whic~
publish their proceedings and exchange published proceedings with Ca_h~
fomia, including Alaska which is published as a part of the Grand Juris~
diction of the State of Washington, Hawaii which is a part of the Grand

208

209

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Jurisdiction of the State of California, and the District of Columbia
which publishes separate proceedings, have been reviewed. All such proceedings so reviewed have been submitted to the Editorial Staff of the
California Freemason and, so far as limited space permits, some of these
reviews are in turn published in the California Freemason.
The review of the proceedings of the Grand Lodges with whom the
California Grand Lodge is in correspondence reveals that there is almost
no change in their respective problems and the solution thereof.
Losses, especially due to the large number of deaths and suspensions
for non-payment of dues, continue at a -rather alarming rate. One fact
stands out with sharp darity. We need enlightenment, vital leadership
from men who are not hesitant to look at the changes that have taken
place and who are willing to face the challenges which our modem world
presents. We need men who have the ability to research, analyze, plan
and implement: we need men who can quickly appraise the ability of
other Brothers so that consistent, imaginative, vigorous attack upon our
problems will be made.
Current records show that there are four million Masons among the
200 million plus people in the United States, or 5 %, and a quarter
million 'Masons among the 20 million inhabitants of Canada, or 8%.
The one question which occurs to all of us : "Is Masonry free?" The
answer is "No." Too many of our Brethren have interpreted the phrase
"Free Mason" as free from attending Lodge, free from fulfilling obligations voluntarily assumed, free from giving effort or time to take part in
degree work and other activities for the welfare of the Lodge and the
Craft.
Freemasonry is not free because its rights, lights and benefits can
only be purchased with time, effort and sacrifice. Let us start now to
attend and sacrifice a few other pleasures to support our great Fraternity
in which we claim to have so much pride. Anyone of us can wear a ring
or a pin and proudly state : " I am a Mason." Let us by our daily actions
prove it to ourselves and others.
Some of the problems confronting all jurisdictions are a continuing
decline in membership, lack of real interest in Masonic matters, changes
in population, civil rights and how it affects our Fraternity, the failure on
our part to appeal to more young men to enter our Masonic Craft.
Fraternal organizations are on trial during these unsettled times and
it behooves us all as Master Masons to be vigilant as to our conduct and
activity as Freemasons. As in the past. Masonry will arise out of its
apparent lethargy, but only through the joint efforts of its membership.
When one considers the Masonic stature of previous ·correspondence,
it is with considerable trepidation that this review has been written
during the past twelve months. While these articles are not intended
to be the writer's personal thoughts and work, they are intended to re-

fleet as accurately as possible the general trend and developments of
Masonry in other areas of the United States and around the world.
The Correspondence Committee has had an enjoyable and interesting
experience to follow proceedings of other Masonic Jurisdictitons and the
cause of Masonry during the year. It is hoped that this article has
brought understanding of the progress and problems of other jurisdictions closer to us, and possibly given us thereby a dearer insight into our
own problems, and an inspiration to work with greater effort for the
future of our ;Masonry in California.
Our Grand Master, Chester R. MacPhee, has taken the initiative in
discussing racial problems and, while they will not be settled for a long
time, he has not hesitated to bring them to light that we may all be better
prepared to understand them and what is the best solution therefor.
One Masonic Jurisdiction, in order to seek out the reason or reasons
that members of our Fraternity permit their membership to lapse for nonpayment of dues, sent a letter to each as he was dropped from its rolls. A
great nuumber replied, some by sending money for reinstatement and,
surprisingly, none specifically placed the blame on Masonry itself, but
rather these Brethren stated that they had failed Masonry. Invariably,
these letters indicated that these Brethren felt as though they were
unimportant and unwanted in their Lodges because of the lack of any
type of communication other than the usual request for payment of dues,
all of which indicates that the lack of communication with our membership on a regular basis is a weakness which we must overcome. The value
of communication is indicated by the fact that one jurisdiction experienced the reinstatement of 38% of those dropped for non-payment of
dues by direct communication with them.
We move that this -report be filed as read, and that the portion
thereof relating to finance for the Correspondence Committee for the
ensuing Masonic year in the sum of $440.00 be referred to the Finance
Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE W. BURCH, Chairman
