COMBINED REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
INFORMATION AND RESPONSIBILITY AND
SPECIAL SUB-COMMITTEE FOR THE
COMMUNICATION OF THE FUNDAMENTALS OF
FREEMASONRY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Th~ following material is the report of the Standing Committee on
Masonic Information and Responsibility, consolidated with that of the
Special Committee of Study for the Communication of the Fundamentals of Freemasonry.
.The Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility, constitutionally composed of 30 members and interlocked with the four Research Lodges of this Jurisdiction, succeeded the Masonic Education
Committee. The Committee was organized to present Masonic Education to the Brethren of California and Hawaii in workshop form.
At the last Communication, where the Committee received its authorization, it was instructed to assume guidance of the above named Special
Committee.
By virtue of its succession to the former Masonic Education Committee, we are also charged "to assist the officers of the constituent Lodges
in planning programs which would instill profound understanding of the
precepts of the Fraternity" (Proceedings, 1969), and "to promote and
correlate the work of the Research Lodges: review all Research Lodge
materials intended for publication: review all correspondence contemplated by Research Lodges with Grand Lodges of other jurisdictions:
to regulate the display and sale of approved publications of the Research
Lodges" (Proceedings, 1967) .
The workshops, our primary project, are the brainchild of our
projected services to the Lodges of this jurisdiction have continued to
multiply as described herein.
The Workshops, our primary project, are the brainchild of our
Grand .Master, M. W. Chester R. MacPhee. They had their genesis
some six months before you elected him to the high office to which he
has brought so much luster. He met weekly, and frequently more often,
with from six to a dozen Past Masters and Officers, for extended sessions. Finally in June of 1969, the plans for the Workshops began to
crystallize. With his guidance, encouragement and inspiration we were
ready for the initial three pilot sessions held in Los Angeles, Fresno and
San Francisco immediately following the 1969 Communication. After
conclusion of the year-end holidays and installations the program was
expanded throughout the Jurisdiction.
During this Masonic year 47 Workshops were held, including two

in Hawaii. Twenty-five were held in Northern California and twentytwo in Southern California. The division line is drawn from San Luis
Obispo to Bishop.
These Workshops were and shall continue to be voluntary as to attendance. It is our conviction that they will be worthy of perpetuation
only as long as they continue to be of interest to the Masons of our
Lodges.
One hundred ten Brethren have taken part in the Workshops this
year. Thirty of the participants are members of the Committee: the
others, volunteers. All are qualified and trained, active Masons. Workshops have been held in every part of the Jurisdiction. The aim is to
place one within reach, that is within 50 miles, of each Lodge. To accomplish this it has been necessary for some panelists to make a 300 mile
£ound trip. One of our Workshop Directors found it necessary to drive
over 700 miles. Programs have been presented to audiences of less than
10 and in some panel Workshops more than 200 were in attendance. The
size of the audience was not the criterion. Effort was expended to secure
as many qualified, local panelists as could be found . Expansion of this
group is being planned for the coming year. The panelists work from
prepared material. even to the introductions they must offer to conserve
time and to maximize audience participation.
The cooperation of the lnspectoral Corps and the Assistant Grand
Lecturers has been outstanding and has contributed largely to the early
success of the program.
The programs tJsed in the Workshops were determined over a yea£
ago in August. They were based upon two questionnaires sent to all
Senior Wardens and Inspectors of the Jurisdiction. The suggestions received resulted in the preparation of twelve subjects for presentation. We
have closed this year with sixteen subjects, as the need for additional
subjects became apparent from requests received.
In 1970 we have again sent out similar, though modified, questionnaires to the Senior Wardens and the Inspectors. We feel it is necessary to check performance, desirability of times selected, and procedures in addition to the subjects to be covered. The response this year was
quite informative. We have learned, for instance, that the "how to"
subjects related to the operational health of the Lodge, and the subjects
dealing with the principles of Freemasonry are far more interesting to
our members than some of the other subjects of a more general nature.
This information will cause a change in this area. There was an overwhelming response to the question, "Can you supply local panelists if
we furnish them the material and train them?" Unfortunately the affirmative replies were not accompanied, in many cases, by names and addresses of nominees. We would greatly appreciate receiving those names
and addresses even now.

212

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

We learned that there is practically no interest in revising the order
of the ritual work in our degrees. And the question relating to the times
chosen for presentation of the programs could well have been answered
by a shotgun, though there were a few suggestions which will improve
the scheduling in the year ahead.
The area of activity which was inherited from the Masonic Education Committee is that of publication ·review for the Research Lodges.
This was carried on by approximately ten members and associates who
are dedicated and well qualified reviewers. They examine and sometimes
offer editorial advice on all material published by the Research Lodges
for outside dissemination. It is their function to endeavor to make sure
the material is suitable to be published in this Jurisdiction with particulru:
care to avoid esoteric material and to follow the policies as expressed by
this Grand Lodge. We believe that this should be a cooperative venture
and we have striven to work, not as censors but as associates, to facilitate the important work o~ these Lodges.
Under the title of Inter-Grand Lodge Reseatth, we have this year
re-established orderly and fraternal relationships with all forty-eight
other Grand Lodges in the United States. By authority of the Grand
Master and with the guidance of the Grand Secretary, we have divided
the foreign jurisdictions into two groups of twenty-four Grand Lodges
and have maintained correspondenc e with each group. This is a completely different function from that of the Correspondenc e Committee.
We call your attention to this so that you will not be drawn into a
natural ·confusion.
It is our practice to share our materials and studies with comparable
Committee Chairmen and Grand Secretaries of other jurisdictions. We
find that they reciprocate and that the interchange of material is growing.
Most other Grand Lodges have Education Programs, usually in four
phases: they bracket the degrees with instruction before, during and
after. Massachusetts , for example, requires participation in area workshops before permitting a new member to sign the by-laws of his Lodge.
Generally, educational programs are separated from the coaching of
candidates.
For post-candidate status, our plan of education is popular. Our
system, however, is unique in limiting length of presentations and in the
promotion of the maximum of audience participation. This approach is
also used by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.
Much of the basic material for the idea of our blue folders, "Freemasonry, A Way of Life," and our orange folders, "Freemasonry, Does
It Concern Me?", was drawn from such sources. Other material. now
being accumulated, will be used in further projects if and when authorized.

You will note that the foregoing activities have all been prepared by,
and presented by the Committee. There is another area which we have
assigned entirely to a different group: The Special Committee of Study
for the Communication of the Fundamentals of Freemasonry. This is the
area of programs prepared entirely as a service to individual Lodges, and
to be administered by the officers of the Lodges under the sponsorship
of the Masters. In addition to the preparation of the program material.
the Special Committee stands ready to provide counselling and, when
requested, to implement those programs which are new to the Lodges.
This year all operations under this group are in pilot stage. Several
groups within the Committee are working with a number of Lodges,
monitoring the results and, with the feedback information, •restructuring
the plans of action. It is expected that within the next year at least one
of these programs will be sufficiently perfected so that it can be released
generally.
The Special Committee has this year completed the up-dating of
re-publication of "From a Rough to a Perfect Ashlar" and forwarded it
to each Lodge for insertion in the Lodge Manual. indexed under Education. Another accomplishment of this Committee since January has been
the preparation of the Grand Master's Bulletin to provide a direct contact
between the Grand Master and the Lodges. It also serves to furnish the
Master with material he can deliver to his Lodge Education Committee.
Alternatively this material may be used for filler in his Trestleboard. The
Bulletin provides each Master with a calendar of .M asonic Events within
this Jurisdiction for fas information and for that of the members of his
Lodge. It has initiated a Foster Father, or Widows and Orphans program in pilot form. This program has not been officially named as yet,
nor has its coverage or procedure been fully standardized for general
presentation. The program is undergoing test and reporting from about
ten Lodges at this time. A Bulletin Research project has also been instituted wherein trestleboards of all Lodges in the Jurisdiction are submitted for review and analysis. It is anticipated that the results of this
study will be published in the coming year, redounding to the benefit of
all our Lodges. Trestleboard inserts for our Lodges, on a quarterly basis,
have also been provided to assist our Lodge bulletin editors. Similru:ly,
material of a different kind has been provided for our concordant bodies:
specifkally the Scottish Rite, the York Rite and the Shrine Temples. A
Guide Lines program has been prepared and made available for inLodge education in pilot form.
This Guide Lines prog·ram is the original one, around which the
Special Committee was generated. It is reflected in the revised insert in
the Lodge Manual. This program, which had to be divorced from candidate education by the Special Committee, has now been put together in
such form that several Lodges are doing individual experimentation with

their own member-education committee. We feel con8dent that our
Lodges can handle their own programs when provided with the material
and plan of operation. It is to be hoped that with the aid of the pilot
Lodges we may modify and further improve the plan of operation.
Now, returning to the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility, composed of thirty members: we have moderated the Workshops with these members because more intensive training is desirable for
leading this activity according to its basic plan. It is amazing to note the
number of revisions, both of program and tactics. that have resulted from
this procedure. These moderators operate under the direction of the
Workshop directors. The latter supervise both the training and the
scheduling.
The Committee generates and staffs new projects as they develop,
and assigns them to their areas of specialization. Under development is a
program of special Lodge therapy. Workshop programs to cover such
things as selection of officers, training of officers and management of a
building Lodge have been prepared. These are intended as "teasers" to
indicate to the officers of our Lodges that, no matter how precarious their
Lodge's health has become, the problems are not unique nor are they
incurable. Lodge therapy will be available on call for those Lodges which
wish to have such assistance in regeneration. You will 8nd, later in the
year, a small series of open, public panels for the service of Lodges of
given areas. They will be informed that friends may be invited to learn
openly "What Masonry is and What Masonry Does, Today." These
programs will be repeated in an area about once every five years.
Under consideration is a review of the Funeral Service to cover
cremation and the deposit of ashes. The results of the study will be
presented to the Ritual Committee for consideration and possible preparation. We are also researching a pamphlet on the Examination of
Visitors, which also will be referred to the Ritual Committee. Studies are
also being made on a booklet on Common Customs and Masonic Courtesies: a booklet on definitions of common Masonic words and their
Masonic uses; a pamphlet on a factual. condensed history of Masonry:
and another on a factual, condensed history of Masonry in the United
States. In these instances the work will probably be done in conjunction
with the Masonic History Committee.
We had the opportunity this year to visit the Hawaiian part of the
Jurisdiction with the Grand Master on his visitation. Taking advantage
of that opportunity, we produced two Workshops on the Islands. We
were also successful in lining up the personnel necessary for the production of these programs in the Islands. It is the consensus of this Committee that no Mason should be denied full participation in the
advantages and programs of this Grand Lodge. regardless of the remoteness of his home or Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1969 Communication Kern River Valley Lodge U.D., which
had been under dispensation for only two months, did not apply for a
charter and their dispensation was continued. They have now petitioned
this Grand Lodge for a charter.
Their representatives have submitted the records of the Lodge for
examination by the Committee on Charters and have appeared before
this Committee. We find that the records meet all the requirements of
our laws and the interviews have been most satisfactory.
This Lodge is located in the community of Kernville, which was
originally agricultural in nature, but has now become a residential and
recreational area due to the development of Lake Isabella. The new
Lodge is serving an area with a population of approximately 20,000
within a thirty mile radius. There is ample Masonic interest, as evidenced
by the fact that the Lodge has ·received 31 petitions while under dispensation. Through the generosity of Masons in the area, a Masonic Temple
has been built and will be deeded to the Lodge, free of debt, when
chartered.
It is the unanimous recommendation of the Committee on Charters
that a charter be granted and number assigned to this Lodge as follows:
Kern River Valley Lodge No. 827 in the unincorporated community of
Kernville, in the county of Kern.
No new Lodges were instituted during the past year.
There has been referred to the Committee on Charters that portion
of the Report of the Grand Secretary relative to the change of meeting
place of certain Lodges which are listed and that portion dealing with
the consolidation of Presidio Lodge No. 354 and Parnassus Lodge No.

1. It is recommended that a joint activity be undertaken next year by

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes: The report of the
Committee on Youth Activities contains two recommendations involving
policy consideration by the Grand Lodge. Your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes reports as fellows:
1. The Committee on Youth Activities recommends that the reg~
ulations concerning fund raising activities by members of the
three youth groups be more dearly defined.
1969 Annual Communication Resolution No. 17 was adopted.
the
At
This resolution called for the preparation of a clear and concise policy
manual to aid in compliance with our laws. The manual is in the process
of being completed and in accordance with the resolution will be widely
distributed. We, therefore, feel that the present recommendation of the
Commmittee on Youth Activities is already being implemented.
2. The second recommendation is that the Committee on Youth
Activities be designated as a Standing Committee rather than
as a Special Committee.

since to do so would require legislation and, since the entire California
Masonic Code is now in the process of revision, we believe no action
should be taken until the revision is complete. The designation might then
be reassessed, if it is deemed necessary to do so. We do not, therefore,
present any motion or resolution.

concurrence in the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge~ F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Cemeteries respectfully submits the following
report of their activities for the Masonic Year 1969-1970.
Columbia Cemetery, located in the Columbia State Park, is in good
condition. The :weeds were sprayed again this year, a little late in the
season by the Future Farmers of America in Sonora but this apparently
had little effect. It was later mowed by the same organization. The Future Farmers in Sonora have been doing this work for us for several
years for what we consider a most reasonable fee. It helps t~em by giving
them some practical, on the job experience and adds to their treasury.
famestown Cemetery: This cemetery, like the Columbia Cemetery,
was also sprayed by the Future Farmers of Sonora. The results here
were fair but they still had to go in later and mow some ?f ~he weed~.
Attempts are still being made to get some of the broken rails i~ the s~ht
rail fence replaced. It is hoped that it will be done before this co~ing
spring. Trimming of the oak trees is being held up for re-evaluatt~n.
Some of the limbs which were thought to be dead are now sprouting
..
.
new growth.
Both the Columbia and Jamestown Cemeteries are m good condition
and under the direct supervision of Brother Marcel Baer of Sonora.
Fiddletown Cemetery: Due to an early dry season, it was not a~vis­
able to bum leaves and weeds at the Fiddletown Cemetery. There is no
water available in this cemetery and the dry grass on the adjacent property created a hazard. The local disposal company has agreed to leave
a large suitable container for the next clean-up .. The cost for the use
and removal is estimated at $15.00. Some of the live oak trees that were
removed have started to sprout again and present a problem. We have
been advised that they can be poisoned and this is being done. The
Amador Agriculture Commission has. been spraying th~ weeds ~t a cost
of approximately $20.00 per acre. This ~as h.elped con~iderably in keep.
ing the weeds to a minimum. The practice will be continued.
Two burials have been made in the Fiddletown Cemetery this year.
Early in the year Mrs. Ada Bessie Howdy was buried in the Howdy
family section which is designated as Plot No. 17. In March, Brother
Luther Chase was buried and a second lot was sold to Mrs. Chase for
future use. These lots are designated as numbers 41 and 42 on our map.
Fiddletown Cemetery is in good condition and is under the direct
supervision of Brother Vincent V. Lake of Lodi.
Peter Lassen Grave in Susanville: The work of cleaning, repairing
and preserving the Peter Lassen ·g rave and two monuments has progressed in a most satisfactory manner. The bases of b~th monuments
have been reinforced with steel and concrete, cement curbings have been
put around each of them and the area covered with cinder rock. The

223

old original marker is in a bad condition due to weather and vandalism.
A chain link fence has been placed around it and a protective roof covering installed. It has made the area most attractive and will prevent
further damage by people carving their initials in the stone or chipping
off pieces as souvenirs. A new redwood turnstile gate has been installed
at the entrance and the memorial rock at the entrance has been reinforced.
Some work remains to be done at this grave but it is in good condition. This work has been under the supervision of Brother J. Wilbur
Combes and the Inspector, Elmer Glenn Van Tassell.
Michigan Bluff Masonic Cemetery: All the necessary survey work
has been done and the maps for filing are complete and have been approved by the Placer County Public Works Department. All necessary
documents have been turned over to Judge Ronald Cameron. We are
waiting for him to grant us title to this cemetery. Our share of the attorney fees and other costs to date in the amount of $179.69 have been
paid. There may be some additional nominal expense later.

they attend Grand Lodge in such capacity only.

F1:ancisco has been taken from the published records of the California
State Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of
Hawaii to San Francisco has been taken from the published records of
air lines, in accordanc e with Sections 174 and 176, California Masonic
Code. No compensation is allowed to members from San Francisco or
the immediate vicinity. Compensa tion of members from the State of
California has been computed on the basis of ten ( 10) cents per mile, the
rate fixed by the Committee on Finance. Compensa tion of members from
the State of Hawaii has been figured on the basis of published first class
round trip air rates of regularly scheduled major air lines, from Honolulu
to San Francisco, plus inter-islan d air fare to Honolulu when necessary.

To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge~ F. & A. M. of California:
The Retirement Income Plan for the benefit of employees of the
Grand Lodge and its agencies was made effective January 1, 1955 for
employees of the Masonic Homes of California and was subsequen tly
amended as of January 1, 1956 to cover employees of the Grand Lodge
of California and as of December 8, 1958 to cover employees of compo•
nent organizations.
Amendme nts to the original Plan during the years of its operation
have provided substantia l improvements for covered employees. It is
the opinion of this committee that a new study of the Plan should now
be made in light of current practices and trends. To this end, our actuaries will be requested to meet with this committee.
During the current Grand Lodge year, a change in actuaries has
been made and we are now represente d by the firm of Coates and Craw•
ford. In addition to the able representa tion which this firm affords, it is
anticipate d that there will be a savings in fees for actuarial services rendered.
Analysis of the report furnished by the actuaries for the calendar
year ended December 31, 1969 for the Masonic Homes of California
shows that there were 106 covered employees in the Plan and that 27
employees eligible for retirement benefits are now receiving annual pen•
sions totaling $14,651.00. A similar report for the Grand Lodge of California and its components shows that there were 15 covered employees
in the Plan and that 16 employees eligible for retiremen t benefits are now
receiving pensions totaling $21,128.00 per annum.
Employer pension obligations for covered employees as of October
1, 1961 were fully funded at that time. Current contributions to the
Plan consist of an employee contribution rate of 3% per annum on regular salary plus the employer contribution rate which is determined from
time to time by the actuaries. The contributions by employer and employee, together with gains kom investments, were calculated to main·
tain the Plan on a sound financial basis.
However, during the calendar year 1969, and to date in 1970, the
portfolio of investments held as security for pension obligations has
suffered losses which can be considered above average due to investment
policies carried out by the Trustee for the Plan and to the unsettled condition of the securities market. The latter has ,r esulted in some securities
currently held in the portfolio having a market value less than cost.
This situation requires an adjustmen t in the employer service contribution rate for the calendar year 1970. Based on calculations prepared
by the actuaries, your committee reports that for the Masonic Homes
of California the employer contributi on rate on covered payroll will in·

Your Retirement Pension Plan Committee is of the opinion that component organizations should bear their share of employer contributions
and the following resolution adopted last year by the committee but not
implemented by action of Grand Lodge is now offered:
"WHERE AS. at the 1958 Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California, a resolution was adopted including in the Masonic
Homes of California Retiremen t Plan employees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, the Boards of Relief and the Masonic Clubhouses with the further provision that Grand Lodge should pay the
employer' s portion of the premium for the several entities joining the
Plan, and
"WHERE AS, each of these entities operate on their own budgets,
and
"WHERE AS, it seems unfair to require non-member Lodges of said
Boards of Relief to indirectly support Boards of Relief activities without
obtaining any benefits from the same,
"NOW. THEREF ORE. BE IT RESOLV ED that the Retiremen t
Plan Committee recommends to Grand Lodge that each of the component entities, members of the Masonic Homes of California Retirement
Plan, be required to assume their full responsibilty under the Plan by
being obligated to pay its fair share of employer's premium required for
participating employees of the several componen t entities."
Adoption of this resolution will reverse action taken at the 1958
Annual Communication (see pages 60 and 61, 1958 p,roceedings) whereby Grand Lodge approved payment of employer's contributi ons for
agencies by Grand Lodge.
Your committee has reviewed the provisions in the Retirement Income Plan and Trust Agreemen t relating to rights and powers of the
Trustee to hold, invest, reinvest, manage and administer the Fund for
the benefit of the members, annuitants and beneficiaries under and in
accordanc e with the Plan. The contended sole power of the Trustee in
this connection is debatable in the opinion of this committee.
We therefore recommend that in connection with the proposed study
of the Plan by our actuaries and this committee, a revision of applicable
sections in the Plan be made placing authority for the investment and

We suggest, in view of anticipated increased activities and meetings

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Report of the Committee on Retirement Plan has been referred
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. Said report contains
a resolution that each of the component entities which is a member of the
!retirement plan, which plan is called the "Masonic Homes of California
Retirement Plan," be required to assume its share of the employer's
premium required by its participating entities.
The total premium required by the Retirement Plan naturally de~
pends upon the number of employees of the different entities whose em~
ployees are within the plan. Since 1958, for example, the employees of
Boards of Relief may participate in the retirement and each such em~
ployee contributes 3% of his salary into the funds. Although the em~
player of such employee is one or another of the Boards of Relief, the
employer's contribution is paid by the Grand Lodge rather than the
actual employer. a Board of Relief or some other entity. Your Commit~
tee on Retirement Plan has recommended that each particular employer
pay its own share of the employer's premium. This Committee approves
the policy inherent in the recommendation. I move the adoption of said
resolution and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recom~
mends a "yes" vote.
Adopted.

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1970

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its twentieth year of activity,
and herewith renders its report for the twelve months ended June 30,
1970. Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background
and basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule, in modified form, was adopted by and for
Grand Lodge at the 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges
a Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent
Lodges. but Grand Lodge makes the services of its Investment Advisor
available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are making use of this service.
The following is Moody's report of activities for Constituent Lodges
for the year ending June 30, 1970:

The Investment Committee hopes that the Lodges are making full
and continuing use of this valuable service.
We would also like to call your attention to the fact that there is a
circular issued by Grand Lodge regarding the investment of funds by
Constituent Lodges. which is available at the Grand Secretary's office.
It is my understanding that a copy of this circular or reprint of Section
403 with respect to investments by Constituent Lodges has been inserted
in the new Lodge Manual.
Since its inception, the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. This has now been changed so that the Committee
meets every two months. Between meetings the business of the Com~
mittee is conducted by correspondence or telephone. The Committee is
available at all times, should special meetings be advisable or necessary.
As stated, we have just completed twenty years of operations. The
following is a summary of the consolidated market value of the securities
owned, plus investable cash, together with a record of dollar income

on these investments, beginning with November 30, 1950, and for each

During the past year secuTities were sold at prices yielding $648,~
779.04 less than cost. Since the inauguration of the Prudent Man Rule
in 1950, sales have increased the total asset value by $6,360,269.99. Sales
always remain a part of capital assets, and are never included in income
totals. With respect to the Endowment Fund, no capital assets are ever
withdrawn.
Endowment Fund contributions made through the Lodges during
the year amounted to $919,392.16. Other contributions to the Endow~

and Donations (organizations and individuals) $7,610.14. Gifts and
Bequests to the General Fund amounted to $1.315,442.70 (which also
includes real estate and items other than stocks and bonds). The
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees determines how these gifts and bequests are allocated-such allocations are made in accordance with
specific bequests, or in the absence of such at the direction of the Trustees. The Endowment Fund contributions remain in that fund, and only
the income is used.

expanded our acreage in Coachella Valley where we are operating about
350 acres of citrus. Much of this acreage, both in Florida and in Coachella Valley, is young and will not show a profit for several years.
"Our land development subsidiaries continue to do very well and
we feel quite optimistic in spite of the contingen t liabilities that these
subsidiaries have generated . The future of any land development in this
area appears to be based on the ability to obtain financing and we would
have to solve this problem before undertakin g any new projects."
The entire portfolio is listed in the Grand Treasurer 's and Auditor's
reports, and therefore is not included herein. The securities are always
held in safekeeping for account of Grand Lodge by the Trust Department of the Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One Montgom ery
Street office, San Francisco.
We have had excellent attendanc e at our Investmen t Committee
meetings during the year, as has been the case since this Committee was
organized . It was a pleasure to have Most Worshipf ul Chester R. MacPhee, Grand Master, and members of our Grand Lodge elective line
present and for luncheon at a number of our meetings.
Again we come to that portion of the Investmen t Committee report
where we try to summarize in a few words our thoughts as to the financial and investment outlook. We asked our Investmen t Advisor to prepare a statement for us, and it follows:
"We believe that the economy is in a period of important transition.
The current period of pessimism and uncertaint y resulting from the
sharpest stock market decline since World War II, concern about the
financial viability of the Wall Street community, considerable domestic
social unrest and the Vietname se and Middle East conflicts have resulted in changing dynamics of the economy.
"Our investments in the portfolio continue to be made in accordanc e
with the Prudent Man Rule. The bonds being purchased continue to be
high grade, and stocks being accumulated are of companies with excellent managements, strong market positions, sound financial structures ,
good product lines, and above-ave rage earnings prospects.
"Historica lly, the performan ce of the United States economy has
been characteri zed by periodic structural shifts that extend for meaningful time periods and create opportunities for significant changes in
investment strategy. We intend to pursue a conservatively aggressive
approach to our investment manageme nt."
We again repeat that our course of action can be quite different
from that of an individual for a variety of reasons. This statement is
made so as not to unduly influence individuals in their personal investment programs.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his staff, and to the Grand
Lodge officers who attended meetings from time to time. My thanks

also to the members of the Investmen t Committee for their wholehear ted
and generous cooperation at all times.
Respectfu lly submitted on behalf of the Investmen t Committee:

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTE E ON
CODE REVISION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Committee as it is presently constituted has for the last two
years, by direction of Past Grand Master Crigler and Grand Master
MacPhee, worked to revise the existing California Masonic Code.
At 6.rst it was thought that an earlier endeavor to rewrite the entire
Code was the procedure to follow. However, after a detailed review of
the existing Code and a meeting with the elective line Grand Lodge
officers and Elbert Davis, Past Grand Lecturer, it was decided to utilize
the basic Code and to delete duplications, remove inconsistencies, and
make as little substantive change as necessary.
With these guide lines in mind, your Special Committee has completed a draft of the proposed revised California Masonic Code Annotated, which has been disseminated in limited quantities for review.
It is the sincere belief of your Committee that an annotated Code as
used before presents the most practical and efficient method of setting
forth our Masonic Law. The proposed revised Code has, however, in
some instances, incorporated some of the annotations in the basic Code
Sections. In some cases, several annotations, by rewriting the basic sections, have been eliminated. These might be considered as substantive
changes, but the Committee has been careful to do only such combining
where the annotations have in effect become law by being consistently
invoked, or the annotations did much to relieve the confusion registered
by the wording of the basic section.
We are also recommending to Grand Lodge that a new format
be used for the California Masonic Code Annotated. This format is a
loose-leaf binder where pages can be inserted or removed with legislative changes, without the need for an annual pocket part.
Also, the proposed revised Code has a new numbering system. This is
being done to give the revised Code elasticity so that it can be used for
many years without the need for additional revisions.
Your Committee has also prepared the proposed revised Code so

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

241

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

240

that all forms used by Grand Lodge may be found in a special appen~
dix at the back of the book. Each form will be numbere d to correspo nd
to the Code Section from which it stems. Such a procedur e will make it
easier to locate all the forms, and as a form is not trul;y a part of the
Californ ia Masonic Code but only the means to carry out the intended
purpose of the Code, they can be changed from time to time as deemed
appropri ate by the Grand Secretar y's office.
The draft of the proposed ·revised Californ ia Masonic Code Anno~
tated has had limited review by the elective line Grand Lodge Officers.
the members of the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General
Purposes , as well as the Grand Secretar y and persons he has asked to
assist in this endeavor. Also, the Committee has been very fortunate to
have had the untiring assistanc e and counsel of Elbert (Bill) Davis, Past
Grand Lecturer. His knowled ge of Masonry and Californ ia Masonic
Law has been a source of guidance througho ut the work. To him we owe
a deep debt of gratitude. Our work is not, however, completed. Further
review of the draft must be made in conjunction with Jurisprudence and
Policy and General Purpose. Also, the cross referencing must be <:om~
pleted as well as an appropri ate index prepared .
With the status of the draft at present we expect all the remaining
matters can be attended to and that during 1971 the Revised Code can be
printed and distributed.
The Committee requests a budget of $2,250.00 for the coming year.
Respectf ully submitted,
HARLAN P. HUEBNE R, Chairman

REPOR T OF SPECIA L COMM ITTEE ON
COMM ERCIA LISM
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism herewith submits its report for
the year just ending.
Our symbolic lodges and concorda nt bodies (Scottish Rite and York
Rite) have presente d no serious problems. Constan t supervision and at~
tention, however, are required as to the appenda nt and prerequisite
organizations. The infractions occurring during this past year have been
of minor nature. No Masonic trials have resulted from any of the
violations.

Substant ially all of the infractions of our laws, rules and regulations
have been handled through discussions with the offending parties and an
understa nding that said parties will cease and desist from future
violations.
Example s of the kinds of infractions handled during this iyear are
hereinaf ter briefly mentioned so that violations of similar characte r will
not occur in the future:
A violation occurred by the act of a Shrine club arrangin g with a
newspap er to issue a "memorial supplem ent" in the paper publicizing the
50th annivers ary of the Shrine club. The club failed to advise the news~
paper that no Mason or Shriner could advertise in the said supplement.
When the supplement was published it appeared that a number of in~
dividual Masons and Shriners had place advertise ments in the said
supplement. (The Shrine club did not receive any of the proceeds from
such advertisi ng.)
A full explanat ion was made by the Presiden t of the Shrine club to
this Committee. It was apparen t that the violations were the result of
ignoranc e of the individuals.
Another type of violation encounte red was the illegal formation of
an organiza tion called "Interna tional Masonic Radio Network ." The
formation thereof was commenced by a member of this jurisdiction. The
organiza tion was to require that all members be Master Masons or members of the Eastern Star; dues were to be $3.00 per annum; and a Directory was to be published listing the names of the members and their
radio call letters. The first Director y containe d approxim ately 26 pages
of names of members.
This matter came to the attention of the Committee prior to the
mailing of the initial Director y to its members. We have now been advised that all of said Director ies have been destroye d; that no Drrectories
shall be published in the future.
The main violation of our rules and regulatio ns was in the creation
of what purports to be an organiza tion requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition to membership. Section 332.1 in the 1969 Supplem ent to the
Californ ia Masonic Code prohibits any Mason residing within this jurisdiction from becoming a member of any such organiza tion unless such
organiza tion existed in the jurisdiction on Septemb er 27, 1957.
In addition to attemptin g to handle violations of our rules and regulations, the Committee has acted in an advisory capacity. when requested, in order to avoid violations:
Ben Ali Temple wished to sponsor and produce a rodeo at the California State Exposition and Fairgrou nds. The proceeds were to be used
for expenses in operatin g the Temple. In order that there be no violation of our rules and regulations. the Potentat e requeste d approval from
the Most Worship ful Chester R. MacPhee , Grand Master of Masons in
California. The matter was referred to this Committee which advised
1

Received by Grand Master. Referred to Committees on Finance
(budget allocation), and on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
At the 1969 Communication a resolution was presented that the
Committees on Commercialism and on Policy and General Purposes prepare a policy manual on permissible and prohibited practices as to commercialism, fund raising and related activities.
Such a manual in incomplete form is at hand. If it were finalized and
published at this time it would be necessary to key it into the present
Masonic Code, for it could not be keyed into the revision which is not
adopted at the moment. To finalize, publish and distribute a manual
keyed to sections which might be renumbered, re-arranged or modified
would be ill advised.
Therefore, I move that the preparation and presentation to the Grand
Lodge of a Manual on Commercialism be continued to the 1971 Annual
Communication. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes."
Adopted.

REPORT OF SPECIAL IN-DEPTH STUDY COMMITTE E
1969 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMME NDATION NO. 4
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Pursuant to a recommendation made by Grand Master Crigler to
Grand Lodge at its 1969 annual communication, a resolution was adopted
"that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to make
an in-depth study of the administration and operation of our Grand
Lodge and its entities toward effecting any possible economy or increased
efficiency."
The resolution was implemented by Grand Master MacPhee by the
appointment of the following committee to pursue the In-Depth Study.
Chairman: W. Stanley Davis, C.P .A. and member of the Grand
Lodge Committee on Taxation.
Member: Jam es Craven, Public Accountant and member of the
Board of Trustees, California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Member: Guy B. Mize, P.G.M., Trustee, Masonic Homes of
California and former member of the Special Finance Study
Committee and the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance.
The committee met immediately to organize and establish a course of
action. Recognizing the extensiveness of the task, the committee, with
the approval of Grand Master MacPhee, invited Phil N. Myers, P.G.M.,
a former member of the Finance Committee and of the Masonic Homes
Board, and currently chairman of the Grand Lodge Audit Committee together with John A . .Sickenberger, Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance, and also a former member of the Special Finance
Study Committee, to serve as consultants to the committee.
The committee was directed to include all entities ultimately involved
financially with the Grand Lodge. In addition to the Grand Lodge itself
this was to include the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic Foundation, and the California Masonic Memorial Temple. The
committee included consideration of the Retirement Fund for employees
of Grand Lodge and its entities. The survey did not indude the Board
of Control or the Committee on Lodge Financing or other committees
of the Grand Lodge.
Your committee held a series of meetings, reviewed various reports
prepared in previous years by public accountants and by members of
Grand Lodge engaged in special studies, visited the Masonic Homes at
Decato and Covina, surveyed the Grand Lodge office as it relates to the
operations of Grand Lodge and the administrative functions of the Masonic Homes, the Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation. In the course of these meetings, we discussed various problems
with individuals who met with the committee. Your committee was
acutely aware of its responsibility not to criticize or to commend without

245

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

thorough knowledge and consideration. In short, its aim was to review
the administration and operations as objectively as possible.
In connection with the annual audit performed by a public accounting firm for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1969, the auditors prepared
two supplemental reports of operations of the Grand Lodge and its entities. One report dealt with the Grand Lodge, the California Memorial
Temple and the California Masonic Foundation and the other report
dealt with the Masonic Homes of California. The reports were titled
"Memorandum on Accounting Pi'ocedures and Internal Control." The
reports, and the recommendations contained therein, were reviewed
carefully by this committee. We specifically mention these reports and
recommendations as they appear to have created groundless rumors and
baseless speculations throughout segments of this Grand Lodge. Your
committee met with a representative of the public accounting firm and
was assured that their memorandum reports were of a routine nature and
followed a policy of submitting recommendations to all clients after each
examination or audit.
Subsequently, the public accounting firm advised the Grand Master
by letter (Exhibit A ) of the conference with this committee and emphasized that their recommendations were not designed to be critical of the
officers and employees of the various Masonic entities. On March 10,
1970, Grand Master MacPhee issued a comprehensive twenty-one page
commentary, accompanied by several exhibits, designed to lay unsupported rumors to rest, his report going to those brethren engaged in the
management of the several Grand Lodge entities mentioned in the socalled memorandum reports prepared by the public auditors.
This report is divided into four sections: organization, accounting,
internal control and mechanization.

It also appears clear that it is the intention of Grand Lodge that the
administration of these policies is to be carried out through designated
officers of the Grand Lodge. It was not by accident that the Code provides that the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer also act as the
Secretary and as the Treasurer of constitutional boards.
At this point, we recommend that the Code be amended to make clear
that the Grand Treasurer is the Treasurer of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple in view of the fact that the Grand Treasurer acts fully
in that capacity at the present time.
Your committee finds no reference of any kind to the California Masonic Foundation in the Code. We believe that it is in the best interests
of the Craft that the California Masonic Foundation be covered in the
Code as are the other entities of Grand Lodge, and we so recommend.
We further believe that the same organizational pattern should be
followed whereby the Grand Master appoints the trustees and the Grand
Secretary and the Grand Treasurer act as the Secretary and as the
Treasurer of the Foundation.
Your committee believes that it is a sound requirement that the
Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer be responsible, when so
designated, for the implementation of established policies of the Grand
Lodge and its entities. This procedure is sound and is the only way the
organization can fu~ction. A continuing observance of good organization contributes more than anything else to economy and efficiency of
operations.
Most of the administration of the affairs of Grand Lodge and its entities takes place in the office of the Grand Secretary. Most of the personnel are designated as Grand Lodge employees but some are designated
as Masonic Homes employees. For the most part these employees work
interchangeably for all organizatitons. The personnel designated as Masonic Homes employees are not eligible for California Unemployment
Insurance and subject the organization to a higher rate for workmen's
compensation insurance than applies for other employees doing similar
work in the Grand Lodge office.
Your committee recommends that all clerical-administrative personnel in the Grand Lodge offices be considered to be employees of the
Grand Lodge and under supervision of the Grand Secretary. Their duties should be defined by the Grand Secretary and all of said personnel
should perform such work as is administratively necessary for each of
the entities of Grand Lodge. The cost of all clerical-administrative personnel would then be under review of the Grand Lodge Finance Committee. The entities other than Grand Lodge would reimburse Grand

ORGANIZATION

The organizational structure of Grand Lodge is complex. It is comprised of the Grand Lodge governed by the officers elected by the Grand
Lodge. The Grand Master in turn appoints trustees to govern the
Masonic Homes, the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the
California Masonic Foundation, which become semi-autonomous bodies.
The Grand Master also appoints members of various boards and committees such as the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, which adds to
the complexity of the organization.
There is no question but that the Grand Master, acting for the Grand
Lodge, as prescribed by the California Masonic Code, determines the
general policy of the entire organization. The trustees of the several constitutional boards in turn determine the operating policies of their several
entities. For example, the implementation of operating policies of the
Memorial Temple is carried out by its manager who is appointed by the

246

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Lodge pro rata for administrative costs as determined by the Grand Secretary and approved by the Finance Committee in consultation with the '
Grand Secretary and the entities involved.
AccouNTING

Directly or indkectly most of the functitons of the Grand Lodge office are involved with accounting. They include maintaining records of
nearly a quarter of a million members, custodianship of over fifty million dollars of assets. and annual receipts of approximately two and a
half million dollars. Four separate corporations are involved and five
general ledgers are required. Ten employees are engaged in the accounting and membership records, six secretaries are employed, three employees work in the supply room. all administered through the office of
the Grand Secretary. It is truly a large and complex operation.
Your committee has reviewed the operations and the functions of the
various employees. We are satisfied that the work is performed economically and that the personnel is required due to the singular demands
of the organization.
The end result of most accounting work is in reports. We have reviewed the various statements prepared in the Grand Lodge office and
believe most of them are desirable and necessary. It is recognized that
there is danger of the officers and trustees, or other officials. of Grand
Lodge and its entities making ever increasing requests for reports and
statements. It is also well recognized that, once established, reports and
statements are seldom discontinued and tend to proliferate.
Your committee did not believe that it was essential for it to attempt
to evaluate the present reports and statements. We do recommend that
the necessity of each report be examined by the officers or trustees of the
organization that requires it and that outdated or unnecessary reports
be eliminated. We would suggest also that the frequency of reports be
considered and that semi-annual or quarterly reports. rather than
monthly reports, be employed wherever possible.
Accounting is performed on a cash basis modified only slightly by
recognition of some prepaid items. Under this method of accounting.
revenues and expenses generally are recorded at the time of receipt or
payment of cash.
From time to time recommendations have been made that an accrual
method of accounting be adopted. It has been claimed that satisfactory
measurement of operating results can be achieved only in this manner.
Such a system would require that income be ·r ecorded when earned and
that expenses be recorded when incurred. This would, for example, require recordings of dividend income when declared instead of when received. It would require amortization and accumulation of bond premium
and discount.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

247

Your committee has considered carefully these suggestions. We point
out that Grand Lodge and its entities are not a business in a normal
sen.se. I.n addition. your committee is aware that most non-profit organizations m the n~tu.re of frate~nal groups find cash basis accounting adequate and that 1t 1s not considered to be an improper method for such
organizations.
. The principal interest in accounting data for a non-profit organization, such as ours, is in the flow of cash which is well provided for by
our present method. Accrual accounting necessarily would lead to estimates whi~h ma! provide less accuracy and informaton than the present
met~od. Financial statements that show income that is not immediately
a~ailable for use. or expenses that have not been paid could make unduly
difficult the understanding of the financial statements. Your committee
has considered the increased costs of clerical work that accrual accounting would require and cannot justify the cost.
Some recommendations for accrual accounting have been made on the
basis that it would demonstrate a more accurate financial statement for
the Masonic Homes. for example, by considering depreciation. future
care c~mmitments an~ other items primarily of interest to governmental
agencies. Your committee believes that if such information becomes essential. adequate supplemental reports may be prepared without changing the basic present methods.
.~e ·reco_mmend that the accounting method of Grand Lodge and its
en~1tles continue to be the present cash basis modified only by certain prepaid expenses.
From time to ti~e recommendations are made and occasionally
adopted that depreciation expense be charged on long term assets and
that allowances for depreciation be shown in the balance sheets. This
is desirable in commercial enterprises but is generally understood to be
meaningless in non-profit organization accounting. Such a practice would
only make sense if funds were set aside to an amount equivalent to the
depreciation provided. The funding of reserves for depreciation is unnecessary and undesirable and injects in the financial statements an expense that does not involve the flow of cash. It should be pointed out that
any replacement of depreciable assets would come from contributions
and from reserves derived from other sources.
Your committee recommends that depreciation not be charged on the
books of any of the entities of Grand Lodge.
A recommendation was made that responsibility accounting be
adopted. This involves control of costs by identifying the costs with
the person or department responsible for the incurring of the cost. It is
usually considered as the relationship between the budget and the accounting systems. Your committee considered the suggestion and believes
that adequate responsibility accounting already exists in the Grand

The code provides:
( 1 ) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secret ary to collect all
moneys due the Grand Lodge, keep a correct account thereof
in proper banks, and pay the said money, within ten days
after its receipt to the Grand Treasu rer.
( 2) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secret ary to establish in
some bank an operati ng fund in such amoun t as the Grand
Master may approve, from which he shall pay such bills,
claims and deman ds upon the Grand Lodge.
( 3) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secret ary to draw warran ts
upon the Grand Treasu rer for all approp riation s by the
Grand Lodge, for all orders of the Grand Master to meet
cases of emerge ncy that maiy arise in a recess of the Grand
Lodge, and for reimbursement of the operati ng fund for such
amoun ts as have been disbursed in payme nt of bills, claims
and deman ds upon the Grand Lodge, but in the presen tations

(4) It shall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer to receive all

thereof. and immediately upon receipt of said moneys, to

as are not recorded in accordance with generally accepted
accounting principles.

Your committee is convinced that the Code provides excellent internal control with responsibilities soundly divided between the Grand
Treasurer and the Grand Secretary, subject always to review by auditors. Further, we recommend that the procedures set forth in the Code
be strictly adhered to and not be deviated from for convenience or otherwise and, if for any reason the Code is not operable it should be changed.
Your committee believes that by all implication where the Code provides the duties of the Grand Secretariy and the Grand Treasurer they
apply with equal force to the other entities of Grand Lodge where the
same individuals serve, or should serve, as Secretary and as Treasurer
bylaw.
Your committee does not suggest that major deviations from the
Code exist but has observed various minor alternatives which have developed which could weaken the internal controls provided. As an example, the auditors made an observation on the control of the facsimile
signatll!I'e plate used in the check signing machine. Actually, according
to the Code, there is no reason for the Grand Treasurer to have a facsimile plate in the Grand .Lodge office. The Grand Secretary has the
duty of paying all bills from the operating fund. The Grand Treasurer
or the Assistant Grand Treasure would periodically sign checks to reimburse the operating funds.
Auditors have made observations concerning one weakness in internal control concerning membership of the Grand Treasurer on the Investment Committee. They were concerned about too much authority
being centered in one individual. They pointed out in their memorandum
report that the Grand Treasurer, as a member of the Investment Committee, can implement authorized security transactions , can sign checks in
payment for same, and is associated with an investment firm through
which some of the security transactions have been cattied out.
Over the many years of its existence, the Grand Lodge of California
has been singularly blessed with a continuing succession of great
Masons, leaders in the business and financial worlds, who have lent
their talents to our Grand Lodge in the office of Grand Treasurer and as
investment counsellors. None of our leaders of the past stand higher
than our present Grand Treasurer who has given so much and so freely
of himself to Masonry and to this Grand Lodge.
The comments of the public auditors bear no personal connotation s as
to any of our fine Grand Lodge staff of employees or to Grand Lodge
officers. The comments were solely on a technical point-that of the
possibility of conflicting interest at some future time. We must agree that
the comments of the public auditors point up a weakness in internal control and an unfair position in which to place any Grand T,reasurer.
Our general review points up an organization al problem which gives
this committee concern and that is in the Code reference to the Invest-

Your committee considered the Retirement Fund to be an entity
which was involved financially with Grand Lodge and accordingly reviewed its operations. The Retirement Fund, originally created for the
benefit of employees of the Masonic Homes of California was subsequently amended to provide retirement benefits for employees of the
Grand Lodge and other of its entities. It is now operated as a common
fund to provide pensions for those covered under the terms of the Retirement Plan and Trust Agreement. As such we believe a more correct
designation of the Plan would be the Grand Lodge Retirement Income
Plan and we so recommend. The fund is audited by public accountants
designated by Grand Lodge. The acturial work is performed by actuaries designated by the Retirement Pension Plan Committee. The trustee

Your committee has read an interim report of the Grand Lodge Audit

tee consider the question as to whether an Audit Committee will be necessary after the end of the current Masonic year. The Audit Committee points out that with regulations clearly setting forth definite ceilings
on reimbursable expenses adopted by Grand Lodge at the 1969 Annual
Communication, auditing of expense claims could be performed under

e agree that the work of the Audit Committee is a duplication of

any type of expense .that the public auditors be requested administratively to so extend their audit tests. We are also of the opinion that a
program of test checks could be performed by the Finance Committee to
insure conformity with Grand Lodge regulations. In times past, test
checks by members of the Finance Committee were valuable in giving
them a more complete understanding of the over-all financial picture of
Grand Lodge.
In concluding these comments on internal control, your committee
wants it to be known that no serious deficiencies were observed. There
is administrative respect for internal control and constant attention is
being given to it.
MECHANIZATION

The volume of accounting transactions and the requirements for
membership information suggests that modern data processing methods
may be used to advantage by the Grand Lodge. Such suggestions have
been made and there may have been implied criticism that a mechanization program has not been further advanced.
Your committee is well aware that data processing by modern
electronic equipment is a difficult and very expensive program. It would

251

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

be relatively easy to rush such a program into being: however, the risk
of failure is real and the waste of large development costs is possible.
Successful data processing installations are the result of excruciating
plannin g. It should also be appreci ated that such installations do not
general ly result in savings of personnel or money, but they may contribute operating advanta ges.
We have been impressed with the sound approac h of the Grand
Lodge staff to the problems of mechanization. It was found that thr:
Grand Secretary, the Assista nt Grand Secreta ry and the Chief Accoun ting Officer are well versed in data processing and have been considering
machines, methods and costs for a number of years.
We were further impressed with the records already handled by data
processing methods which include data on endowm ent fund contributions, accounts payable distributions and expense summaries for the Masonic Homes. The mailing list for the California Freema son is prepare d
by modern data processing methods. The billing of the annual returns is
machine calculated and printed. At the present time, installation is in
process for machine recording of all cash receipts.
The present program of careful analysis and cautious progress is
sound and should result in successful and economical development.
Grand Lodge is indebte d to its administration in that it did not become
involved with an impetuous and costly program common to so many data
processing installations.
Your committee recommends that funds be made available for outside consultants if or when they appear to be desirable and that, at a
proper time, Grand Lodge might consider a special committee of its members knowledgeable in data processing to assist in further development.
SUMMA RY

This committee was charged by this Grand Lodge to make a study
toward effecting any possible economy or increased efficiency.
Your committee believes that this report conclusively illustrates that
economy and efficiency can only derive from a cohesive organization of
Grand Lodge and its entities. Under the Code, there can be but one
Grand Master and he with ultimate power over Grand Lodge and all
entities. There can be but one financial officer, the treasurer, responsible
for all the cash and other designa ted propert y of Grand Lodge and all
entities. There can be but one administrative officer, the secretary, responsible for the administration of the Grand Lodge office including
accounting for Grand Lodge and all entities. The functions and responsibilities of these elected officers cannot be by-pass ed or nullifled by
non-observance of the Code requirements.
Anythin g other than this cohesive organization is difficult to contemplat e and could only result in waste, inefficiency and probabl y chaos.

Your Committee to Study Boards of Relief was requested by The
Most Worshipf ul Chester R. MacPhee, our Grand Master, to make
recommendations to this Grand Lodge as to the following questions:
1. Should Boards of Relief be abolished?
2. Should Boards of Relief continue as presently established?
3. Should the duties of Boards of Relief be ·restri:cted, expanded,
defined, modified, or otherwise considered?
4. Should the name of the Boards of Relief be changed?
Our Grand Master also personally wrote to the Masters of the
Lodges in this Jurisdiction, requesting that they write to this Committee,
giving the views of the officers of the Lodges as to whether or ~o.t. t~e
Boards of Relief should be retained and, if so, what the responsibilities
and activities of the Boards of Relief should be.

letters from 85 Lodges as of the date of this Report, which is generall!
considered to be a good percentag e for replies to a general letter of this
type, and we will give you a tabulation of the contents of the.se letters:

favored the abolishing of Boards of Relief. Some of those suggesting that the Boards of Relief be abolished stated that the!
did not belong to Boards of Relief and had not had any experience with them.
Some of the Lodges did not outline any particular duties which
they felt should be handled by Boards of Relief an~. of c~urse, the
suggestion s as to the duties of Boards of Relief varied from
Lodge to Lodge, but we will give you a tabultion of the recommended activities of Boards of Relief. as follows:
1. 23 Lodges felt that Boards of Relief should handle investigations requested by other Grand Jurisdictions or other Lodges
outside the area of the Board of Relief.

On the question of changing the name of the Boards of Relief, there
were 19 Lodges which recommended that the name be changed to
Masonic Service Bureau, or some similar name, and others made passing
reference to this st1bject.
Your Committee has met and considered all of the information that
we have accumulated, and have also met with the Board of Control and
discussed with them their problems and their philosophy with regard to
Boards of Relief and, after carefully considering the recommendations
of the Lodges and others and investigating the activities of Boards of
Relief and the questions submitted to us by our Grand Master, are unanimous in making the following recommendations:
1. That Boards of Relief should be continued.
2. That the name of the Boards of Relief be changed to "Masonic
Service Bureau," or some similar name with the word "Masonic" as the first word in the name. We feel that by having
"Masonic" as the first word in the name and listing it in the
telephone books in this manner, it will be easier for Masons,
families of Masons, mortuaries and others to locate this
Service Bureau.
3. That all Boards of Relief be listed in the local telephone books.
4. That all Boards of Relief be encotli'aged to develop a committee of Masons who are either retired or in a position to leave

260

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

their employment and attend Masonic funerals. We feel that
Masonic funerals are one of the most important means of
building a good image of Freemasonry and that every effort
should be made to have them properly conducted and attended
by as many Masons as possible.
5. We believe that Boards of Relief should be encouraged to develop a Speakers Bureau to furnish speakers to Lodges or
other groups who may be interested in the activities of the
Boards of Relief. Too many Masons do not know that there
are Boards of Relief and too many others do not know of the
service they render to our Masonic Fraternity.
6. We recommend that the California Freemason publish a list
of the Boards of Relief in California, with their addresses and
telephone numbers, so that every Mason in California can
locate any Board of Relief in California.
7. We recommend that the Boards of Relief be encouraged to
develop a committee to visit Masons in Veterans Hospitals and
Sojourners who are sick or infirm.
8. We find that there are many occasions when an officer or Past
Master of the Lodge is not available to conduct a Masonic
funeral. and do it properly, and on many occasions, such as
those involving two or more funerals in one day, it is necessary
to have a group of qualified Masons who have the time and the
willingness to conduct a Masonic funeral. Many of these
Brethren who are perfectly willing to help wherever possible
are living on retirement pay, Social Security, or limited incomes, and cannot afford to drive 50 miles or more for this purpose, and that it should be discretionary with the Boards of
Relief to pay mileage to such a Brother, but he should only be
paid mileage at prevailing Grand Lodge rates and not a fee.
The foregoing recommendations are general recommendations to
improve the service which Boards of Relief can render to the Masonic
Fraternity, and involve a more liberal construction of the word "relief"
than has been given by the Report of the Board of Control to this Grand
Lodge in 1969.
To clarify the duties and responsibilities of our Boards of Relief,
your Committee has caused its Chairman to present to this Grand Lodge
a Resolution on Boards of Relief to amend Section 603 of the California
Masonic Code relating to Boards of Relief. This Resolution was presented.as a tentative recommendation of your Committee but, after a full
investigation, your Committee now unanimously recommends the adoption of that Resolution with the following changes:
1. In the 23rd, 24th and 25th lines, change the phrase "and such
other proper Masonic activities as may be requested by the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

261

Lodges belonging to the Board of Relief, all under the supervision of the Board of Control" to the words "and such proper
Masonic activities as may be authorized by the Board of Control as provided in Section 263 of the California Masonic
Code, subject to appeal to and review by the Grand Master or
the Grand Lodge.", and change "report annually to the Grand
Lodge," in the 26th line, to "report annually to the Board of
Control."
In connection with this Resolution, your Committee has the following
comments:
1. As shown by the fact that 225 relief cases were handled by
Boards of Relief in 1969, this is a necessary function, particularly in metropolitan areas and locations where no one can be
reached at a Masonic Temple during the daytime. Families of
deceased Sojourners and mortuaries do not have a Grand
Lodge roster through which to locate the officers of a Lodge
and there must be some central clearing house which can be
reached during the day.
2. As shown by the reports that Boards of Relief handled or
arranged for 1.019 funerals of Sojourners during 1969, it appears that this is a necessary and proper activity of Boards of
Relief. There is so little time between death and the funeral
that there should be some central place which ·can take over
the arrangepients and check the good standing of the deceased.
If you have tried to contact Lodges through their Masonic
Temples, you know how difficult it is because few have a daytime caretaker. Again, families of deceased Masons and Sojourners do not have a Grand Lodge Roster and, accordingly,
have no way of contacting officers of Lodges except on meeting
nights. The same applies to mortuaries. The officers of many
Lodges cannot leave their work whenever they feel like it and
a Board of Relief should be authorized to conduct funerals
to take care of this problem and certainly are in a better position to have a group of well-qualified men to conduct the
funeral than any individual Lodge. This is important to the
public image of Freemasonry.
3. Investigations to locate Sojourners, whether from other parts
of California or other parts of the world, and the many other
types of investigations requested by other Grand Jurisdictions,
are time-consuming and generally require some knowledge of
how to make this investigation, and again a central location
which can be contacted by other Jurisdictions or Lodges is a
much more effective way to produce results.

262

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

4. Visiting the sick is a service which we owe to our Brethren and
the demands upon the time of an officer of a Lodge in handling
the affairs of his Lodge, looking after his own family responsibilities, and doing the work through which he earns a living,
certainly recommend a central agency to handle these matters.
5. While some areas handle the matter of advising Lodges in the
Jurisdiction of the names of applicants for degrees, this has
been handled for many years by Boards of Relief in other
metropolitan areas, and it appears to your Committee that this
function by a Board of Relief should be permitted. There must
be a central agency for this purpose in any metropolitan area.
For example, you can imagine the paper work and confusion
if over 100 Lodges in one metropolitan area were required to
have their respective Secretaries notify the other more than
100 Lodges of the names of its applicants each month.
6. We see no reason why Boards of Relief should not put on
breakfasts and similar gatherings of the Masons in their area
to let them know about the activities of the Boards of Relief
or honor the Grand Master. Members of your Committee have
attended many such gatherings, some of which have been
attended by over 2,000 Masons. They are an inspiration and
a chance to enjoy Masonic fellowship.
This Report is much longer than your Committee would have desired,
but it appeared to be necessary to cover the subject as thoroughly as
time would permit, and we have accordingly only hit the high spots.
To sum it all up, we unanimously ·recommend that Boards of Relief be
continued and their functions and activities be as clearly outlined as
possible. We unanimously recommend the adoption of this Report and
the Resolution we have presented, as amended.

(1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Lodge Secretary is an elective officer of the Lodge
and the connecting link between Grand Lodge and his constituent Lodge,
carrying on most of the communication between the Grand Lodge and
his Lodge, advising the Master and other Lodge Officers in legal procedure and other matters excepting ritual and esoteric work, and
WHEREAS the Lodge Secretary is the direct communication with
every member of his Lodge and in many cases the only Officer in the
Lodge who the member knows and communicates with, and
WHEREAS many Secretaries are Past Masters of their Lodges, all
should be recognized and have as much voice in Grand Lodge proceedings as, say, the Junior Warden. Compare the duties of the Wardens
(Sec. 489 & Annotations a thru d) with those of the Secretacy (Sec.
493, 1st thru 11th, Annotations a thru k. Sec. 494, 495, 496 1st thru 4th,
Annotations a & b, and Sec. 497.), and
WHEREAS most Secretaries serve their Lodge for many years and
do not wish to be "in the line" but rather concentrate on the "mechanics"
of helping their Lodge and thereby Grand Lodge especially the Grand
Secretary and his staff with his sustaining knowledge, and
WHEREAS a Lodge can and sometimes does at times, function
without its Master, its Senior Warden or its Junior Warden, it would
soon founder and be helpless without its Secretary, especially at its
stated meetings.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that Article II, Sec. 8 of the
Constitution be amended to include the Secretary in the list of those com-

Referre d to the Commi ttees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purpose s, and on Finance.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution number one has been referred to the Committee on Policy
and Genera l Purpose s. It propose s an amendm ent to Article II of the
Constit ution of the Grand Lodge to make the secretaries of lodges members of Grand Lodge by virtue of their office as secretar y.
In the "where as" paragra phs of the resolution it is stated, "many
Secreta ries are Past Masters of their Lodges " and it is also stated, "most
Secretaries serve their Lodges for many years and do not wish to be 'in
the line .. .'." The latter stateme nt is not accurate. The roster of lodge
officers for 1970 lists the names and address es of secretaries of 702
lodges and shows that 508 of them are Past Masters and only 194 are not
so designa ted. It thus appears that of the 702 secretaries listed, 508 are
at this moment members of the Grand Lodge.
If our Constit ution were amende d as this resolution proposes it
would give each secretar y a full vote in the Grand Lodge, as the Master
and each Warde n present ly possesses. As I read to you a moment. the
propone nts state most Secreta ries serve their lodges for many years. The
result of adoptio n would be to invest a substan tial part of the voting
power of each lodge in one man over a span of .five, ten, fifteen or more
years. Under our present system there general ly is a continu al but gradual change in those who wield the voting power in each annual communication. Perhaps , this was in the mind of those who framed the Constitution when they provided that the Past Masters of each lodge, who
are present have, collectively but a single vote.
Incidentally, I have examin ed the constitutions of a score of other
Grand Lodges and have not found any in which the secretaries are
given a vote by virtue of their office as secretar y. The closest approac h
is the Grand Lodge of Kentucky. In that jurisdiction, if the Master and
both warden s are absent, the secretar y may cast one vote.
We are authoriz ed by the Committee on Finance to state that the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

265

resolution does not involve matters of finance and that committee will
not present any further report.
To get the matter before the Grand Lodge, I move the adoptio n of
resolution number one and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "no" vote.
