Referre d to the Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and
Genera l Purpose s.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Propose d Resolution No. 2 affords an opportu nity to summarize
briefly the parliam entary procedu re which has been followed for the
past nineteen years as to resolutions and the reasons therefor.
Our Californ ia Masoni c Code requires that a proposal to change
our law or policy must be filed not less than ninety days before the
opening of a Communication, that copies thereof be mailed out at least
sixty days before the opening, and that the proposa l must be referred
to an appropr iate committee for report before it is voted upon. None of
these steps actually present s a resolution to the Grand Lodge. To get

266

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

a resolution before you, and to conserve time, one of the committeemen
giving a report moves its adoption and the Grand Lecturer seconds that
motion. Neither, thereby, signifies that he favors adoption: each is
merely getting the resolution before you for voting.
A committeeman who presents a report as to how the committee
believes you should vote will add a statement at the end of his reportthe Committee on XYZ either recommends a "yes" vote or a "no" vote.
We believe this procedure, followed for the past nineteen years, is
generally understood and it eliminates the confusion which f.requently
existed before its establishment.
Resolution No. 2 would change this procedure by eliminating the
motion to adopt and the second thereto. In effect, it would provide that
the act of flling was in itself equivalent to a motion to adopt and second
thereto. Do not forget, however, that what would be before you for
voting would be the resolution in the exact words flied prior to the Communication.
.
Each year numerous resolutions are filed in which the authors have
not attempted to spell out an amendment to a Code section but have
written "Resolved, that the appropriate sections be amended" or (I
quote from Resolution No. 1 ) "that any ordinance in conflict or omission
be changed." Resolutions which this year fail to spell out the amendment are Nos. 1, 6, l l, 12, 18, 20, 21, 3l,33and34.
In each of these instances it would appear to be necessary for the
Committee on Jurisprudence to frame the words of an amendment which
would accomplish the purpose of the proponents. If proposed Resolution
No. 2 were in effect, conventional parliamentary procedure would require a motion to amend the resolution as flied, a second thereto and a
vote whether it should be amended: if the aiyes won it would then be
necessary to move to adopt the resolution as amended and !l'eceive a second thereto. Resolution No. 2 either requires such procedure or it prohibits voting on any words except those found in the draft originally
flied.
The same situation would be present if the document flied ninety
days before the opening contained an error or failed to refer to all Code
sections involved.
It thus should be apparent that the adoption of Resolution No. 2
would, in most instances, require a motion to adopt something and a
second thereto, perhaps two motions and two seconds.
To get the resolution before the Grand Lodge, I move the adoption
of Resolution No. 2. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes
recommends that you vote "no."
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
In the opinion of your Committee on •Jurisprudence, the proposed
language sufficiently expresses the intent of the proponents of Resolution No. 2, except that in both Section 76 and Section 781, C.M.C., the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

267

last sentence of the present language which provides that "When the
report of said Committee is presented the vote shall be taken on the
amendment," should be deleted since that languge would be superseded
by the proposed Resolution.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 2 as so amended.
A majority voted against the resolution.

(3)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. a Lodge representative may be entitled to more than
one vote for his Lodge, and
WHEREAS. in a voice vote the presiding officer does not know
how many votes each voice is legally voting, and
WHEREAS. it is impossible in a voice vote to accw-ately determine
numbers of votes as opposed to volume of voices.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED THAT: Article VI. Section
39 of the Constitution of the California Masonic Code be amended to
read-"All voting on all resolutions at the Annual Communications of
the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of California shall be by
secret ballot" biy the following method:
1. Use the same kind of paper ballot as prepared for the 1969 Annal Communication, making sufficient yes and no ballots for each reso•
lution.
2. Issue ballots to the proper Lodge representative ( s).
3. Begin discussion of resolutions to be considered.
4. Immediately prior to calling the Grand Lodge from labor to refreshment, stewards will collect votes on all the resolutions on which
discussion has been declared closed.
5. Stewards will count the votes while the Grand Lodge is at ref.reshment.
6. The stewards will record the vote-count with the Grand Secretary to be held by him until the next session of labor, at which time the
Grand Master will render the decisions of the votes taken on the resolutions.
Respectfully submitted,
VESTER B. LAWRENCE, M., No. 634

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution proposes voting on all resolutions at Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge by secret ballot.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully reports that it is

unable to prepare legislation to implement this resolution because it is
incomplete. The resolution as presented does not cover voting on motions to declare a ,resolution out of order, to amend it, to table it, or motions to adopt recommendations or resolutions presented with committee reports.
Since the necessary elements are not included in the resolution, they
cannot now be added in view of Section 104 of the C.M.C. which requires resolutions to be presented at least 90 days before opening of
Grand Lodge.
The resolution provides for the Stewards to collect the votes and
count them "while the Grand Lodge is at refreshment." There are
only two Stewards in the Grand Lodge, and it is obviously impossible for them to count the ballots. Not less than 50 votes are taken at
each Annual Communication on resolutions of various kinds. Most of
such voting takes place on the last business day of Grand Lodge, namely,
Thursday. Since the result of balloting would not be available under
this resolution until F,riday, the business of Grand Lodge could not be
completed in the manner provided by the Constitution of Grand Lodge
We therefore recommend a "no" vote on the resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated its concurrence in the recommendation of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
A majority voted against the resolution.

INSPECTORS' VOTE
(4)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Inspectors have no vote at the Annual Communication
of Grand Lodge, their participation in balloting being limited to their
status as one of the Past Masters of their own Lodge, who collectively
have a single vote; and
WHEREAS, the knowledge, wisdom, and experience of the Inspectors in Masonic affairs throughout our jurisdiction, which includes administration and planning in addition to ritual. is in many instances more
comprehensive than that of some appointive Grand Lodge Officers who
are each entitled to one vote; and
WHEREAS, our Constituent Lodges would benefit from the judicious balloting by the Inspectors on all matters affecting Masonry; and
WHEREAS, an Inspector is the representative of the Grand Master, and as the supervising official over the affairs and activities of the
Lodges in his District he in effect is acting as an Officer of the Grand
Lodge, and renders substantial services as such throughout the year:
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED: That in order that
Grand Lodge may benefit at our Annual Communications from the wide
range of knowledge and experience incorporated in the individual Inspectors, that each Inspector be allotted one full vote.

MASONS AT SIGHT-PHYSICALLY HANDICAPPED
(5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:

.•

WHEREAS. it is an established fact that many Sovereign Grand
Jurisdictions in the United States as well as Foreign Jurisdictions welcome into membership men who are well qualified for Freemasonry but
who have some minor physical defect which would prevent their complying with the normal requirements of degree work, and
WHEREAS, for several years this Grand Lodge has received resolutions which. in different ways. have attempted to lift the restrictions
of Sec. 511 C.M.C. pertaining to the requirement that the applicant
must be ... "physically able to conform 'substantially' to what the several degrees respectively require of him.". and
WHEREAS, it is the opinion of many Freemasons that the failure
of these many resolutions has been due primarily to the fact that the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

270

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Representatives to Grand Lodge were uncertain as to the extent of disability that might be acceptable, and
WHERE AS. Sec. 545d C.M.C. states, "Physica l disability suffered by a candidat e after he has received one or more degrees is n? bar
to his advancement." This statemen t testifies to the fact that a physically
disabled man is capable of learning the art and this capability of learning
the art should determine his acceptability!, and
WHERE AS, rather than to modify the ritual to enable the physically handicap ped applicant to comply "substan tially" to what would
be required of him (perhaps to his embarrassment and that of the officers), and
WHERE AS, this resolution would not disturb or modify the C.M.C.
law as it now pertains to "physica lly quali6ed" men. It seeks only to
add a means by which men who are highly desirable and who would
be a substant ial asset to Freemas onry but are not phiysically qualified
might attain membership. and
WHERE AS, it is possible for this Grand Lodge to restore to the
Grand Master the power, for the limited purpose only, of investing handicapped men with the degrees at sight; that this might be accomplished
at annual meetings, one in the North, one in the South: that such investiture must be subject to the fact that the applicant had previously been
investigated and elected by the individual Lodge to receive the degrees
at sight; that having been invested with the degrees in this manner, n.o
dues card would be issued until the candidat e had demonstrated his
proficiency in the degrees by means of a special examination in the
teachings of Freemasonry, no less comprehensive than that demande d
of those taking the degrees in the normal manner.
NOW, THERE FORE. BE IT RESOL VED that a special committee be appointe d by the incoming Grand Master. to investigate and
report at the next Annual Communication, on the extending of the powers of the Grand Master to confer the degrees in the manner herein set
forth.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE P. CALDERW OOD, P.M. No. 327
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes , and on Ritual.
The Committee on Ritual did not report.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 5 deals with the continuing concern of many of the
Brethren relative to the physical requirements for admission to Masonry
in this Grand Lodge.
The proposer suggests that power be given to the Grand Master to
invest the degrees of Masonry upon physically handicap ped men at

271

sight following election of such men by a Lodge and that such investiture be accomplished at two annual meetings expressly held for the
purpose, one in the North and one in the South.
The resolution itself calls for a special committee to be appointe d
by the incoming Grand Master to study this suggestion for extendin g
the powers of the Grand Master and to report at the next Annual Communication.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes , without repetitive
consideration of the argumen ts for and against admission of the physically handicap ped, does not favor this resolution for the following reasons:
1. We believe that there should be no change in the restriction in
this jurisdiction that the Grand Master may not make Masons at sight
except in a regular Lodge upon unanimous consent of the members there
present (see C.M.C. 121, Annotati on b).
2. It is Masonic custom that each of the first three degrees be conferred individually, and we believe there should be no break in this
long-accepted tradition.
3. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes , in reporting on
Resolution No. 24, will propose the establishment of an in-depth study
of the entire problem of admission of the physically handicap ped. To
also have a special committee with the limited assignment proposed in
Resolution No. 5 would then be unnecess ary since the suggestions of
the proposer, contained in Resolution No. 5, could and presumably
would be included in the total study which can be conducted by an indepth study committee.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 5 and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes unanimously recommends a "no"
vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 5 proposes that Grand Lodge ., restore to the
Grand Master the power, for the limited purpose only, of investing
handicap ped men with the degrees at sight," and that this might be
accomplished at annual meetings, one in the North and one in the South,
subject to the applicants having been investigated and elected by the
individual Lodge to receive the degrees at sight; and further that a special committee be appointe d to investigate and report at the next Annual
Communication on extendin g the powers of the Grand Master to confer
the degrees in the manner set forth in the resolution.
As appears from this 1'esolution, it is more than a resolution for appointment of a special committee, but expresses the ultimate purpose
to be accomplished, namely, to have the Grand Master make Masons
at sight of persons who cannot conform to our ritual.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully submits that such

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

a purpose is not within the power of this Grand Lodge, since it is an
attempt to change one of the Ancient Landmarks.
We cannot restore to the Grand Master the power mentioned in the
resolution, because the Grand Master already possesses that power
under the Eighth Landmark, which was acknowledged and adopted by
this Grand Lodge more than a century ago. It is "The prerogative of
the Grand Master to make Masons at sight in a regular Lodge by unanimous consent of the members present." (C.M.C., Appendix, p. 342)
Since the Grand Master possesses that prerogative, the Grand Lodge
cannot direct or require its exercise, nor limit it nor extend it, nor can
it be exercised in regional meetings, but only in a regular Lodge by unanimous consent of the members of that Lodge then and there present.
We submit that the resolution contemplates the violation of an
Ancient Landmark and we therefore recommend a "no" vote.
(NOTE: Following the above reports the proponent of the resolution, in consideration of favorable action to establish an in-depth study
of the entire matter of the physically handicapped, withdrew Resolution
No.5.)

COMM ITTEE AND BOAR D CONS ULTA NTS
(8)
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHER EAS. all Committees, Commissions and Boards of the Grand
Lodge are composed only of members of the Grand Lodge: and
WHER EAS, the assistan ce of members of Constit uent Lodges
who do not qualify as members of Grand Lodge is sometimes desirable,
by reason of special talent, knowledge, availability, or geographical location; and

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, Grand Masters, in the past. upon occasion have named
certain brethren as consultants to specified committees, but the status of
such brethren and their right to reimbursement for necessary expenses
has required individual directives by the Grand Master; and
WHEREAS, the practice concerning consultants should be confirmed and its terms specified by legislation;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That in addition to
the regular membership of all standing and special committees, commissions and boards, the Grand Master, under special or demanding circumstances, may appoint as a consultant to a committee, commission or
board, any member in good standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction. The
Grand Master may remove a consultant at any time. The number of
consultants appointed by the Grand Master to the various committees,
commissions and boards shall not exceed a total of ten during such
Grand Master's term of office. Such consultants shall perform services,
render advice, and attend committee meetings. as may be directed by the
chairmen of the committees to which they are assigned, but shall have no
vote therein. They shall be entitled to reimbursement for necessary expenses incurred in the discharge of their duties on the same basis and
subject to the same provisions and restrictions, as members of the committees which they serve.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED: That the foregoing provision be
suitably added to the California Masonic Code, either as now constituted, or as it may be revised, irrespective of whether the revision is
adopted before or after action on the present resolution.

We estimate, however, that the appointment of up to ten consultants
as contemplated by Resolution No. 8 and reimbursement of their expenses on the same basis as regular committee members would involve
an expenditure of not less than $2,000.00 in any one year and would
probably not exceed $5,000.00
Recognizing the value of the proposal, we concur in the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and, if Resolution
No. 8 is adopted, would propose to include an amount of $5,000.00 in
the Grand Lodge budget for the fiscal year July 1, 1970 to June 30, 1971,
to provide for this expense.

The Committee on Finance:
As to Resolution No. 8, your Committee on Finance is concerned
with expenses that may be involved and its effect on the annual budget
of the Grand Lodge.
It is well known, of course, that the employment of consultants can
be costly. In this case it is apparent that the cost involved may vary
considerably. depending upon the number of consultants a Grand ,Master may see St to appoint, the location of such consultants, the number
of meetings a particular committee may find necessary and various other
factors.

277

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution confirms the use of Consultants to Committees and
provides for their reimbursement. In 1967 then Grand Master Laurence
E. Dayton stated "There are among the Craft in California many brethren with special knowledge and experience in particular fields of Grand
Lodge activity, but who, never having served as Master of a Lodge, are
not members of Grand Lodge and accordingly are not eligible for appointment to a Grand Lodge Committee. They are nevertheless willing
to contribute their talents. Instances frequently occur in which the
services of such brethren would be useful and would enhance the efforts
of a particular committee. These sources of competence and interest are
largely untapped. Their use will extend meaningful participation more
broadly among the Craft and, by augmenting the skilled personnel available to them, add to the success of many Committee programs. It should
be the policy of Gral}d Lodge to seek out and wherever possible, enlist
the aid of these brethren in a consultant or advisory capacity and I so
recommend.''
Grand Lodge approved this recommendation and consultants have
been appointed to Committees such as Public Schools, Masonic Foundation, etc., by Grand Masters since 1967. These brethren have rendered
invaluable service to this Grand Lodge. The Committee on Policy and
General Purposes believes that, since these consultants perform duties
comparable to those of regular Committee members, they should be entitled to the same reimbursement for their expenses.
The ·restrictions im::orporated in this resolution concerning the number of consultants not exceeding ten, that appointment be for special
and demanding circumstances and that the consultant be a member in
good standing of a Lodge in this jurisdiction are, in the opinion of the
Committee, proper safeguards.
I move the adoption of Resolution No. 8 and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence is of the opinion that while in gen-

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 11 proposes a change in our policy and procedure of
holding securities in its corporate name in order to facilitate delivery of
securities for transfer in good delivery form because of the paper work
and, at times, lack of the required signatures of certain members of the
Investment Committee named as nominees.
The investment portfolio of the Grand Lodge and its components has
increased in size to a point which necessitated a change in our policy and
procedure to a more generally accepted business practice of large cor..
porations and financial institutions. You Committee therefore recommends having a custodian nominee, such as a bank or trust company,
with full fiduciary responsibility to effect timely transfers of security
transactions. Such transfers to be made only upon authorization, by a
resolution, from the components of the Grand Lodge that own securities,
such as the Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M., the Masonic Homes
of California, the California Masonic Memorial Temple, the California
Masonic Foundation and aniy other entity of Grand Lodge hereafter
established. We therefore submit that the fifth paragraph of this resolu ..
tion be amended as follows: Strike out the words, "in the name of a
nominee designated by the Investment Committee," and reword the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

283

phrase to read, "in the name of a custodian nominee designated as the
repository of such securities, provided that such custodian nominee shall
at all times be a bank or trust company chartered by the United States
of America or by the State of California."
Your Committee moves that the resolution, as amended, be adopted
and recommends a "yes" vote.
We are authorized by the Committee on Finance to state that there
is no matter of finance involved and that they will not render a separate
report.
The Investment Committee indicated its concurrence in the recom..
mendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The resolution requests this Committee to prepare legislation which
would authorize Grand Lodge and its controlled boards to have title to
its securities held in the name of a nominee or nominees designated by
the Investment Committee for the purpose of expediting the transfer of
securities.
To carry out the purpose and requests of the resolution, the following
resolution is presented:
RESOLVED, That a new section numbered 245.1 be added to the
C.M.C. to read as follows:
"Title to securities of every kind and nature, including but not
limited to stocks, bonds, debentures and notes, belon·ging to the
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund,
the California Masonic Foundation, or any other entities or funds of
Grand Lodge or under control of Grand Lodge, may be held in the
name of a nominee or in the name of a custodian nominee designated
as the depository for such securities, with full power to substitute or
change such nominees from time to time, which nominee shall
always be a bank or trust company chartered by the United States of
America or the State of California."

.
The Committee on Masonic History indicated that the body of its
report to Grand Lodge at this Communication contained remarks reftecting the attitude of the Committee with respect to this resolution.
The Committee on Finance:
There has been referred to the Committee on Finance Resolution
No. 13 which proposes the rebuilding of the Masonic Temple. fo~er1y
occupied by Quittman Lodge No. 88 at North Bloomfi~ld, Cahf?~ia ..
The suggested method of financing this proposal, m our opmio~, ~s
impractical and should be accomplished by recognition of the. cost within
our per capita assessment instead of Grand Lodge requesting all con.stituent ·Lodges to contribute at the rate of 20¢ per member, leaving it
to the option of eat:h Lodge as to how the money be raised as proposed
in the resolution.
Your Committee on Finance appreciates fully the enthusiasm of the
proponents but must necessarily be mindful of. our ever-incr~":1g costs
of operation. We estimate an increase of 27 f m ou~ per cap.ita. m order
to fund this proposal which we do not feel appropriate at this time. We
recommend a "no" vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 13 has to do with the proposed rebuilding of the
Temple of Quittman Lodge No. 88 as part of the total restoration of the
pioneer town of North Bloomfield, Nevada County. The California St~te
Department of Parks and Recreation has establishe~ the Malakoff .Diggings State Historical Park and the Temple of Quittman Lodge, if restored, would be in this park.
A very similar resolution was presented at the 1969 Annual C?mmunication but it was not adopted, partly because of lack of sufficient
information concerning the rights and requirements of the Grand Lodge

in connection with the restoration project. The 1969 resolution also called
for authority to solicit contributions from the Lodge members throughout
the jurisdiction to raise the necessary- funds for rebuilding the Temple of
Quittman Lodge.
Resolution No. 13 is in very simil<l1' form and content to the proposal
of last year. The primary difference is that the resolution now asks Grand
Lodge to request all Lodges of the jurisdiction to contribute at the rate
of 20¢ per member for rebuilding the Masonic Temple at North Bloomfield, Nevada County.
The proposers of Resolution No. 13 state that all objections !l'aised
by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes respecting last year's
resolution have now been satisfied. This is not correct. The Committee's
concern about clarification of the arrangement and relationship between
the Grand Lodge and the State Department of Parks and Recreation has
been satisfied. But, as was stated in our report on this proposal last year
... "We believe it is not good policy to authorize the solicitation of contributions from Lodge members throughout this jurisdiction for any
purpose other than one of Masonic charity. If a project of the sort
proposed is worthy as a Grand Lodge project, then it should be supported in uniform proportion by all of the Lodges within the jurisdiction." We reiterate this position. Further, we do not believe that a
"request" by Grand Lodge for contributions from all of the constituent Lodges is anything but solicitation.
In last year's report respecting the Malakoff Diggings State Historical Park proposal this Committee called for the appointment of a special committee to Btudy the entire matter of Grand Lodge responsibility
and participation in the area of historical site restoration and preservation. Unfortunately no committee was appointed. We still believe that
this should be done, because we believe it is necessary to establish
proper policy in this important field.
Your Committee further feels that the proposal to rebuild the
Masonic Temple at North Bloomfield is worthy and that it should be
accomplished, and we commend the Brethren who have worked so
diligently and with so much enthusiasm toward that end. We do, however, strongly believe that Grand Lodge must establish a firm policy
respecting proposals of the kind submitted in Resolution No. 13 before entrance into any contractual arrangements with the State, or any
other agency or organization, as well as before any financial commitments are made.
We' renew our suggestion and request for the appointment of a
committee to develop a proposed policy for Grand Lodge, and we also
want it understood that this Committee unanimously favors the restoration of the Quittman Lodge Temple. However. we believe that the point
of commitment for the project has not been reached, and we accordingly urge a "no" vote on Resolution No. 13.

The Committee on Ritual has considered Resolution No. 14 proposing an amendment to the Installation Service to provide for a Flag
presentation at public installations by an Honorary Marshal or a
group approved by the Inspector.
Our law requires that the Flag of our Country be displaiyed at all
meetings of our Lodges. At the annual election of officers and at such
other meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag
must be formally presented at the Altar by the Marshal and received
in the manner prescribed by the Grand Lecturer.
There is no logic whatever in permitting the Flag to be informally
taken out of the Lodge in order to have it again presented while the
Lodge is at refreshment for the purpose of installation. The proposed
resolution does not provide just how the Flag is to be taken out of the
Lodge room, nor by whom.

to the Flag by requiring the pledge of allegiance to be given at the

ALTAR LIGHTS
(15)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 6 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, some Inspectors of Masonic Districts have advised
the Masters of their respective Lodges that it is contrary to Masonic
regulations to use other than ordinary blue bulbs in their altar lights,
and
WHEREAS, the blue in such light bulbs is symbolic in the same
way that the word "East" is symbolic in Lodgerooms that happen to
be geographicall~ situated in other directions than East and West,
and
WHEREAS, there are presently no restrictions in the California
Masonic Code in regard to the type or color of altar lights that may
be used by a Masonic Lodge, and
WHEREAS, there are presently available for purchase by Masonic
Lodges, altar lights which are amber in color, and in which the fllaments
are made in the shape of a square and compass. and
WHEREAS, in the opinion of many individual Lodge members,
such lights are beautiful, and in harmony with the spirit of Masonry:
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the following
section be added to the California Masonic Code:
Section 329.1. Altar lights. There is no Masonic authority for
restricting the type of altar lights to be used in a Lodge, either as to
color, or as to the shape of the 6laments contained within the light bulbs.
Respectfully submitted,
EUGENE E .WILKINSON, P.M.,
ALFRED L. GERRIE, JR., M.,

The Committee on Ritual:
This resolution proposes a new section 329.1 of the C.M.C. to
declare that there is no Masonic authority for restricting the type of
altar lights to be used in a Lodge or as to color or shape of filaments
contained in the light bulbs.
It is true that there is no provision of the Code as to the type of
lights to be used at the Altar. There is in fact no requirement that
there be electric lights, and there are Lodges which use candle lighting.
However, the lights to which we are referring are the Lesser Lights,
and good taste alone should dictate that they should be subdued in
tone and in candle-power.
The use of filaments in the shape of the square and compass were
ruled out more than 20 years ago by the late Arthur M. Warren,
P.G.M., when he was Grand Lecturer, because the filaments were an
affectation, and because it would be incongruous for the Lesser Lights
to contain any of the Great Lights. Our ritual prescribes the location of
the Great Lights. The explanation of the Lesser Lights, as well as the
Great Llghts, is esoteric * * * * * Consequently, it would be meaningless to embellish them with the proposed adornment or any other adornment.
Your Committee on Ritual therefore moves the adoption of the
resolution and recommend a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated its approval of the resolution as to form and stated it carries out the purpose of the proponents.
A majority voted against the resolution.
STATEWIDE PUBLIC SCHOOLS WELFARE

(16)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS the more than 240,000 members of the Fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons of California and Hawaii unqualifiedly
subscribe to the belief that an educated and enlightened citizenry is the
first great care of a prog·ressive society and that upon our Public
Schools depends the hope for the perpetuity of a free and untrammeled democracy and
WHEREAS we believe that the Founding Fathers of our nation
established our Public Schools so that our iyouth could receive an
adequate education, without any deterrent, according to their separate
needs. and
WHEREAS we view with alarm the unrest that has encompassed

293

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 16 is in two parts:
First - That the Masonic Fraternity earnestly urges that the duly
elected School Boards, School Administrators and Instructors, at all
scholastic levels, endeavor to inculcate the high principles of self esteem,
morality and unreserved patriotism in the minds of students of Public
Schools of California and Hawaii.
Second - That copies of this resolution be made available to all
news media and to the leaders in education throughout this jurisdiction.
The California State Education Code alreadiy provides as follows:
Chapter 3, Article 1, Section 7851; Each teacher shall endeavor to
impress upon the minds of pupils the principles of morality, truth, justice,
patriotism, and a true comprehension of the rights, duties and dignity
of American citizenship, to teach them to avoid idleness, profanity,
and falsehood, and to instruct them on manners and morals and the
principles of a free government.
This is in essence what the first part of the resolution proposes. We
also feel that direct participation in Public School problems, by Masons,
is preferable and more effective than resolutions made available to the
news media and leaders in education.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion
that we should assist the local School Boards in implementing the

294

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

present California Education Code, by providing the Public Schools
with material on such programs as Washington's Birthday and other
patriotic observances. That the Lod·ges or District Officers Associations
provide for participation by one or more Master Masons in School
Board meetings, and also that Lodges arrange for a public meeting
with School Administrations and Teachers to discuss Public School
problems, and to give assistance in helping to solve them, and that the
Public Schools Committee be charged with implementing this program
under the direction of the Grand Master.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes moves the adop~
tion of the resolution and recommends a "no" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution No. 17, if adopted, would grant permission to the gov~
erning Body of the Scottish Rite Temple in San Diego to place a Square
and Compass sign directly below the Scottish Rite emblem on the pylon
and located on the property of the San Diego Scottish Rite Masonic
Center.
In order to better acquaint the members of this Grand Lodge with
the background of this resolution, the following is a brief history of what
has thus far transpired with regard to the display of the Square and
Compass at the Scottish Rite Temple in San Diego.
The Scottish Rite in San Diego purchased a bowling alley and con~
verted it into a temple where Blue Lodges, youth groups and concordant
bodies meet. The pylon in question was already in existence as part of
the original construction and was adapted to display the emblems of
these groups in a vertical line. The Scottish Rite, as the owners of the
temple, quite naturally displayed its emblem at the top of the pylon and
emblems of other organizations were added below as they became
tenants.
Several members of the tenant Lodges, at their expense, manu~
factured an illuminated sign displaying the Square and Compass and
installed it below the Scottish Rite emblem on the pylon. During the time
the Square and Compass was displayed, it is the understanding of the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes, that it was the predominant
emblem on the pylon and the one that flrst caught the attention of mo~
torists driving by, especially at night, as it was brighter than any of the
other signs. After a period of time, the question was raised by several
brethren in the area as to whether or not the Square and Compass could
appropriately be displayed beneath the emblem of one of the concordant

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

bodies. Because of the controversy that followed, the Square and Compass was removed. It was then suggested that the Square and Compass
be placed at the top of the pylon and the Scottish Rite emblem placed
below but, because of the expense involved in modification of the signs
and the pylon, it seemed not economically feasible.
At the last Grand Lodge Communication a resolution was introduced
that would have allowed the display of the Square and Compass in any
position with reference to any of the other concordant emblems. As th~s
resolution would have created a new ordinance and hence afiected this
entire Grand Jurisdiction, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommended a "no" vote.
The resolution presently under consideration, however, would apply
only to the Lodges in the Scottish Rite Temple in San Diego and would
not create an ordinance for the rest of this Grand Jurisdiction. The
majority of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes
that the proposed location of the Square and Compass in this particular
instance is in good taste and in keeping with Masonic propriety.
I move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence has indicated that the language of
the resolution is sufficient to accomplish the purpose of the proponents
and has authorized us to say that they will not render a report.
Adopted.

PERIODS COVERED-TREASURE R'S REPORTS
(19)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the duties of the Treasurer of a Constituent Lodge in
this Jurisdiction, as presently set forth in the By-laws under Section 348
of the California Masonic Code, include the submission of financial
reports to the Lodge in February and August of each year, for six months
periods ending June 30th and December 31st, and
WHEREAS, some Lodges prefer to operate on a fiscal year other
than the calendar year, and
WHEREAS, with Elections and Installations of Officers being generally held in December of each year, many Lodges prefer to end their
fiscal year on November 30th, thus enabling the outgoing Master to 9ive
a complete report of his year to the Lodge before the election of the new
Master, and
WHEREAS, in such cases, the mandatory dates of February and
August make it necessary for the Treasurer to submit four financial
reports to his Lodge instead of two:
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that Section 348, Bylaws, Article V, Duties of the Treasurer, Section I, be amended as follows: The second sentence, reading:
"He shall, at the Stated Meetings in August and February of each
year, submit a report in full of the monetary transactions of the Lodge
for the six months periods ending on the preceding June 30th and
December 31st, respectively"
shall be deleted, and shall be replaced by the following sentences:
"He shall semi-annually submit to the Lodge, at a Stated Meeting, a report in full of the monetary transactions of the Lodge, each
such report to cover six months, or one-half, of the Lodge's fiscal
year. The Stated Meeting at which such report is made shall be no

the period which the report includes."

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 19 proposes to amend Section 348, Article V, Duties
of the Treasurer, Section 1 of the Uniform By-Laws.
A careful study of the effect of this resolution if adopted discloses
that a Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction could adopt any fiscal year that
may suit its convenience to report the monetary transactions of the
Lodge. This concept of reporting. as outlined in the resolution, would
create a chaotic condition as this Grand Jurisdiction is composed of more
than 700 constituent Lodges. Resolution No. 19 fails to recommend
amending Section 350, Article V, Section 1 of the By-Laws, pertaining
to the duties of the Sec'l°etary. whose duties in financial reporting must
obviously coincide with those of the Treasurer. Hence, if this resolution
is adopted, the Treasurer and Secretary might be presenting their
financial reports at different times.
Section 348, as it presently stands, defines definite dates for the
Treasurer's reports for the sake of uniformity as concerns the Grand
Secretary's office and the respective Inspector of the Masonic District.
Your Committee believes this is a sound and practical businesslike
method of reporting. There is nothing in the California Masonic Code
to prevent a Lodge from preparing an interim financial ·r eport at any
date desired for internal reporting.
In order to put this resolution before this Grand Lodge we move the
adoption of the resolution and recommend a "no" vote.
The Committee on /urisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence is of the opinion that adoption
of this resolution would ·create confusion because it would permit the
Treasurer of the Lodge to report on a fiscal year basis, whereas under
Section 493-2nd, C.M.C .• the Secretary of the Lodge is required to
report on a calendar year basis. The lodge members could not know
whether the Treasurer's report coincided with the Secretary's report.
We therefore recommend a "no" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

WEARING OF PAST MASTER'S APRON
(21)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. it has been customary in the several Lodges in the
jurisdiction of California for the Brethren of the respective Lodge or
the Lodge to present the retiring Past Master with a Past Master's
Apron, and
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code is totally void of any
documentation authorizing the Past Master's Apron as a legal piece of
Masonic wear, and
WHEREAS, at the installation of officers in 1969 the Past Masters,
including those performing the installation •ceremonies, were denied the
privilege of wearing the ·Past Master's Apron which is contrary to the
unwritten established custom for several years, and
WHEREAS, the Grand Master, Grand Lecturer, Deputy Grand
Lecturers and Inspectors have taken the liberty to individually dictate
when Past Masters may or may not wear the Past Master's Apron, and
WHEREAS, this flexibility exercised by the Grand Master, Grand
Lecturer, Deputy Grand Lecturers and Inspectors is not commensurate
with the Masonic customs and ritual to preserve the customs and ritual~
istic ceremonies of the Fraternity.
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED, that a section be added to
the California Masonic Code establishing the PAST MASTER'S
APRON as a legal piece of Masonic clothing to be worn only by Past
Masters.

DEFINE MEMBER IN GOOD ST ANDING
(22)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there are numerous references in the California
Masonic Code (CMC) to a "member in good standing," to cite a few
Ordinances-301, 302, 303, 304, 308, 358, 359, 432, 447, 451, 452, 557,
580 and 601: all of which are subject to individual interpretation, and
WHEREAS, a definition for a member in good standing does not
appear in the CMC but must be individually determined based on either
precedence or inference, and
WHEREAS, it is not the intent of the fraternity to differentiate
between a member in good standing and other categories of members
based on payment of dues as strongly implied by Ordinances 447c, 557b
and432~3.

NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that a member in good
standing is defined as a member who has been regularliy initiated an
Entered Apprentice Mason, passed to the degree of Fellow Craft and
raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in a just and legal manner;
and does not stand suspended or expelled from any regular Lodge of
Masons, and holds no membership in a Lodge which is not regular, or
have been dimitted from a regular Lodge for less than a year or have
made Application for Affiliation within the year if the year has been
exceeded. This Ordinance clarifies all Ordinances in question relative
to a member in good standing but does not negate the t"equirement for
having dues paid in advance for the purpose of dimitting or forming a
new Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
J. PARKS, S. W .. No. 89
B. G. MAY, M .. No. 89

PROGRAMS AT INSTALLATIONS
(23)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there is some confusion among the Craft as to whether
or not any type of program may be scheduled for a meeting called for
the annual Installation of Officers of a Constituent Lodge, other than
the actual Installation itself, and
WHEREAS, it is desirable for the encouragement of attendance at
such Installations, that musical and vocal selections be offered, and
speakers on Masonic subjects be presented, especially at open Installations, for the enlightenment of the general public regarding Masonry,
and
WHEREAS. it is most desirable that, when convenient, presentations of Masonic 50 Year Veteran Buttons be made at such Installation
meetings. in order that the public may witness such presentations, and
that the recipients' wives and friends be enabled to see them thus honored, and
WHEREAS, in the past, certain Lodges have been denied such
privileges by order of Grand Lodge Officers. and
WHEREAS, such actions tend to cause unhappiness among the
Fraternity. causing members of Constituent Lodges to feel that they are
being governed by executive decree, instead of by Masonic law, as set
forth in the California Masonic Code:
NOW, THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that the following
section be added to the California Masonic Code:
Section 474.1 Programs allowed at Installations. Any Constituent
Lodge of this Jurisdiction, when holding a meeting for the purpose of
installing newly elected or appointed officers. may also schedule, in
addition to said installation, musical and vocal selections, or present a
public speaker on any subject determined by said Lodge to be appropriate
for the occasion, or may present 50 Year Masonic Veteran Buttons to
any qualified recipients, or schedule any other type of program that they
deem in good taste and appropriate for the occasion, and that does not
coll'flict with any other provisions of the California Masonic Code.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM G. MOHN,
MILTON J. SEIDEL,

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
(24)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth are the principal
tents of our fraternity, and
WHEREAS, our present physical qualifications adopted of necessity for the protection of the Brethren when operative Masonry was in
force, and
WHEREAS, these qualifications have continued through the ages
solely to maintain uniformity in ritual, which has excluded many men
of good character from joining our ·ranks, and
WHEREAS. the ritual is one of the tools which is used to teach
candidates the above tenets, and any workman worth his keep will adapt
his tools to accomplish his purpose, and
WHEREAS. since we no longer work in operative Masonry. but
speculative only, the stringent physical requirements are contrary to the
fundamental principles of Masonry.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that section 511 of the California'Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
· "511. Moral and physical qualifications. An applicant for the
degrees of Masonry must be a man: no woman or eunuch: free
born, being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman: a believer in God and a future existence: of moral conduct: capable
of reading and writing: having no maim or defect in his body except the loss of limb or limbs or other impairment which can be
remedied with aid of a prosthesis, thereby rendering him capable
of learning the art, and physically able to conform substantially
to what the several degrees i'espectively require of him."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that section 512 be amended to
read as follows:
"512. Sound discretion required. The question as to the phys-

SHORTEN FORFEITURE PERIOD
(25)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. &A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, a dedicated Mason, having joined the Fraternity of
his own free will and accord, should desire to make steady and rapid
advancement through the Degrees, and
WHEREAS, failure to do so within a •r easonable period, without
extenuating circumstances, can only be regarded as lack of interest
toward Masonry in general, and his Lodge in particular, and
WHEREAS, two years can certainly be considered a reasonable
period for establishing proficiency to receive the 2nd and 3rd Degrees,
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that Section 546 of the California Masonic Code be revised to read as follows:
Section 546. FORFEITURE OF FEES: If a candidate does
not present himself properly qualified for the Second and Third
Degrees within a period of two years from the date of his initiation
as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall direct the Secretary to
forward to such candidate, by registered mail to his last known
address, a notice advising him that unless he shall present himself
for advancement on or before a specified date (at least sixty days in
advance) his fees for the unconferred degrees and all of his previous
contributions will be declared forfeited.
On the date specified, the Master shall declare the fees forfeited
unless further time shall have been granted by a vote of the Lodge.
A candidate thus denied advancement shall be considered only as
an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft with the right of applying
for the remaining Degree or Degrees, and paying the fees and con-

307

Respectfully submitted,
RALPH W. GAINES, P.M .• No. 226
RoY G. SCANNELL, P.M., No. 341
WARD W. GRUSH, M .• No. 226
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 25 proposes revision of Section 546 California
Masonic Code, which now provides that if a candidate does not present
himself properly qualified for the Second and Third Degrees within a
period of five years all fees and contributions shall be declared forfeited.
This resolution proposes reducing the five year period to two years
except where extenuating circumstances may exist.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that no particular good will redound either to the Fraternity or to such
Lodge or Lodges now affected by Section 546. It opens the door, moreover, to differences of opinion as to what may or may not be "extenuating
circumstances." Shortening the period will convey no significant financial
advantage to the Lodge and remedial physical or mental treatment that
might well be impossible in two years might result favorably in five years.
To bring the matter before the Grand Lodge for action, I move the
adoption of this reso)Jition. The Committee recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reports that in the opinion of the
Committee the legislation proposed is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents and is in proper form.
A majority voted against the resolution.

OPTIONAL THIRD DEGREE LECTURE
(26)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the third degree ceremony is so long and fatiguing on
the candidate that he is unable to fully absorb the lengthy lecture which
followsWHEREAS, many members are unwilling to sit through the lengthy
lecture and leave the lodge room before it starts WHEREAS. some jurisdictions allow it to be given at a future date
because of the reasons mentioned above WHEREAS. the third degree lecture differs from jurisdiction to
jurisdiction both as to content and as to length -

308

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

WHERE AS, what was practical in one period of history is not
necessar ily practical at a later date WHERE AS, many jurisdictions have and are making revisions,
additions, and deletions in our ceremonies (for fascinating developments
in this area see the Grand Lodge of Iowa's "Compa nion to the 1Moni~
tor") WHERE AS, poor attendan ce at degree meetings is a serious prob~
lem and the adoption of this resolution is one of the many things we
can do to help solve this problem WHERE AS, a shorter third degree lecture would be heartily wel~
comed by candidat es, brethren and visitors WHERE AS, the third degree is so meaningful. impressive and
inspiring that it can stand on its own merits without an unduly long
explanat ion thereafte r WHERE AS, a meaningful lecture of one half the present length
would command the candidat e's complete attention WHERE AS, about half the present third degree lecture could be
omitted with little or no loss, by saying in the proper place (and there is
a preceden t for this) ("21 words expunged by order of Grand Master" )
and by omitting the third section (pages 33 and 34 of the Monito r)THERE BY BE IT RESOL VED that an optional third degree
lecture of about half its present length, be prepared by the Grand Lodge
for lodge use.
Respectf ully submitted,
JOHN R. NoCAs, P.M., No. 537
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes , and on
Ritual.
The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual, to which Resolution No. 26 was referred,
proposin g that Grand Lodge provide a shortene d Third Degree Lecture,
"about half its present length," that is, one which would save perhaps
fifteen minutes in length, has carefully considered this proposal.
Since the brother proposing this resolution has carelessly introduced
into his resolution a change in the esoteric work, we ask the Grand
Master to direct the Grand Secretar y to expunge that portion of the
resolution from the written record of the proceedings.
What is proposed by this Tesolution is an innovation. The author
and every other member of this Grand Lodge, on his installation as
an officer of his lodge, solemnly acknowl edged that "it is not in the power
of any man or body of men to make innovations in the body of Masonry ."
Furtherm ore, it is prohibited by Section 555 of the Californ ia Masonic
Code which permits changes in the ritual "for the purpose of having it
remain as it was handed down from time immemorial," and by Section

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

309

554 which requires that "Each degree conferre d and all lectures must
be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and
recognized by the Grand Lodge."
The portions of the lecture which the author of this resolution wishes
to eliminate are not a mere recapitulation of the ceremonies but are
explanat ory and instrm:tive, reciting the history and explanation of the
legend of the Third Degree, which is listed in the Appendi x to the Code
as the third of our Ancient Landmar ks, supposed to be unchangeable.
This Grand Lodge and our Grand Masters for many years have
repeated ly urged more education for candidat es, and we have set up
Committees and Research Lodges for the purpose of spreadin g Masonic
educatio n and knowledge. The most importan t place to begin this educa~
tion is when the candidat e is receiving his degrees, when he is most
receptive. The opportun ity thus afforded for impressing him with the
meaning of his degree will never come again. The ceremony is once
in a lifetime for the candidat e and it should not be shortene d or rushed.
If the only criterion in conferring a degree is how quickly we can com~
plete it, have we not lost sight of our entire purpose? Your Committee
on Ritual has long believed that the length of a well~conf erred degree or
lecture should not he judged by time in minutes and seconds but rather
in the quality of the presenta tion. Is the saving of fifteen minutes in the
lifetime of a Mason ·really worth it? Furtherm ore, the burden of officers
having to learn an additiona l optional lecture more than offsets any
alleged benefit which can arise from the saving of a few minutes of time
during the degree.
As a proposed exception to Sections 554 and 555 of the Code,
adoption of the resolution would require a flve~sixths vote.
We move the adoption of the resolution hut strongly urge a "no"
vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has thoughtf ully
consider ed this resolution and •recommends a "no" vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

OPTIO NAL APRON LECTU RE
(27)
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHERE AS, the reception of his apron is a milestone in the life of a
Mason WHERE AS, the Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M., apron
lecture is far less expressive and meaningful than that used or permitte d
to be used in many other Grand Jurisdictions THERE BY BE IT RESOL VED that the following apron lecture
be optional, and allowed to be given by any brother, in this Jurisdiction.

310

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

(Note: this is the optional apron lecture of the Grand Lodge of Illinois,
A. F. & A. M., and used with variations by other Grand Lodges.)
"My brother, I now present you this lamb-skin or white leather apron.
It is an emblem of innocence and the badge of a Mason- the distinguished badge of a Mason.
It may be that in the coming years, upon your head may rest the
laurel wreaths of victory: from your breast may hang jewels fit to grace
the diadem of an eastern potentate : nay more than these, with light added
to the coming light, your ambitious feet may tread round after round of
the ladder that leads to fame in our mystic circle, and even the purple
of our Fraterni ty mary rest upon your honored shoulder s: but never again
from mortal hands, never again until your enfranch ised spirit shall have
passed upward and inward through the pearly gates. shall any honor so
distinguished, so emblematical of purity and perfection, be conferre d
upon you as this which I now bestow. It is yours to wear th·r oughout
an honorabl e life. and at your death to be placed upon the coffin which
shall contain your remains, and with them laid beneath the clods of the
valley.
Let its pure and spotless surface be to you an ever-pre sent reminder
of a "purity of life and rectitude of conduct, " a never-en ding argumen t
for nobler deeds, for higher thoughts , for greater achievements; and
when at last your weary feet shall have come to the end of life's toilsome
journey. and from your nerveless grasp shall drop forever the working
tools of life, may the record of your life and actions be as pure and spotless as this fair emblem which I placed in your hands tonight: and when
your trembling soul shall stand naked and alone before the great White
Throne, may it be your portion to hear from Him. who sitteth as the
Judge Supreme, the welcome words: "Well done, thou good and faithful
servant! Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."
Respectf ully submitted,
JoHN R. NocAs, P.M., No. 537
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes , and on
Ritual.

DEGREES - CHARTS, SLIDES, MUSIC
(30)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code, under Section No. 554,
Annotation v, prohibits the use of charts, slides and films in Degree
work in California Constituent Lodges, and
WHEREAS. it is commonly accepted among educators that visual
aids are a most effective tool for use in imparting information to the
human mind, and that there is a great deal of truth in the old saying,
"One picture is worth a thousand words," and
WHEREAS, for many years visual aids in the form of charts and
~lides were permitted for use in California Lodges, and were of great
interest and help to the candidates as well as to those Lodge members
who were present to witness the Degrees, and
WHEREAS, it is the sincere belief of many individual Masons that
the prohibition of such visual aids is one of the many reasons for the
apparent loss of interest in Masonry, and the non~attendance by Lodge
members in this Jurisdiction, and
WHEREAS, it is most desirable, and important, that Masonry
should ?ot handicap any sincere workers in the craft by failing to provide
them with the necessary tools with which to pursue their labors:
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that in the California
Masonic Code, Section No. 554, Annotation v be deleted in its entirety,
and that it be replaced with the following wording:
v-A Lodge may use musical and/or vocal selections, during or
after the conferring of a Degree, such as singing "Nearer My God
to Thee" or "The Holy City," and may also illustrate the lectures by
the use of charts or slides, if such procedure be authorized by a
majority vote of the Lodge members present when the matter is put
to a vote. A Lodge may not, however, authorize those in charge of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

313

conferring a Degree to wear any costumes, other than normal Ma~
sonic attire, during the conferring of a Degree.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM A. BRADY,
WILLIAM G. MOHN,
P.M., No. 599
P.M .• No. 599
MILTON J. SEIDEL,
ALFRED L. GERRIE, JR.,
P.M.. No. 599
M., No. 599
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes, and on Ritual.
The Committee on Ritual to which was Teferred Resolution No. 30
proposing the addition to the Code of a new section which would permit
a Lodge to use musical selections during or after the conferring of a
degree, and may also illustrate the Lectures by use of charts and slides,
has carefully considered the Resolution and wish to report as follows:
The Proponents of this Resolution state that for many years visual
aids in the form of charts and slides were permitted for use in California
Lodges. This statement is incorrect: charts were at one time used, but
the use of slides has never been permitted. Further, the charts were
prohibited biy Former Grand Lecturers if they depicted esoteric matters,
which they practically all did. It is incongruous to our Masonic Obliga~
tions that any of the secrets of Freemasonry could ever be reproduced on
charts, slides, or any other manner of visual conveyance.
Ancient Landmark twenty third is, "The Secrecy of the Institution."
In 1908 this Grand Lodge adopted a clear declaration as to the secrecy
of its Ritualistic work which is still binding upon us. That declaration
included the following points:
1. Freemasonry has as essentials, certain secrets of Ritual which it
forever conceals and never reveals to any person in the world except its
own members.
2. These Ancient mysteries are communicated from the instructive
tongue to the attentive ear and are safely lodged in the Faithful Breast:
And any other mode of communication in Ancient Craft Masonry is
most positiveliy forbidden in solemn form and manner.
3. So likewise is forbidden the writing, printing or marking in any
manner whereby the same becomes legible or intelligible to any person,
lest these secrets might become known to the profane.
4. No individual Mason is exempt from the obligation of profound
secrecy, and no human power can authorize him to write, print or mark
Masonic secrets in any manner whatsoever.
5. The Secrets are Ancient Landmarks of P.reemasonry, and no body
of men inside or outside of Lodge or Grand Lodge, has power to make
innovations in Ancient Craft Masonry.

315

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is no excuse or justification for any, that men are eager to break
these laws, or that men have broken them before, or that in other degrees
or orders of American Masonry, cipher Rituals may be in common use.
Our duty and obligation as Ancient Craft Masons compel our obedience
to these ancient regulations.
This same policy was followed in 1938, when the Grand Lodge
ruled that, "Any slide, map, chart or picture of any nature, showing in
part or in whole the secret work of the three degrees of Masonry, is con~
trary- to the laws of the Fraternity, and is a violation of the obligations
of the Order, and no Lodge in this Jurisdiction shall use such equipment
in any way, nor shall it, or any 1Mason be in possession thereof." That
ruling has never been repealed, nor is it sought to be repealed by this
Resolution.
The enforcement of this Ruling brought forth a Resolution in 1957,
and the appointmen t of a Special Committee, headed by an outstanding
Public School Educator, a former Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge.
The Committee was expressly charged by the Grand Master, that the
question of Visual Aids be thoroughly explored and a report presented
to the forthcoming Communication "which will dispose of the question
once and for all." Questionnai res which were sent to every Lodge in
California, as well as 48 other Grand Lodges in the United States, re~
vealed that a majority of the Lodges did not think that Visual Aids
would enhance the effectiveness of the Degrees. An overwhelming
majority believed that present practices were adequate and should be
retained without modification except as the Ritual Committee approved.
The Committee concluded that the Masonic Law of California, based
upon an Ancient Landmark, prohibited the use of any chart, slide or
picture showing in any part or in whole the secret work of the degrees.
They ,recommended no change in the presentation and Lectures of the
three degrees as now constituted, and added that "the uniform high
quality of California work is a tribute to present procedures. " They
concluded that ph'Ysical representati ons should not be a part of any
Ritual, but that they might add to the "Degree environmen t." They
suggested that Masonic education programs might be built around visual
expressions of the three degrees, but that they should not be a part of
our Ritual, and should only be designed to supplement the degrees.
They further recommended that if their recommendations were ac~
cepted, a program should be developed, consistent with California
standards, supported by written or audio commentary: that their use
should be optional and subject to conditions to be outlined by the
Committee.
The foregoing report was adopted by the Grand Lodge in October,
1959, and we think, as did the Grand Master at that time, that it should
"dispose of the question once and for all."

Your Committee on Ritual therefore moves the adoption of the
resolution but recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes thoughtfully con~
sidered the resolution and recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reports that in the opinion of the
Committee the legislation proposed is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents and is in proper form.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PAID UP MEMBER SHIP-- 50 YEAR MEMBERS
(31)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS , The Grand Lodges of several Masonic jurisdictions
other than California honor their veteran members by remitting their
dues in advance, and
WHEREA S, it is becoming increasingly difficult for older members
to maintain paid up status in the face of inflation, and
WHEREA S, The Grand Lodge of California does not relieve its
veterans of the requirement that they pay dues.
NOW THEREFO RE BE IT RESOLVE D that the Grand Lodge
of California adopt the policy of issuing its 50 year members a paid up
membership.
Respectfully submitted,
ALBERT H1TcHEN, P.M., No. 209

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes, and on Finance.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 31 would adopt the policy of having the Grand Lodge
automatically issue a paid up membership to all fifty year Masons.
Under our present Code, Lodges may now remit dues for members
of over 75 years of age or forty years membership. A Lodge may re~it
dues for any member when the paying of dues would create a hardship.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that many
fifty year members have the means of paying dues and are proud
our
of
to contribute toward the support of their Lodges and Grand Lodge. This
resolution would reduce the income of the Lodges and increase the pro~
portion of Lodge funds required for per capita tax.
Since the means of remission is now available where it is needed or
desired, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels that this
resolution should not be adopted.

603. Boards of Relief. Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction or located in areas near the concurrent jurisdiction of such Lodges may form

319

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

During the past two years this Board of Control has studied the problems of the Boards of Relief.
They are many, varied and further complicated by the wide divergence of opinion of the persons connected with them.
Last year a special committee appointed by the Grand ·Master recommended that the Boards of Relief be discontinued as a June 30, 1970.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, however, believed
that some of the function of the Boards of Relief, particularly the operation of blood banks, to be vital to Masonry. Even though by the strict letter of the law they were not legally the responsibility of the Boards of Relief, they should be continued until an alternate method could be found
for handling these functions.
In this, the Board of Control concurred although in our report we
stated that we believed that the Boards of Relief, in the concept in which
they were originally formed had outlived their usefulness.
We believe that our Board has delved further into the problems of
the Boards of Relief system than any other board or committee and yet
we have no ready solution to the problem.
We are aware of an intense campaign by individuals who reportedly
are in favor of not only retaining the Boards of Relief but of expanding
their duties. We believe these people have a right to be heard. How
much weight is to be given this small but vociferous minority is for Grand
Lodge to decide. We do not know the contents or the authors of these
letters as this information has not been turned over to us.
However, numerous persons have expressed opinions to us regarding
our statement that the Boards of Relief have outlived their usefulness.
Some have agreed. A few have recommended not only the continuance,
but the expansion of their duties.
We have been impressed by one significant fact-not one Mason has
expressed to us this latter opinion who was not on the payroll of the
Boards of Relief system or in a position to be strongly influenced by it!
We believe that the Brothers who presented Resolutions 32 and 33
are sincere in trying to solve the deep set and long standing problems of
the Boards of Relief. However the problems are too complex to be
solved by either or a combination of these. At least another year of intense study will be required before a practical approach to legislation can
be made correcting this problem.
This study should include, but not be limited to, a tabulated questionnaire, worded so as to elicit basic information, circulated to every
active Mason in the Jurisdiction. It should also give heavy weight to a
searching questionnaire to the entire lnspectorial Corps who are probably closer to individual problems of the Craft than any other single
group, as well as being the best informed.
In order that this Grand Lodge may have the opportunity to study

this problem in depth, your Board of Control recommends a "no" vote
on both Resolutions 32 and 33.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 32 delineates the proper duties and responsibilities of
Boards of Relief based upon the careful and thorough study of the Special Committee on Boards of Relief.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes the proposal of the Special Study Committee retains all the vital and timetested services of Boards of Relief and provides a very satisfactory arrangement for their organization and governance. We believe the present day functions assigned to the Boards of Relief require they be more
correctly designated as Masonic Service Bureaus.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 32 with the proviso
that where the words "Board of Relief" appear there be substituted
"Masonic Service Bureau" and that all necessary changes be made in
our law to accomplish the change of name. The Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote on the revised resolution.
The Comittee on furisprudence reports that the proposed legislation
is sufficient but suggests the following amendments in order to further
clarify the activities of the Boards of Relief:
Delete the words "and such other proper Masonic activities as may
be requested by the Lodges belonging to the Board of Relief, all under
the supervision of the Board of Control" appearing on lines 23, 24 and
25 and substitute the following: "and such proper Masonic activities as
may be authorized by the Board of Control as provided in Section 263
of the Califoronia Masonic Code subject to appeal to and review by the
Grand Master or Grand Lodge."
Delete the words "report annually to the Grand Lodge" on line 26
and substitute "report annually to the Board of Control."
With these amendments the Committee recommends adoption of
the resolution.
(NOTE: By separate action Grand Lodge agreed to consider
Resolution No. 32 with the substitution of "Masonic Service

Committee on Policy and General Purposes. The proponents of

Control shall have the power to promulgate basic rules and regulations
governing the operation of Masonic Service Bureaus, with the approval
of the Most Worshipful Grand Master and of the Grand Lodge of
California.
The rules and regulations promulgated by the Board of Control for
the operation of area Masonic Service Bureaus should take into consideration the individual requirements of each Bureau to enable it to best
serve the interests of Masonry in such area.
Area Masonic Service Bureaus should be centers of Masonic service
and information to all Masons residing within its territorial jurisdiction,
without in aniy way usurping or performing any of the rightful duties
and responsibilities of the Worshipful Masters of Masonic Lodges
within such areas.

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and
General Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered and
agreed unanimously that, with one exception, the statements made and
the recommendation for amendment of Section 685, annotation ( d),
fairly and accurately represent a widespread opinion and endorsement
among the membership of the Fraternity in this Grand Jurisdiction.
The Committee does not concur in the representation that "the game
(Bingo) has no public connotation of gambling" because where Bingo
and its associated titles are concerned the public is not, and cannot
be, "fully aware of the non~commercial nature of the event." On the
contrary, even where such an event is held in a church, we are justified
in suspecting that the game is "Bingo" for which cash has been received,
that it is a "game of chance" and that it is contrary to the law of the
State of California.
It was because of this connotation of a fund~raising or ·gambling de~
vice that Annotation ( d) of Section 685 was approved by the Grand
Lodge in 1955. Even where prizes are donated or pt"ocured from Lodge

324

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

refreshment funds and no charge is made to the participants, the connotation of gambling still remains. The game of Bingo or Lotto or a similar
game under any other combination of five letters in title is a "game of
chance" and its usage for any purpose would create in the public mind
a connotation of gambling.
To bring the matter before the Grand Lodge for action, I move the
adoption of this resolution. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "no" vote.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.. F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with the requirement of our Code, Certified Public
Accountant s have made their annual audit of the records of Grand
Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California. the California Masonic Memor~al Temple and the California Masonic Foundation for the fiscal year
ending June 30, 1970. Copies of these audit reports have been reviewed
by this Committee and we invite your inspection in the published reports
and proceedings.
It requires some time for a public accounting group to become familiar
with our transactions and the requirements of our Fraternity. Until they
do become conversant with our practices, they are of little help in the
important area of guidance so necessary to improve our procedures and
accounting for the activities of Grand Lodge and its entities. Our records for the past three fiscal years have been examined by three different firms of accoutttants. We believe that the complex nature of our
operations warrants more continuity in our yearly audit program.
For theflscal year ended last June 30 Grand Lodge expenditures were
well within the budget adopted at last year's Communication. This
budget totaled $530,650 while actual expenditure s came to $485,047.
There were the usual instances where budgeted amounts were more than
the actual amount needed. Conversely, where certain programs exceeded
the original estimates, or no budgets were provided, we requested the
Grand Master's approval of supplemental appropriatio ns totaling
$23,065. We recommend your approval of his action.
Our total expenditure of $485,000 represented a new high in Grand
Lodge history. A substantial portion of the increase over the previous
year was due to the impact of the policy of providing for payment of
travel and lodging for the Grand Lodge line and for Committee and
Board members. Printing costs increased by $12,000, salaries and related costs by $6,000, Veteran Buttons by $3,000 and Postage, Telephone and Audih:osts by $7,000.
The per capita tax of $1.85 for Grand Lodge use, approved at our
1968 Communication, provided the bulk of our income in the 'Year ended
last June 30. This, together with some increased return on our invest-

become a Grand Lodge expense and therefore included in the per capita
tax. Prior to that time, these items of expense had been borne by the
Homes through reimbursement to Grand Lodge. Your Committee on
Finance is definitely of the opinion that such expenses should not be an

Homes as such expenditures are productive of contributions by Masons
to the Endowment Board which produces income to cover the expense
of operation of our homes. We accordingly recommend that the action
taken at our 1968 Communication be reconsidered by the Grand Master
in due course.
CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION

We have provided $15,000 in the budget as a result of request from
the Foundation for funds pending sale of the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse. We
have been assured that the California Masonic Foundation will be truly
self~sustaining following the completion of the sale.
Your Committee on Finance did not review the Foundation's operat~
ing budget for the 1970~71 fiscal year.
Such matters in the Grand Master's Message and in the several
resolutions and reports which have been approved by this Grand Lodge
and now require funds have been provided for in the following proposed
budget.
